title: StateBench: Testing how language models track state changes over long documents
abstract: Back to Articles StateBench: Testing how language models track state changes over long documents Enterprise Article Published November 3, 2026 Upvote 5 Kyle Wiggers Ai2Comms Follow allenai 📄 Tech Report | 🤗 Data | 💻 Code We’re introducing StateBench , a benchmark for long-context state tracking —how well language models keep track of information about entities in long documents as they evolve. State tracking underlies tasks from reading code, where variables are assigned and reassigned, to following a story as characters physically move around and objects change hands. For example, if a mystery novel states that “John gave Mary the knife” right before a murder occurs, it’s important to know that the state of each character has changed. However, not all state-tracking problems are created equal: some require only finding the latest update; harder ones require following a chain of changes, where one missed step can throw off the final answer. For example, a harder variant of our mystery state tracking would be if John gave Mary the item in his backpack, with it previously known that Edward put a knife in John’s backpack. Transformers have well-documented theoretical limits on hard variants of state tracking with long dependency chains, helping motivate recurrent and hybrid architectures such as Gated DeltaNet that carry a running memory forward. Existing state-tracking tests tend to focus on the hardest cases, but as these designs become more common, researchers need to know which kinds of state tracking each architecture can handle. We would like to understand the differences between architectures not just on the hardest kinds of state tracking, but also on the simpler, potentially more common kinds. To this end, we developed the StateBench benchmark to capture state-tracking problems of different complexity, which we used to evaluate the differences between language models with different architectures. We find that recurrent and hybrid models can generalize much farther than transformers when trained directly on these tasks, while frontier models including Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Sol and Luna still break down on harder forms of state tracking as inputs grow longer. Four levels of state tracking StateBench consists of four difficulty levels that permit increasingly complex state update operations. For programmers, these levels of state tracking complexity can be understood as allowing different types of variable assignment operations: R-trivial problems use immutable assignment. A variable’s value never changes, so the model only needs to recover what it was first set to. In code, this looks like let x = 4; in everyday life, it’s like a birth date—it stays fixed. Aperiodic problems allow reassignment by value. The model needs to find the most recent value and can ignore earlier ones. In code, this looks like x = 4 followed later by x = 2; in everyday life, it’s like a thermostat, where the latest setting determines the current temperature. Soluble problems add self-referential updates. Each update builds on the current value, so the model has to carry changes forward rather than simply find the latest assignment. In code, this looks like x = x + 5; in everyday life, it’s like a game score, where each point adds to the running total. General finite problems add assignment by reference. One variable can take on another variable’s current value, creating dependencies across updates. In code, this looks like x = y or swapping two variables. Imagine a magician hiding a ball under one of five cups, then repeatedly swapping their positions. Finding the ball means keeping track of how those swaps change its location. This illustrates the S₅ state-tracking problem: following how successive swaps rearrange five objects. It belongs to the hardest of our four levels and is discussed in previous work on the limits of state tracking . These levels can be intuitively understood in terms of variable assignments, but they also represent theoretically motivated distinctions in state tracking rooted in Krohn–Rhodes theory, a branch of algebra that describes how state-tracking problems – which can be viewed as word problems over finite monoids – can be decomposed into atomic primitives. Each level in our hierarchy corresponds to a class of state-tracking problems that can be built out of a different set of primitives. To compare the four levels fairly, we start with a general finite sequence of variable assignments and derive three easier versions from it, producing four comparable StateBench problems—one at each difficulty level. All four use the same number of variables and distinct values, with assignments appearing at the same points in the sequence; only the type of assignment changes. What we found Pretrained models We tested a range of open pretrained models on the r-trivial, aperiodic, and general finite levels of StateBench to see where their state tracking breaks down, and whether different architectures fail where theory predicts. Under standard theoretical assumptions, transformers can handle r-trivial robustly (and soluble and aperiodic to some degree) but are predicted to fail on general problems. In contrast, Gated DeltaNet with a more flexible memory update can, in principle, handle all four levels. We started with open pretrained models, where the training data and context lengths are fully documented. These included two 7-billion-parameter models, Olmo 3 (a transformer) and Olmo Hybrid (which adds Gated DeltaNet layers), along with smaller models with 275 million and 2.7 billion parameters. All of these models were pretrained on the same data; none had seen contexts longer than 64,000 tokens during training, and we tested most of them on inputs well beyond that length. When we scored each model, almost all performed well on r-trivial problems, lost accuracy on aperiodic ones as inputs grew, and stayed at chance on general finite problems. Problem format mattered here—the 275-million-parameter hybrid and Gated DeltaNet models scored near the ceiling on RULER-style r-trivial problems but were near chance on the same problems framed as spreadsheet edits. That gap is one reason StateBench tests the same underlying problem in several formats. Frontier models We then tested four frontier models – Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 Sol and Luna – asking them to read each sequence of variable assignments and generate the final value of every variable. All four performed well on r-trivial and aperiodic problems. But on soluble and general finite problems, accuracy fell sharply as inputs grew longer, dropping to 13% or lower on the longest general finite problems. One likely factor is sensitivity ; at these harder levels, many more steps can affect the final answer, leaving less room for a model to miss an update without getting the result wrong. Models trained directly on the task Next, we investigated whether models’ difficulty with the harder levels reflects limits of the architectures themselves, or whether pretraining simply doesn’t teach models to solve them. Targeted direct training is a more favorable setting that reveals to what degree state-tracking issues come from the underlying architecture and optimizer rather than the data used to pretrain a model. We trained several 275-million-parameter models from scratch on StateBench: two transformer variants, two hybrids, and two Gated DeltaNet variants with different memory-update constraints. The models trained on sequences of up to 256 assignments and were tested on sequences as long as 64,000 assignments, or 250 times the maximum training length. The architectures began to diverge as sequences grew longer. Gated DeltaNet and hybrid models generalized almost perfectly on r-trivial, aperiodic, and soluble problems out to the longest sequences we tested, tens of thousands of assignments.

title: Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language
abstract:
Back to Articles Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language Enterprise Article Published November 3, 2026 Upvote 3 Praveen Venkateswaran praveenv Follow ibm-research Anupama Murthi anupamamurthi Follow ibm-research Hamid Adebayo harmedox Follow ibm-research Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all. Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other. Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language , and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it. Why decks are hard for small models A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at. It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from. It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent. There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them. Build it like a human: a designer and a coder Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter: The designer reads the plan and writes a structured JSON brief: the palette, the type system, and for each slide its layout, its exact content and a short design rationale. The coder takes one slide's spec from the brief and writes the pptxgenjs JavaScript that draws it, preceded by its reasoning. Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster. We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×. Synthesizing decks and their reasoning There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides. Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example: "Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance." The coder reasons about geometry: "The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart." The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example. The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest. What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions. Steering a deck in plain English Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives , short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]] : ## Rollout plan
- March: pilot with two teams
- May: security review complete
- July: rollout to all of engineering
- September: company-wide launch
- November: first adoption review
[[make this a timeline]] The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead. The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase. Category Example directive Layout [[make this a timeline]] Tone [[be candid, no spin]] Audience [[this is for the board]] Order [[lead with the ask]] Leaving out [[no pricing]] Emphasis [[highlight the headline number]] Figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive. Building a check-and-repair harness Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first. Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned. First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black.

title: CWE-bench v2: More coverage, quality, and transparency
abstract: Back to Articles CWE-bench v2: More coverage, quality, and transparency Published November 3, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 5 Gonzalo Gonzalez chalo2000 Follow collinear-ai Ajay Jagannath ajayjagan2511 Follow collinear-ai Nazneen Rajani nazneen Follow collinear-ai Nathan Habib SaylorTwift Follow CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI , CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set , so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai . Our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough. As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true: Does the instruction read like a realistic instruction and not an evaluation setting? Can every graded behaviour be inferred from the instruction? Does the verifier check for correct behaviour and not for specific structure of one fix? Does the starter code fail and the reference fix pass? Does the original functionality still work with the new fix? Do the verifiers fail memorized solutions like the known upstream patch? Every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set. Results Results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file ( how ). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space , where new models are added through a PR on the Space. Open-weight models, from the dataset page: All evaluated models, including API-only ones: Of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands. On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92. Run it from the Hub Every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json . Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself: harbor run --repo "https://huggingface.co/datasets/collinear-ai/cwe-bench" -d cwe-bench@2.0 -k 4 \ --agent <agent> --model <model> -- env docker \ --allow-agent-host <model API host> -k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once: hf auth login --token $HF_TOKEN --add-to-git-credential The tasks are also tagged rl-environment : the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.

title: Transformers Model Integration Contracts
abstract:
Back to Articles Transformers Model Integration Contracts Published November 3, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 12 +6 Tarek Ziadé tarekziade Follow On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention
(SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens.
During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict.
Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months. When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged
it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built
around it. Why bugs reach main Transformers supports over 750
model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus
200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also
test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention
kernels. The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on
real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs
busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a
regression, it may already be in main. Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture : a small
model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower
layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files
unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests"
against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study ,
the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint
is 1,227 MB. This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU
runners, but their fixtures run on CPU. Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and
checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5
bug would have passed a forward pass just fine. Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a
chance to catch bugs before they reach main. Introducing Model Integration Contracts transformers-mic is a proposed
standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has
three parts: a fixture : the shrunk model described above, published once and pinned a usage path : a runnable Markdown example of something people do with the
model, such as generating text or running a training step baselines : the outputs recorded when running that example, reviewed by a
human The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the
baselines. A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint:
compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected
results. We publish them in huggingface-mic . For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital
of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading
the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt: inputs = tokenizer( "The capital of France is" , return_tensors= "pt" )
outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 4 , do_sample= False )
new_tokens = outputs[:, inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ]:] print (tokenizer.batch_decode(new_tokens, skip_special_tokens= True )) It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies
that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md . A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions
used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it
used, so we can reproduce it later. On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes. The UMT5 regression We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small
UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28 .
Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training
loss by about 0.20. One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path.
Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only
helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint. We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check
failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step
took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup. The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details. How models are shrunk The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer
layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no
use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear. The recipe now has four steps: Shrink the configuration. Start from a real checkpoint and reduce
hidden sizes, attention heads and depth. Keep the different layer kinds,
including mixtures of sliding and full attention or dense and MoE layers.
Some architectures need extra rules to keep their components compatible.
We also look at the model's own Transformers tests: the ModelTester in test_modeling_<model>.py already picks a small config by hand, so we
take its sizes for any width our generic rule doesn't know by name. Keep preprocessing unchanged. Preserve vocabulary, special tokens and
input dimensions, and copy tokenizer and processor files byte for byte.
Loading and preprocessing are part of what we want to test. Build and validate the weights. Try seeded random weights and change
the inputs to check that the model responds. If it doesn't, try training
it on the contract's small batch of examples. Reload the saved model and
check that outputs, loss and gradients are finite. Reject failed builds. Freeze and record. Save the accepted weights and measure repeatable
outputs on a known-good Transformers build. Review the baselines for each
supported platform and precision, then publish a pinned snapshot. CI reuses
it; it does not rebuild the fixture for every PR. We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the
conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail. The Llama 4 Scout shrink report shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7
million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from
48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style. Building MICs with agents Our CLI, tmic , creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new
model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure
the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed
expectations require human review. To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model : pip install "transformers-mic[runtime]" "hf-doc-builder @ git+https://github.com/huggingface/doc-builder.git" hf auth login
tmic run org/model --local-only --fixtures-only --no-history --bill-to '' It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your
machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything.
For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed
to your own account ( --bill-to '' ). The CLI docs cover the individual steps. We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge
case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from
model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space . Random vs Overfit With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in
the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path. So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green".
We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible
in its outputs.

title: NVIDIA Shows 3 Ways to Speed Up MoE Inference on DGX Spark, Lifting Ling-3.0-flash Throughput 42.5%
abstract: NVIDIA’s latest technical blog shows how to speed up mixture-of-experts (MoE) inference on one DGX Spark . The test model is Ant Group inclusionAI’s Ling-3.0-flash , a 124B-parameter MoE with 5.1B active parameters. NVIDIA stacked three optimizations: a new MoE kernel backend, an FP8 output layer and built-in speculative decoding. On all 1,319 GSM8K questions, decode throughput rose 42.5% with no statistically detectable accuracy change. So why is it relevant for Devs? DGX Spark is a desktop system, not a data center node. NVIDIA’s results show a 124B MoE serving single-user requests faster on that desk-side box. The technical post also shows where MoE decode time goes, and how to cut it. DGX Spark is NVIDIA’s desktop system built on the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip. It offers 128 GB of unified memory and 273 GB/s of memory bandwidth. Peak compute is up to 1 petaFLOP of sparse FP4. NVIDIA rates it for inference on models up to 200B parameters. In the NVIDIA technical post , the NVIDIA team profiled Ling-3.0-flash-fp4 at batch size 1. Decoding was memory-bound: reading model weights drove execution time. Two operations stood out, the MoE computation and the LM head that scores the vocabulary. That points to two levers: move fewer bytes per decode step, and generate more tokens per verification round. The baseline followed the official W4A8 recipe. It used FlashInfer MXFP4 MoE kernels, CUTLASS dense GEMM and an FP32 LM-head path. On a synthetic 32K-input, 2K-output test, it ran at 27.71 ms per token (36.09 tokens per second). 1. Humming MXFP4 MoE kernels: NVIDIA swapped FlashInfer’s MoE backend for Humming , an independent kernel library. Humming uses NVRTC to compile kernels at runtime for the actual matrix shapes, data types and GPU. That includes the narrow 768-wide expert layer. Each kernel compiles in seconds. The FlashInfer CUTLASS path compiles 97 targets with ninja, on the order of tens of minutes. Throughput rose 9.3% to 39.45 tokens per second. 2. Online FP8 LM head: The LM head is a 157,184 x 2,560 matrix stored in BF16. Every generated token reads all of it. Quantizing only this layer to FP8 at load time halves those reads. Setting SGLANG_ENABLE_FP8_LM_HEAD=1 enables it. It cannot be combined with the baseline –enable-fp32-lm-head option. Combined with Humming, throughput reached 43.94 tokens per second. That is 21.7% over baseline and 11.4% over Humming alone. 3. MTP speculative decoding with NEXTN: Ling-3.0-flash ships with a built-in NEXTN prediction layer, so no extra draft model is needed. It drafts three tokens, and the model verifies four positions at once. Verification costs about 2.26x a normal decode step. The main cost is MoE, not attention. Verifying four tokens can activate up to 32 experts instead of 8. On the synthetic test, an average of 3.90 tokens were accepted per round. Throughput jumped to 102.88 tokens per second, up 185.1%. The three techniques do not overlap. Humming and the FP8 LM head cut the cost of each step. MTP cuts the number of steps. The integration trap: Stacking these is not automatic. With FP8 LM head and MTP both on, the draft must share the full LM-head module. Otherwise the framework silently falls back, and the draft interprets FP8 weights as BF16. Accept length drops to 1.00, and throughput falls below the unoptimized baseline. The NVIDIA team advises checking at startup that each optimization is active. NVIDIA points to the Ling cookbook notebook for enabling both together. Synthetic tests flatter speculative decoding, so the NVIDIA team also ran all 1,319 GSM8K questions. It used 5-shot prompting with chain-of-thought, temperature 0.6, top_p 0.95 and top_k 29. With all three optimizations, time per output token fell from 26.45 ms to 18.56 ms. Decode throughput rose 42.5%, from 37.81 to 53.89 tokens per second. Mean latency dropped 24.5%, from 15.21 to 11.49 seconds. Accuracy moved from 96.89% to 96.82%, a change NVIDIA calls statistically undetectable. Accept length here was 2.68, versus 3.90 on synthetic data. The NVIDIA team gives three reasons for the gap. Synthetic outputs are more repetitive, so drafts are accepted more often. The synthetic test used greedy decoding, while GSM8K used sampling. GSM8K answers are also short, with a median near 310 tokens versus a fixed 2K. Ling-3.0-flash belongs to Ant Group inclusionAI’s Ling 3.0 family , released under the MIT license. The open-weight lineup also includes Ling-3.0-tiny , a 7.9B MoE with 1.3B active parameters. Both come with base checkpoints and FP8, INT4 and GGUF builds; flash also has FP4. OpenRouter also lists inclusionAI’s vision-language, finance and health variants built on Ling 3.0 Flash. Ling-3.0-flash is built to keep per-token cost low: On its model card , inclusionAI reports 56.6 on SWE-Bench Pro and 72.4 on SWE-Bench Multilingual. It also reports 93.2 on MathArena AIME 2026 and 87.0 on HMMT Feb 2026. Artificial Analysis results shown on OpenRouter list 85.5% on GPQA Diamond and 55.4% on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The hardest reasoning tests remain tough: Humanity’s Last Exam scores 22.7 self-reported and 23.7% independently. API pricing: Artificial Analysis lists InclusionAI’s API at $0.075 per 1M input tokens and $0.22 per 1M output tokens. That blends to about $0.05 per 1M tokens, using its 7:2:1 cache-hit, input and output mix. It measured output speed at 231.7 tokens per second, third of 26 models in its class. On OpenRouter , Novita and DeepInfra list $0.06 input and $0.18 output. Against peers: Artificial Analysis lists higher blended prices for comparable models. Step 3.7 Flash is $0.18, Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite $0.33 and GPT-5 (medium) $1.34. These figures compare price only; they are not quality-adjusted. Quantization costs little quality: inclusionAI’s quantization table compares BF16, FP8, INT4 and FP4. FP4 scores 83.68 on GPQA-diamond versus 84.97 in BF16. IFBench moves from 74.49 to 73.87, and ArcPrize from 68.75 to 68.06. SciCode shows the largest drop, from 41.24 to 38.43. The FP4 checkpoint is the one NVIDIA ran on DGX Spark. NVIDIA’s full analysis is on the NVIDIA Technical Blog . Model weights and recipes are on Hugging Face , the SGLang cookbook and the Ling cookbook . The post NVIDIA Shows 3 Ways to Speed Up MoE Inference on DGX Spark, Lifting Ling-3.0-flash Throughput 42.5% appeared first on MarkTechPost .

title: Soniox STT v6 Adds Agent Text Input and Echo Filtering for Voice Agents
abstract: Soniox has released Soniox STT v6 , the latest generation of its speech-to-text API. Soniox STT v6 is a speech-to-text model that reads what a voice agent says while hearing the caller. It uses that text to recognize short replies and to drop the agent’s own voice. The release ships as stt-rt-v6 for streaming and stt-async-v6 for files , across 60+ languages. In a cascaded voice agent, STT usually hears only the caller. It never sees the question being answered. Short answers suffer most. In Soniox’s docs , “River Roast” becomes “River Road” and “a tow” becomes “a tour.” The second problem is echo. Agent audio leaks back through speakerphones and laptops, gets transcribed as user speech, and the agent interrupts itself. You enable it with one flag in the start request: "enable_agent_text_input": true . It is only available on stt-rt-v6 , not the async model. While the agent speaks, you stream its words on the same WebSocket as the caller’s audio. Each message is a small JSON frame: {"type": "agent_text", "text": "...", "end_of_segment": true} . Timing matters. Messages carry no timestamps, so the model places text where it arrives in the audio stream. Soniox recommends sending each piece 500 ms to 1 second before playback, paced by TTS timestamps. On barge-in, you flush what was already played, send end_of_segment: true , and drop the unplayed rest. The agent’s text never appears in the returned transcript. With agent text input on, v6 knows what the agent is saying. It uses that to separate leftover agent audio from caller speech and filter it out. It keeps listening during playback, so callers can still interrupt. It does not replace acoustic echo cancellation. It handles what your existing AEC leaves behind , so keep AEC on. There is one formatting change to test before upgrading. v6 writes “15 dollars and 20 cents” as spoken, not “$15.20”. Hyphens in codes appear only when spoken. Soniox has not published v6 accuracy or latency numbers. Its benchmarks page still reports v5 on the open-source Pipecat STT benchmark . It uses 1,000 real-world samples and measures semantic WER plus time to final segment (TTFS). On it, stt-rt-v5 scores 1.34% semantic WER, 83.3% perfect transcripts and 260 ms median TTFS. Its P95 latency is 305 ms. Azure posts the lowest WER mean at 1.21%, but at 1,016 ms median latency. Pipecat figures from the Pipecat STT benchmark README . Soniox numbers are for v5, since v6 has not been benchmarked yet. Soniox calls v6 the first model that knows what your voice agent is saying. That claim needs a qualifier. AssemblyAI shipped agent context in Universal-3.5 Pro Realtime in July 2026. It also feeds the agent’s replies into streaming STT. The clearer difference is echo. Soniox’s docs describe filtering leaked agent audio using that text. AssemblyAI’s context docs describe no such filtering. v6 is a drop-in swap: change the model name to stt-rt-v6 or stt-async-v6 . The v5 models are deprecated and will be removed on December 15, 2026 . After that, v5 requests route to v6 automatically. Pricing is token-based. Soniox lists about $0.12/hour streaming and $0.10/hour async . Agent text is billed as input text tokens, at $4.00 per 1M on real-time. Check out the Soniox STT v6 announcement , the agent text input docs and the v6 changelog . title: OpenAI Introduces Pando: A Git Backend That Cuts Median Push Latency ~80%
abstract: OpenAI has introduced Pando , a new Git backend that now serves all development in its monorepo. The OpenAI Pando Git backend keeps the standard Git client and protocol. Engineers and Codex agents still run git push and git fetch as before. Only the server changed. OpenAI team reports median push latency fell nearly 80%. Pando now delivers nearly a petabyte of Git data per day. Pando is a Git-compatible server backend from OpenAI that scales concurrent pushes and fetches for a monorepo. It was written in Rust and reached production in 10 weeks. One engineer designed the core and teams of Codex agents implemented it. It has served production traffic since April 2026. Codex multiplied parallel work. OpenAI’s commit chart shows commits landed on master up 1,378% in Q3 2026 versus Q1 2024. Its Q4 2026 estimate is +2,442%. Each push now triggers many CI fetches. By late 2025, fetches and pushes slowed, merges failed, and reliability at times fell below 90%. OpenAI concluded the bottleneck was how it served Git, not Git itself. Pando drops 2 assumptions that most Git servers treat as requirements: 1. Repository-wide consistency : Conventional servers order every ref update repo-wide, so unrelated pushes wait. Pando uses causal consistency instead. Each branch is serialized on its own, and clients only conflict when pushing the same ref. The tradeoff: a reader viewing several branches may see them at different points in time. 2. A unique packfile per client : Standard servers build a fresh pack per fetch. Pando stores each pushed pack as an immutable blob. A “ref version” goes into a scalable metadata store. A push needs O(1) metadata reads and writes. A fetch needs O(log Δ) reads, where Δ is the ref-version gap to close. With millions of branches, a full ref advertisement can exceed 100 MiB. Pando advertises only the trunk branch as the base for new feature-branch pushes. Any reader with trunk history can then fetch that branch from 1 stored pack. In OpenAI’s monorepo, the median pack was under 20 KiB. Pando returns download links via packfile-uri , an existing Git protocol feature. It sends an empty inline pack. A delivery service called Express caches packs regionally, using consistent hashing, with hit rates above 99%. Each push creates an “L0” pack. Background workers group packs into geometrically larger covers, similar to LSM-tree compaction. The monorepo currently uses covers up to L4. Covers act as a skip list, so pack selection runs in logarithmic time. All figures below are self-reported by OpenAI. OpenAI also ran a 1,000-writer simulation against 3-phase-commit and write-ahead-log designs. It labels these teaching models, not benchmarks. OpenAI wrote a Git conformance suite for agents and added deterministic simulation testing. Agents using GPT-6 Astra wrote Lean and TLA+ specs to find bugs. Pando first ran as a read- and write-through proxy, so traffic moved without downtime. OpenAI ships its own Git build to developer machines and the ChatGPT desktop app. OpenAI fixed client handling of concurrent, interrupted and resumed pack downloads, and added packfile-uri tracing. Its build adds parallel pack indexing and “explicit haves.” Several fixes are upstream. The rest sit in a public patch tracker . Check out the full OpenAI engineering post , the OpenAI Git repository and the patch tracker . title: Zyphra AI Introduces Zyphra Hierarchical Attention (ZHA): A Path to True Subquadratic Attention
abstract: Zyphra has released Zyphra Hierarchical Attention (ZHA) , a sparse attention method built around a tree-structured indexer. ZHA targets a known gap in sparse attention: the indexer that picks tokens still scans the whole context. Zyphra’s technical paper shows ZHA can be distilled into frozen pretrained models with about 4B tokens. On Qwen3.6-35B-A3B it stays close to dense attention on reasoning, agentic coding and 256K retrieval benchmarks. ZHA is a sparse attention method from Zyphra that finds relevant keys by searching a tree. It keeps the full KV cache. The tree only decides which cached keys each query reads. Fixed-state methods like SSMs and sliding windows saturate at long contexts. Fine-grained sparse methods like DeepSeek Sparse Attention score every past token with an indexer. The final attention is sparse, but the indexer still grows with the full context. Near 1M tokens, cited work shows indexing takes 60 to 90% of layer time. ZHA makes the search itself sparse. ZHA splits keys into contiguous chunks and compresses each chunk into a summary key. Summaries are grouped and compressed again, level by level. With chunk size 4, 6 levels cover 4,096 tokens per top node. Summaries come from a small set of learned reference queries . Each reference query gives a tangent-plane estimate of a chunk’s log attention mass. The max over these planes approximates how much attention any future query would give the chunk. At decode time, a query scores the top-level nodes. It keeps the smallest set holding a fraction p of estimated attention mass. It then expands only those children, repeating until it reaches raw KV entries. Top-p makes the budget adaptive. A single-fact lookup touches few branches. A query that needs many scattered facts expands more. The first token is always kept as an attention sink. Zyphra team converted Qwen3.6-35B-A3B with 2 trees: deep (chunk 4, 6 levels) and wide (chunk 256, 1 level). Both use 16 reference queries and p = 0.95. It also trained a MiniMax Sparse Attention (MSA) indexer on 40B tokens, 10x ZHA’s budget. Source: arXiv 2610.42112 , Figure 5. All numbers self-reported by Zyphra. The biggest gap is on retrieval. MSA drops to 77.1% on RULER-13, while both ZHA trees stay above 93%. On LongBench v2, the deep tree and MSA read similar key shares (1.1% vs 1%). The deep tree scores 14.1 points higher. Across 28 tree geometries, RULER accuracy held steady when attending to 10 to 30% of keys. At fixed compression, deeper trees kept accuracy at higher sparsity. A 4-parameter model predicts RULER accuracy from geometry with 1.44-point RMSE. Zyphra released no kernels. It modeled decode latency for one layer at batch size 1 with a roofline. The lightweight setting uses 1 reference query, chunk 8 and p = 0.75. In that model, ZHA beats dense attention near 48K tokens and MSA near 0.48M tokens. At 1B tokens, projected speedups reach 373 to 417x over dense and 52 to 58x over MSA. The blog post adds 32 to 35x and 4.7 to 5.1x at 10M tokens. At 256K, the modeled gains are modest. Pareto-frontier settings reach 1.93x to 2.28x over dense, at 92.7 to 96.4% RULER-13. Routing and selection add their own cost. The base model stays frozen. Only the reference queries train. A KL loss matches dense attention mass per chunk at every level. Qwen and Nemotron runs used 3.98B tokens over 1,900 steps at 32K context. Zyphra reports models under 1B parameters struggled during conversion. Results improved sharply at 4B and above. Check out the ZHA paper on arXiv and Zyphra’s technical blog . title: The Letter Company Releases Letterpress-1: A Coding Agent Built for Growth Engineering
abstract: The Letter Company has released the beta of Letterpress-1 , a coding agent, harness and IDE for growth engineering. The Letterpress-1 coding agent reads a website and its market, then decides what should exist. It builds the change in a sandbox and opens a pull request with a live preview. Letterpress-1 is a growth engineering agent from The Letter Company. It turns site and market signals into pull requests. The letter company team argues that websites, unlike apps, react to outside forces. These include agent behavior, Google rankings, human visits and competitor activity . General coding agents were built to scale codebases, not to act on those signals. The agent is aimed at teams that host their marketing site in git. It is proactive: it suggests the next thing to build. Examples include de-anonymization, landing pages, warmed emails, blog automation and agent telemetry. Letterpress-1 runs in 3 modes : Every change follows the same loop. The agent reads the site, plans and builds in a sandbox. It reviews its own change, then opens a pull request. Each change returns a preview link of your own site . Nothing lands until you choose a preview, a pull request, or a merge after checks pass. Letter team lists 6 surfaces.
