title: Using LLM Summarization in Your Scikit-Learn Pipelines with Scikit-LLM
8 LLM Inference Frameworks You Should Try in 2026
abstract: 8 LLM Inference Frameworks You Should Try in 2026 Compare LLM inference frameworks for production serving, request batching, KV cache management, and efficient deployment. By Bala Priya C , KDnuggets Contributing Editor & Technical Content Specialist on November 3, 2026 in Language Models A model that runs in a notebook serves one request at a time. A production endpoint receives many requests at once, and each one needs GPU memory for its key-value (KV) cache , a slot in the batch, and a response stream. Plain PyTorch or Hugging Face Transformers can serve the model, but you have to build the request scheduling, cache management, and API layer around it yourself. Inference frameworks supply those pieces. They sit between the model and your application and cover token generation, KV cache management, request batching, and the API surface, so you don't build that machinery for every model you ship. With a suitable framework, the same GPU can serve more concurrent requests at lower latency with no change to the model. This article covers inference frameworks for high-throughput, data-center-scale serving, as well as tools designed for local, edge, and low-resource environments. Let’s explore the frameworks. 1. vLLM vLLM is one of the most widely adopted engines for serving large language models (LLMs) at scale, and developers moving off plain Transformers often start with it. Here's why vLLM is great for many practical applications: Uses PagedAttention to manage KV cache memory in small blocks, which packs more concurrent requests onto the same GPU Supports continuous batching, so new requests join a running batch while earlier ones are still generating Ships an OpenAI-compatible server, so existing client code often needs no changes Runs as an in-process library through its LLM class for offline batch jobs and evaluation pipelines, as well as a standalone server Supports NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel GPUs, plus CPUs and TPUs Start with the vLLM documentation , then look at its support for tensor parallelism if you're splitting a model across multiple GPUs. 2. SGLang SGLang pairs a fast backend runtime with a frontend language for describing model interactions, which suits workloads with complex prompting logic. What makes SGLang useful: Co-designs the serving backend and the prompting frontend, giving you finer control over multi-step or branching generations Uses RadixAttention to reuse the KV cache across requests that share a prefix Supports structured outputs and constrained decoding, which are useful for tool calls and JSON-shaped outputs Serves diffusion models for image and video workloads through SGLang Diffusion Offers a server mode and an in-process engine, similar to vLLM's library and standalone options The SGLang GitHub repository is the best starting point, and its docs cover the frontend language in more depth. 3. MAX MAX is Modular's serving framework, and it gives you control down to the kernel level. The following are some useful features of MAX: Runs on both CPUs and GPUs, which helps if your fleet is not GPU-only Allows customization at the model and kernel level, so teams with custom architectures can add support themselves Serves diffusion models alongside standard LLM serving Exposes the same category of tuning options as vLLM and SGLang, such as batch size, memory utilization, and max sequence length, through its max serve command The MAX documentation shows how the serving flags map to your hardware. 4. TensorRT-LLM TensorRT-LLM is NVIDIA's inference library for its own GPUs, and if your fleet is all NVIDIA, that focus tends to pay off in speed. The following features make TensorRT-LLM worth the setup cost: Builds on NVIDIA's TensorRT ecosystem, which targets low-latency inference on NVIDIA silicon Supports in-flight batching and a paged KV cache with block reuse Supports low-precision quantization , including FP8 on H100 and later GPUs, FP4 on Blackwell GPUs, and INT4 activation-aware weight quantization (AWQ) Fits into NVIDIA-centric MLOps stacks, including Triton Inference Server through its dedicated backend The NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM repository has the build instructions and model support matrix you'll need before committing to it. 5. LMDeploy LMDeploy is a toolkit for compressing, deploying, and serving LLMs, with a focus on decoding throughput and quantization. The key features of LMDeploy include: Runs two inference engines: TurboMind , a C++/CUDA engine, and a PyTorch-based engine Uses a persistent batch (its term for continuous batching ) and a blocked KV cache to serve concurrent requests Supports weight-only quantization such as 4-bit AWQ and INT8/INT4 KV cache quantization, which lowers memory use for larger models Supports automatic prefix caching alongside quantization Provides an offline pipeline API and an API server, so you can benchmark it against vLLM on your own model and hardware with the same setup Start with the LMDeploy quickstart guide . Its GitHub repository documents the supported model list and quantization options. 6. llama.cpp llama.cpp is a lightweight runtime written in plain C/C++ with no external dependencies. It supports many model families, including Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, and Mistral. What makes llama.cpp useful: Runs on a wide range of hardware, including consumer GPUs and CPU-only machines Keeps the dependency footprint minimal, which simplifies deployment on constrained devices Includes llama-server , an OpenAI-compatible HTTP server with parallel decoding and continuous batching Suits low-latency, single-request scenarios where a full serving stack would be more than you need The llama.cpp GitHub page is the fastest way to get a model running locally in minutes. 7. Ollama Ollama packages model download, versioning, and local serving behind a simple CLI and API, which makes it a common first inference tool for developers. Why Ollama is super helpful for running and serving LLMs locally: Requires almost no setup, making it the shortest path from "I have a model" to "I have a running endpoint" Handles model pulling, versioning, and local serving through a clean CLI Processes parallel requests per model through the OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL setting and queues additional requests up to OLLAMA_MAX_QUEUE Divides memory into fixed parallel slots, so memory use grows with the parallel setting multiplied by the context length Suits single-user and small-team workloads; for many simultaneous users, vLLM or SGLang add paged KV cache management and continuous batching The Ollama documentation walks through installation, the model library, and concurrency settings. 8. MLC-LLM MLC-LLM is a compiler-based engine built on Apache TVM , and it fits when your target hardware is unusual or your deployment spans multiple platforms. The following features make MLC-LLM different from the rest of this list: Compiles model libraries with Apache TVM, either just-in-time when the engine launches or ahead of time for web, iOS, and Android targets Supports AMD, NVIDIA, Apple, and Intel GPUs Runs on Linux, Windows, macOS, iOS, Android, and web browsers from the same toolchain Provides an OpenAI-compatible REST server with a server mode that raises request concurrency on dedicated GPUs Suits teams shipping the same model across different device types, where one runtime has to cover all of them The MLC-LLM documentation covers weight conversion and model compilation, which web, iOS, and Android deployments need before the first run. Wrapping Up Here's a summary of what we've covered in this article: Framework Best For Concurrent Requests Typical Hardware vLLM High-throughput serving Yes NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel GPUs; CPUs; TPUs SGLang Structured and multi-step prompting workloads Yes NVIDIA and AMD GPUs; TPUs MAX Cross-hardware serving, kernel-level tuning Yes CPUs and GPUs TensorRT-LLM Maximum speed on NVIDIA hardware Yes NVIDIA GPUs LMDeploy Quantized, concurrent serving Yes GPUs (TurboMind targets NVIDIA) llama.

title: Progress on provable inference for large language models
abstract: Chapter 01 : Executive summary Roy Rinberg (Anthropic), Alex Allain (Anthropic); Alessandro Chiesa (EPFL, StarkWare), Miranda Christ (MIT, RESI), Rahul Dalal (Anthropic STEM Fellows Program, Succinct), Giacomo Fenzi (EPFL), Ben Mayer (Anthropic Fellows Program, MIT), Guy Weissenberg (EPFL) Executive summary When you talk to a friend in person, you have many ways to know it is really them: you can see them, hear them, shake their hand. When you talk to an AI model, you have almost none. A user querying a model today cannot check that the responses came from the specific model that a developer claims is responding, as opposed to one secretly substituted in by a routing service for cost reasons, or even by an attacker who has tampered with the token stream. Judging from the model’s output alone is unreliable, even if it produces high-quality responses. Cryptographic proofs of inference solve this problem: they let a model provider commit to a model and then prove that each response was produced by that model. Such proofs could enable applications ranging from consumer products to internal security, and could contribute to a toolkit for verifying compliance with AI pacing requirements. Specifically, we have made progress on a powerful type of cryptographic proof known as a “zkSNARK”, which is uniquely fit for provable inference (owing to its strong hiding and efficiency properties). In this post, we share some of that progress, primarily through a system we call FlashProve. A brief technical summary is as follows: Claude has produced improvements on zkSNARKs for inference, building a system that is substantially faster than prior open-source systems. For a large model (Llama 4 Maverick, 400B-parameter mixture of experts), a single H100 GPU generates proofs at around 110 tokens/second, with a proof size of ~19 MB per 1,024-token request, when in 4-bit quantized weights, using integer arithmetic in prefill. This is ~70-95x the GPU time of running the model itself on vLLM, a common open-source library. Prior open-source systems are orders of magnitude slower, as we discuss in section 6 . Claude found novel ways to apply state-of-the-art tools in the cryptography and security literature, while relying on well-established design principles for cryptographic proof systems. The commitment to the model, and subsequent inference proofs, hide the weights of the model; hiding the architecture of the model is not a goal of this system. Claude is good at optimization, but often makes decisions that are hard to evaluate, especially in large complex systems. We counter this by providing top-level auditable statements in Lean (a formal verification language) for the claimed security guarantees. Today we are releasing five artifacts: The current blog post, which outlines our system and its potential applications; A technical report explaining the details of our system; A (Claude-written) protocol specification document; Executable code that includes: a prover and two verifiers, a fast verifier in C++, and a provably correct verifier in Lean; and Lean proofs for the top level mathematical statements, along with an interactive visualizer of the Lean theorems to aid with auditing. We release our code, Lean proofs, and documentation under the Apache 2.0 license. 1 This research post is meant to share intermediate progress, and not a completed research agenda. We are sharing this explicitly with the goal that others look at what we have done, take it, and improve it. Introduction When a user sends a request to an AI model, today they have no way of knowing for certain that the model they selected is the one that generated the response. For everyday uses, in which users mostly care about the output and not necessarily which specific model produced it, this is a less pressing concern. But there are several cases where such assurance would be useful. For example, independent evaluators who test AI models before and after release need to know that the model they are evaluating is the model being served. Clients who use a model through a third-party routing service want assurance that the tokens came from the model they paid for. And if a cyberattacker modifies the token stream while pretending to be a given model, a user has no way to detect it from the output alone. However, enabling verification of model responses is challenging. Most frontier models’ weights are kept private, and even if the user had access to the weights, checking that a given response was produced by a model with those weights would involve running the model, which requires computational resources far beyond what a typical user (or even evaluator) can afford. The goal of provable inference (PI) is to enable a user with limited computational resources and without any information about the weights to verify that a response came from the requested model. PI is motivated both by a desire to increase customer trust in AI providers, and—because it can be used to provide assurances to independent evaluators and allows providers to demonstrate that they are meeting certain commitments and legal obligations—it also has implications for pacing the frontier of AI development and for AI regulation. One way to implement PI is via a cryptographic object called a zero-knowledge succinct argument: the model provider sends, along with the claimed response, a short proof (say, a few megabytes) that the user can quickly verify (ideally, in seconds on a CPU). If the claimed response deviates from the specified model, the user’s check will fail. Importantly, cryptographic techniques ensure that the proof reveals nothing about the model’s weights. Today, we release FlashProve: an open-source performant prototype for provable inference . For a 400B-parameter mixture-of-experts model (Llama 4 Maverick, 4-bit quantization), we show that a single H100 GPU generates proofs at over 100 tokens/second, with proof size of ~19 MB per 1,024-token request (~70-95 times the GPU time that vLLM, a common open-source library, takes to process prompts of the same length). The release comes with executable code, Lean formalization, and a technical description of the protocol. Our aim is twofold: (i) accelerating and facilitating the development of provable inference; and (ii) demonstrating that zero-knowledge succinct arguments are practical for provable inference. We believe that this progress has meaningful implications for security, in pacing AI development , in providing AI customers with integrity guarantees , in facilitating tooling for auditors and regulators , and more. Trust challenges in AI proliferation The development of artificial intelligence and its growing role in our digital infrastructure and economy raises trust challenges that AI providers must answer. Addressing these and other challenges is facilitated by relying on tools for provable inference (PI). Tools for PI include hardware approaches, software approaches, or a combination of both. Here, we focus on a software-only approach: a cryptographic tool known as a “zkSNARK” ( zero-knowledge succinct argument of knowledge ). Informally, a zkSNARK is a system allowing a prover to convince a verifier , by way of a short “certificate”, that a given computation was executed correctly; crucially, the certificate is zero-knowledge in that it reveals no information beyond what is implied by the computation’s correctness and is succinct in that it’s exponentially faster to verify compared to the proved computation. Below we outline several challenges and how zkSNARKs help in addressing them. Challenge 1: pacing Some proposals to regulate and pace AI development rely on monitoring hardware and how it is used . For example, a provider might be required to devote its hardware to inference rather than to training a powerful new model. The provider might try to cheat by serving cheaper models or using compute in an unexpected way, freeing up resources for training.

title: Bring structured and unstructured data together with Amazon Quick
abstract: Organizations collect data in many forms. Structured data lives in databases and spreadsheets, whereas unstructured data sits in documents, reports, and files stored across file systems. Analyzing both together typically requires switching between multiple tools, running separate queries, and manually correlating results. Amazon Quick addresses this with a unified experience. You can connect structured data through enriched datasets and unstructured data through S3-backed knowledge bases . You can then query both through a single conversational AI agent. In this post, you learn how to: The following diagram illustrates how each component connects to deliver a unified data experience through Amazon Quick. Figure 1: Solution architecture for combining structured and unstructured data in Amazon Quick The architecture has three layers: With this layered approach, you can expand the solution over time. When you add a new data source to the Space, the agent linked to that Space can use it, and responses respect the permissions of the user who asks. To follow along with this walkthrough, you need: This walkthrough uses two types of data: Unstructured documents: Upload these to your Amazon S3 bucket for the knowledge base: Structured data: Download this file to your computer. You upload it directly to Amazon Quick in Step 3: Start by connecting Amazon Quick to your S3 bucket. From the Amazon Quick console, select Knowledge in the left navigation panel. The knowledge page shows available connector types, including Amazon Q Business, Web Crawler, Amazon S3, and third-party options like Google Drive, OneDrive, and Microsoft SharePoint. Under Amazon S3, choose Add . In the Create S3 knowledge base dialog, on the Connect S3 bucket page, provide the following details: Figure 2: Create integration dialog showing the S3 connection fields After the S3 integration is created, Amazon Quick prompts you to create a knowledge base. The knowledge base indexes your S3 content for AI-powered search. Next: Additional settings opens optional settings for document-level access control lists (ACLs) and a metadata files folder. Decide whether to use ACLs before you create the knowledge base, because you can’t change that choice later. This walkthrough uses sample data, so the default settings are sufficient. For details, see Set up and manage Amazon S3 integration . Choose Create . A success banner confirms the S3 integration, and the knowledge base begins indexing in the background. Figure 3: Create knowledge base dialog with the Business Knowledge Base name and content options A dataset is your structured data file loaded into Amazon Quick. By enriching the dataset with semantic descriptions, custom instructions, and correct data types, the AI agent can interpret your data more accurately. It can then translate natural language questions into SQL queries. Amazon Quick ingests the file into SPICE (the in-memory calculation engine) and the dataset appears in your dataset list. The dataset takes its name from the uploaded file, so it appears as Product_Sales.csv in your account. Enriching your dataset with semantic information helps the AI understand your data in business context. The agent uses this context to translate natural language questions into more accurate SQL queries. From the dataset page, choose Edit dataset to enter the data preparation view. In the Transform tab, update data types for columns that were auto-detected incorrectly. For this dataset: Figure 4: Transform view showing data type changes applied to the Product_Sales.csv dataset Select the Output tab to access the dataset-level enrichment fields. Here you provide context that helps the AI understand what your data represents and how to use it. Description: Add a dataset-level description: “Product sales transaction data for AnyCompany, covering orders from FY2024-FY2025 across North America, EMEA, Asia Pacific, and Latin America. Includes order details, customer information, product lines, and revenue metrics.” Custom instructions: Add guidance for how the AI should query this data: TAGS: Sales, revenue, orders, regional performance, product analytics Column descriptions: Select each column in the left panel and add a description. For example: Figure 5: Output view showing dataset details with Description and Custom instructions configured Choose Save & publish to save your changes. The dataset summary now shows the columns with their correct data types and the descriptions you added. Figure 6: Enriched Product_Sales.csv dataset summary showing all 16 columns, data types, and descriptions This enriched dataset provides the structured data layer for your solution. When the agent receives a natural language question about sales data, it uses these descriptions and instructions to generate more accurate SQL queries. Combined with the knowledge base from Step 2, you now have both structured and unstructured data ready to bring together in a Space. Spaces in Amazon Quick act as unified data workspaces. A Space can hold file uploads, dashboards, knowledge bases, actions, and datasets, giving your chat agent a single location to query across data types. From the left navigation, select Spaces and create a new Space. Name it “Business Intelligence Hub”. Add your knowledge base and dataset to the Space: The Space now shows both your knowledge base (unstructured documents) and your enriched dataset (structured sales data) linked as data sources. This is the central hub where both data types come together, giving your chat agent a single place to query across everything. Figure 7 shows the Space with both resources in the Ready state. Figure 7: Business Intelligence Hub Space showing the Product_Sales.csv dataset and Business Knowledge Base Navigate to Chat agents in the left navigation and choose Create chat agent . Amazon Quick presents a prompt builder where you can describe your agent in natural language or choose from templates like Training Guide, Project Coordinator, and Onboarding Helper. For this walkthrough, choose Skip to configure the agent manually. Figure 8: Chat agent creation screen with the prompt builder and sample templates The configuration panel has several sections. Start with the Agent Persona: For Agent Persona instructions, enter: A note appears confirming that your chat agent comes equipped with enterprise guardrails. Figure 9: Agent persona configuration with identity and persona instructions filled in Under Communication style, pick a response style preset. Options include Executive, Technical, and Creative. For a business intelligence use case, select Executive . Under Knowledge Sources , choose Link spaces and select the “Business Intelligence Hub” Space you created earlier. This gives the agent access to your S3 knowledge base and other data sources in that Space. When you link a Space, the agent answers from large language model (LLM) knowledge and the linked resources only. You can also attach reference documents (PDF, TXT, HTML, MD, CSV, DOC, DOCX) directly to the agent for additional context. Amazon Quick extracts up to 100,000 characters of text from the reference documents that you upload. Figure 10: Knowledge Sources section showing the linked Business Intelligence Hub Space Under Customization, configure: Figure 11: Customization section with the welcome message and suggested prompts Choose Launch chat agent . The right panel shows a live preview of your agent with the welcome message and suggested prompts displayed. Figure 12: Launched Business Intelligence Assistant with the welcome message and suggested prompts in the chat panel With the agent running, start with a question about your business results: How did sales change by region in 2025? For this question, the agent combines results from the Product_Sales.csv dataset with the documents in the S3 knowledge base. It returns a response with regional sales breakdowns, trends, and citations that point back to each source.

title: ServiceNow on-behalf-of token exchange with Bedrock AgentCore Gateway
abstract: AI agents that interact with enterprise APIs on behalf of users need to maintain user identity throughout the request chain. Without identity propagation, API calls arrive at downstream services as the application itself rather than the user who initiated the action. This breaks audit trails, bypasses user-level access controls, and violates the principle of least privilege. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. This post shows how to configure AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, for an on-behalf-of (OBO) token exchange with Microsoft Entra ID. An AI agent can then call the ServiceNow REST API while preserving the calling user’s identity. You configure the token exchange on the gateway target, and AgentCore Gateway performs the exchange on each request. The pattern can be applied to other REST APIs protected by OAuth. In production, you can additionally pair identity propagation with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to filter harmful content and validate the agent’s inputs and outputs. The architecture involves three key components connected through AgentCore Gateway: The following figure shows the end-to-end solution architecture, including components within AWS, Microsoft Entra ID, and ServiceNow. Figure 1: Solution architecture across AWS, Microsoft Entra ID, and ServiceNow As shown in Figure 1, the user acquires a JSON Web Token (JWT) to invoke the agent 1. The agent authenticates to the gateway with a JWT token scoped to the agent’s own application registration 2. The gateway then exchanges that token, using the OBO flow, for a new token scoped to the ServiceNow API connector, with the original user’s identity preserved 3. ServiceNow receives a valid token whose preferred_username claim maps to an existing ServiceNow user and applies that user’s permissions to the API call 4. When the agent calls the gateway, it presents a JWT with an audience claim matching the agent’s client ID (for example, 3ff88e17-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXXXXXXXXXX ). ServiceNow, however, expects a token with an audience claim matching its own API connector client ID ( 5d4a7a11-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXXXXXXXXXX ). The OBO flow bridges this gap. AgentCore Gateway sends the inbound token to the Entra token endpoint along with the agent application’s client credentials, the target scope, and a parameter requested_token_use: on_behalf_of . Entra validates that the calling user consented to the delegation, then issues a new token for the ServiceNow API with the original user’s claims intact. Before you begin, you need the following: Start by creating an application registration to represent the ServiceNow API connector. The following screenshot shows the application registration page for the ServiceNow API Connector in Microsoft Entra ID. Figure 2: Application registration for the ServiceNow API connector in Microsoft Entra ID After creating, in the Overview page note the Application (client) ID. In the navigation menu expand Manage and select Expose an API and add a scope named user_impersonation using the default Application ID URI. This scope is what the OBO flow requests when exchanging tokens. The following screenshot shows how to expose an API in Microsoft Entra ID. Figure 3: Exposing the user_impersonation scope in Microsoft Entra ID Next, create an application registration for the AI agent. The following screenshot shows the application registration page in Microsoft Entra ID for the ServiceNow Agent application. Figure 4: Application registration for the ServiceNow Agent in Microsoft Entra ID Note the Application (client) ID for the ServiceNowAgent. Create a client secret on this registration. The gateway needs these credentials to perform the OBO exchange. The following screenshot shows how you can create a client secret on the ServiceNow Agent application registration in Microsoft Entra ID. Figure 5: Creating a client secret on the ServiceNow Agent application registration Then configure the agent application to have API permissions to call the ServiceNow API connector application. The following screenshot shows the API permissions that you need to configure on the ServiceNow Agent application registration in Microsoft Entra ID. Figure 6: API permission configuration in Microsoft Entra ID No changes to the Entra configuration are needed beyond what you would set up for any standard OBO integration between two applications. In the ServiceNow administrative console, navigate to System OAuth > Inbound Integrations and create a new inbound integration (Third party ID token issued by OIDC supporting identity provider). Specify the client ID from the ServiceNow API connector application registration you created in Entra. The following screenshot shows the configuration of the inbound integration in ServiceNow. Figure 7: Configuring the inbound integration in ServiceNow In the same screen, create a new OpenID Connect (OIDC) provider configuration and enter the OIDC metadata URL for your Entra tenant. Map the user claim to the appropriate user field. For example, if your Entra tenant places the user’s email in the preferred_username claim, map that to the Email field in ServiceNow. Clear JTI verification if your Entra tenant doesn’t include it in tokens. Entra uses an internal claim named uti on tokens it issues, which is equivalent to JTI. Consider mapping this uti claim to a jti claim to provide additional replay protection and denylisting. The following screenshot shows how to configure the OIDC provider in ServiceNow. Figure 8: Configuring the OAuth OIDC provider in ServiceNow Finally, in the same screen, create an auth scope for the integration (for example, APIConnector ). The following screenshot shows how to create a new auth scope in ServiceNow. Figure 9: Creating a new auth scope in ServiceNow Limit the auth scope to the Table API, or whichever ServiceNow APIs your agent needs to access, as shown in the following screenshot. Figure 10: Limiting the auth scope to the Table API in ServiceNow After this configuration is complete, ServiceNow accepts authorization tokens with an audience of your API connector’s client ID and resolves the calling user from the preferred_username claim. With Entra and ServiceNow configured, you can now set up AgentCore Gateway to handle the OBO exchange natively. Create a new outbound auth configuration (choose Build > Identity > Add Outbound Auth > Add OAuth client ) in AgentCore and select Customized provider . Enter the client ID and client secret from your agent application registration, along with the Entra discovery URL as shown in the following screenshot. Figure 11: Adding an OAuth client in AgentCore Gateway Expand Additional configurations and select JWT authorization grant as shown in the following screenshot. This tells the gateway to use a JWT-based grant type for token exchange. Figure 12: Configuring the JWT authorization grant Create a new AgentCore Gateway ( Build > Gateways > Create gateway ). When defining the gateway details, expand Additional configurations — optional and select MCP version 2025-11-25 as shown in the following screenshot. This version is required for native OBO support. You can’t turn on native OBO for gateways created with earlier MCP versions. Figure 13: Selecting MCP version 2025-11-25 Configure the inbound identity using your agent’s application registration (select Use existing identity provider configurations ), as you would for any gateway that accepts Entra-authenticated requests. Under JWT Authorization Configuration add the Application ID we documented earlier for the ServiceNowAgent as shown in the following screenshot. Figure 14: Configuring inbound authorization in AgentCore Gateway Add a target to the gateway pointing to your ServiceNow REST endpoint. Define the schema inline.

title: How Gen Digital built Norton Revamp’s AI-curated News Engine with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Web Search
abstract: Your professional reputation now lives online first. Recruiters check LinkedIn before returning a call. Clients review your digital presence before booking a first meeting. For ambitious professionals, that shift is an opportunity: a well-crafted online voice can open doors that a résumé alone never could. But standing out takes more than content generation. It takes real-time awareness of what’s happening right now. A professional building a reputation as a generative AI thought leader needs to react to today’s breakthroughs, not last week’s headlines. And with feeds flooded by AI-generated noise, audiences reward authenticity and timeliness more than ever. Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore made that possible. We built Norton Revamp , a generative AI-powered professional reputation management platform. At its heart is an AI-curated News Engine, powered by AgentCore Web Search, that grounds every content suggestion, goal recommendation, and news feed item in current, cited web knowledge. The platform launched in March 2026, built by a small group of engineers. In this post, we show you how the Gen team builds an AI-curated News Engine in Norton Revamp with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Web Search to help customers turn ideas into engaging social media posts. Unlike chatbots that rely on static knowledge bases, Norton Revamp needs to understand what’s trending right now in each user’s professional domain. A cyber security expert needs today’s threat intelligence. A marketing leader needs this week’s industry shifts. Traditional approaches (custom web crawlers, third-party news APIs, static content databases) each carry trade-offs: infrastructure overhead, stale data, vendor complexity, or data egress risk. We evaluated three alternatives before choosing AgentCore Web Search. Custom crawlers require ongoing maintenance and lag real time. Third-party news APIs added vendor contracts, API key management, and data leaving our AWS environment. Static knowledge bases were perpetually stale. AgentCore Web Search eliminated these concerns. It’s fully managed with zero infrastructure overhead, operates entirely within AWS with zero data egress, and returns cited sources with URLs and publication dates. This makes personalized, real-time news feeds viable at scale. Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a fully managed web search capability, compliant with the Model Context Protocol (MCP). It’s available as a managed connector on the AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Our agent sends a natural-language query, and Web Search returns relevant snippets, source URLs, titles, and publication dates that the model uses to produce grounded responses. This capability powers three core features: Every user gets a personalized content stream surfacing the latest articles and trending topics tied to their goal. If you’re building a reputation as a generative AI thought leader, your feed prioritizes AI breakthroughs, industry analysis, and emerging use cases, sourced in real time through AgentCore Web Search. Unlike a static RSS aggregator, the feed is a goal-aware discovery engine that refreshes with every session. Users receive AI-generated content ideas tailored to trending topics in their space, written in their own authentic voice, with optional AI-generated visuals. AgentCore Web Search grounds every suggestion on what’s happening today . A three-step coaching flow (Analyze, Refine, Post) walks users from initial ideas to published content on LinkedIn and X, with a feedback loop, so the AI gets sharper with every iteration. Users define a goal. The AI builds a personalized roadmap with weekly themes and milestones. AgentCore Web Search feeds real-time trend data into goal generation, so weekly themes reflect current industry movements. The system learns from the past four weeks of activity, refreshing recommendations as users grow. Figure 1: Event-driven architecture of the Norton Revamp News Engine The integration follows an event-driven architecture. When a user sets or updates their professional goal, Amazon Nova (through Amazon Bedrock) generates targeted search queries based on the goal, recent activity, and engagement patterns. The agent sends these queries to AgentCore Web Search, which returns cited results entirely within our AWS environment. Our AI Learning System ranks the results for relevance, recency, and source credibility. The ranked results then serve as grounding context for Amazon Nova Lite to generate content suggestions in the user’s authentic voice. Engagement data feeds back into query generation, making the News Engine progressively smarter. Generative AI and machine learning stack: Infrastructure: React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS on the frontend. Node.js, Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), AWS Lambda, Amazon DynamoDB (multi-table with composite key patterns), Amazon API Gateway, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS), Amazon EventBridge, Amazon CloudFront, Amazon CloudWatch, and AWS Secrets Manager on the backend. Infrastructure managed through Terraform with blue-green deployment for zero-downtime releases. Processing pipeline: The platform runs four pipeline stages: We embedded generative AI from day one, as both the product and the development methodology. The human-AI responsibility split was deliberate: human-owned architecture decisions, security reviews, business logic, and personalization algorithms. AI handled code generation, documentation, test scaffolding, refactoring, and UI component creation. With Claude, we produced 10 or more design variants per concept, compressed design-to-prototype time from weeks to hours and generated 70 percent of UI code with AI. We tested five pricing models in the time previously needed for one. The gamification system went through eight iterations before launching. The measurable impact: 3x faster feature implementation, boilerplate generation accelerated by 90 percent, documentation by 80 percent, test creation by 70 percent, and UI component generation by 65 percent. The trade-off: AI output review consumed 20–30 percent of our time. AI helped with personalization algorithms, the DynamoDB multi-table architecture (which needed experience-based judgment), security implementation, and Amazon Bedrock batch processing optimization. The key insight: AI accelerated implementation, but humans designed how the AI Learning System should adapt to user goals. Product generative AI (Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Nova, AgentCore Web Search) and development generative AI served different purposes, and we kept them separate. We achieved 85 percent code coverage through automated test generation. Critical test areas included content generation quality, AgentCore Web Search result relevance and freshness validation, engagement tracking accuracy, gamification logic, and news feed relevance to user goals. For a product carrying the Norton brand, compliance is non-negotiable. Security checks spanned static code analysis, dependency vulnerability scanning, authentication flows, user data encryption, access control logic, generative AI model output validation, and content filtering. Our security team reviewed all AI-generated recommendations: AI accelerated identification, and humans made final decisions. The result: 99.9 percent uptime since launch with real-time monitoring of generative AI content quality and user satisfaction. For teams considering AgentCore Web Search for real-time grounding: Building Norton Revamp proved that a small, generative AI-augmented team can deliver enterprise software in months. It also proved that Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore can serve as the real-time intelligence backbone for products that need to stay current with the world.

title: Build a semantic layer for agentic AI with EDB Postgres AI and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: In this post, we show how to build a semantic layer for agentic AI using EDB Postgres AI . We run a Strands Agents agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that queries the layer to answer customer 360 (C360) questions. Earlier posts in this series built the same C360 pattern with Stardog’s knowledge graph , Denodo’s data virtualization platform , AtScale’s dimensional model , and Strategy Mosaic’s linked models . EDB Postgres AI puts the semantic layer inside the operational Postgres database as an AIDB extension . Business meaning lives next to the data in standard Postgres COMMENT statements, the join graph comes from Postgres foreign keys, and governance uses Postgres GRANT and row-level security through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint that ships with AIDB. By the end of this post you will know: An agent that answers business questions from live data needs three layers: a model that plans and writes queries, a meaning layer that tells the agent what the data represents, and a runtime that hosts the agent and controls identity and access. The Stardog post in this series introduced this framing. The model layer in this post is Anthropic Claude on Amazon Bedrock , the same as prior posts (model availability varies by AWS Region ). The runtime layer is AgentCore runtime , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. AgentCore Gateway handles inbound authorization, and AgentCore Identity , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, holds outbound credentials for the tool targets, same as prior posts. EDB Postgres AI hosts agents and tools inside the database itself and acts as the connection point for external agents through its MCP endpoint. The meaning layer is where this post diverges from the others. Here it is a SemKB that lives inside the operational Postgres database. The schema and the business definitions are indexed together. Postgres GRANT , row-level security, and column-level grants enforce access, not an advisory system prompt. The sections that follow cover how AIDB builds the layer, how AgentCore exposes it, and how two Postgres roles asking the same question get different answers. The dataset is the Stardog C360 Knowledge Kit , loaded into a single EDB Postgres AI instance in a dedicated c360 schema. The data model has four tables and one derived view. The physical schema is a plain Postgres join graph: a customer in the customers table lives at a location , places purchases , and each purchase references a product. The semantic work rests on three business ideas that column names don’t reveal. State isn’t on the customer row. It lives in locations , reached through the customers.location foreign key, and a comment on that column tells SemKB where to find it. purchases.price records the order total. An agent that reads it as a unit price and multiplies by quantity returns $502,529 for the top customer instead of $27,991.66. Big spender is a term the business owns. Captured as a view with a COMMENT ON VIEW statement, its definition stays in one place that every agent, dashboard, and query reads from. The questions we run through the agent end to end: The following diagram shows the request path from the analyst through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to the semantic layer inside EDB Postgres AI. The analyst authenticates with Amazon Cognito and calls AgentCore Gateway with the issued JSON Web Token (JWT) as a Bearer token. Gateway routes to AgentCore runtime, which plans with Claude on Amazon Bedrock. The agent calls MCP tools through Gateway, which forwards to an Application Load Balancer in the EDB Postgres AI virtual private cloud (VPC) and on to the edb-endpoints MCP server inside AIDB. AIDB serves the SemKB, semantic aliases, and read-only PostgreSQL tables. AgentCore traces go to Amazon CloudWatch, and AIDB captures OpenTelemetry traces as rows in the aidb_otel schema inside Postgres. Figure 1: Reference architecture for EDB Postgres AI and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Two flows cross the boundary between AgentCore and EDB Postgres AI. Inbound: A client calls AgentCore Gateway with a bearer token issued by an Amazon Cognito user pool . The Gateway inbound JWT authorizer validates the token against the Cognito discovery URL. Gateway then evaluates its Cedar policy against the token’s claims to decide which tools this agent, acting for this user, can invoke. It then routes the call to AgentCore runtime. The agent invokes Claude on Amazon Bedrock for planning and answer composition. Outbound to the semantic layer: The agent’s tool call is an MCP request. AgentCore Gateway supports MCP server targets directly. AIDB’s edb-endpoints HTTP server speaks streamable HTTP MCP with HTTP Basic authentication , which lets Gateway treat it as an MCP server target with no translation layer. An Application Load Balancer with an HTTPS listener and an AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificate fronts edb-endpoints on an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance. The ALB URL is registered as the Gateway target. The AgentCore Identity credential provider holds the Postgres role credential and injects it as Basic auth on every outbound request. The agent code doesn’t see the Postgres credential. Observability: AgentCore emits traces for tool calls, large language model (LLM) calls, and token usage to CloudWatch Transaction Search . AIDB captures OpenTelemetry traces for SQL execution as rows in the aidb_otel schema inside Postgres, queryable with ordinary SQL after the database is configured to write them (see enabling telemetry on the source database ). No AWS Lambda is required in this architecture. AIDB already speaks MCP, so Gateway talks to it as an MCP server target directly through the ALB. The Denodo post in this series uses the same ALB pattern in front of its MCP server, and the architecture here is unchanged other than the vendor. These steps assume AIDB is installed and enabled on the EDB Postgres AI instance and the Stardog C360 kit’s four CSVs are loaded into a dedicated c360 schema with the primary and foreign keys shown earlier. Because this layer lives in the same database as the data, there is no second system to deploy and no catalog to synchronize. The semantic layer is defined in SQL, inside the same database as the application that writes the rows. An AIDB semantic knowledge base indexes Postgres schema, not data. It embeds the definition of every table, view, and column (with the COMMENT ON text alongside) into a vector store that an agent can search in natural language. Three authoring tasks help the agent find the right table and column by meaning: writing COMMENT ON statements, defining business terms as views with their own comments, and registering recurring questions as semantic aliases . Comments are the simplest of the three authoring tasks and improve text-to-SQL accuracy the most for both users and agents. The view holds the business definition in one place, so no agent or dashboard has to redefine big spender . The time you spend on comments up front pays off on every query the agent runs afterward. Create the SemKB over the c360 schema. The call registers the name, the embedding model, the target schemas, and the auto-processing mode. The embedding model is a local llama.cpp model ( llamacpp_embeddings ) that ships with the AIDB Amazon Machine Image (AMI). SemKB uses one embedding model per KB, so every entry sits in the same vector space. The AIDB AMI ships with a default SemKB named semkb over public , so creating c360_kb leaves two SemKBs on the instance. When more than one SemKB exists, every aidb.semantic_kb_search call must pass kb_name explicitly. To swap the local model for a remote embedding model, such as Amazon Titan Text Embeddings on Amazon Bedrock , register the remote model with aidb.create_model . Pass its name as the SemKB’s model parameter. The auto_processing parameter accepts Disabled , Live , or Background . Live reacts to schema changes through Postgres event triggers.

title: Building ultra-low-latency voice AI applications on AWS
abstract: Conversational AI is transforming how humans interact with technology. From virtual assistants and AI-powered contact centers to real-time translation and accessibility tools, voice-first interfaces are rapidly becoming the default mode of interaction for millions of users worldwide. Yet delivering a truly natural voice experience remains one of the hardest challenges in AI infrastructure. Users expect human-like responsiveness. Excess latency can break conversational flow and erode trust. To feel natural, AI-generated speech must arrive within the same temporal window as human turn-taking. This post introduces how Cartesia , an AWS Partner specializing in real-time voice AI, uses purpose-built State Space Models (SSMs) and AWS infrastructure to deliver sub-100ms text-to-speech and speech-to-text at global scale. Developers can build voice experiences that feel indistinguishable from human conversation. The demand for real-time voice AI is growing rapidly across industries: Traditional transformer-based text-to-speech (TTS) models struggle with streaming latency because they process entire sequences before producing output. This architectural limitation creates a fundamental tension: higher quality often means higher latency. A new class of models, State Space Models, resolves this trade-off. State Space Models (SSMs) take a fundamentally different approach to processing sequences than transformers, the architecture behind most of today’s AI. Transformers use a mechanism called attention, which compares every element in a sequence to every other element. As a result, the amount of computation grows quadratically as the sequence gets longer. SSMs instead treat a sequence as a system that evolves continuously over time, processing it step by step and carrying a compact internal state forward. This can be converted into a form computers handle efficiently, keeping the cost low for certain long sequences. This efficiency makes SSMs well suited to real-time, streaming data like live speech. Key advantages of SSMs for audio processing include: These properties make SSMs uniquely suited for real-time voice applications where both quality and latency are non-negotiable. Cartesia puts these SSM advantages to work in two production voice models: Sonic for speech generation and Ink for transcription. Cartesia is a real-time multimodal intelligence company that has built a voice AI application, purpose-built on State Space Model architecture. Founded by researchers who pioneered SSM advances, Cartesia’s application is designed for streaming inference at the edge of human perception. The application features two core models, Sonic for text-to-speech and Ink for speech-to-text, both optimized for sub-100ms first-byte latency while maintaining studio-quality output. Sonic is Cartesia’s flagship streaming text-to-speech model, delivering ultra-realistic speech synthesis with sub-100ms latency: Sonic is recommended for teams that want the fastest time-to-production with minimal operational overhead. Call the API and receive streaming audio in real time. Ink is Cartesia’s streaming speech-to-text model, purpose-built for conversational AI applications: Together, Sonic and Ink provide the complete voice AI stack needed to build conversational agents that feel human. If you need data sovereignty, latency control, or compliance, you can deploy Cartesia models directly into your own AWS account. Sonic is delivered as an Amazon SageMaker AI model package through AWS Marketplace, which you deploy to a SageMaker AI endpoint running entirely within your virtual private cloud (VPC). Inference data doesn’t leave your account. The deployment patterns in this section cover Sonic. Ink is currently available through the Cartesia API, which you can purchase through the Cartesia Voice AI Platform listing in AWS Marketplace. Two primary patterns are available for Sonic. Deploying on Amazon SageMaker AI is the fastest path to a managed, in-VPC Sonic endpoint. Sonic ships as an AWS Marketplace model package, so there’s a one-time subscribe step that grants your account an AWS Region-specific model-package ARN. You then create the SageMaker AI endpoint from that ARN, either from the console or with the SageMaker or Boto3 SDK. The following steps follow Cartesia’s official deployment notebook. Run from an Amazon SageMaker Notebook Instance or SageMaker Studio. The AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) execution role needs AmazonSageMakerFullAccess . To subscribe, your role (and you) need aws-marketplace:Subscribe , aws-marketplace:Unsubscribe , and aws-marketplace:ViewSubscriptions . Otherwise, the account must already be subscribed to the listing. Before deployment, choose a supported instance type from the model package’s SupportedRealtimeInferenceInstanceTypes field: If your chosen instance type’s applied value is below your current usage plus your planned endpoint instance count, you may need to request a service quota increase. See SageMaker AI quotas for details. In Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, you can subscribe to its AWS Marketplace model package, create a SageMaker model, and host it on a real-time endpoint. The following four steps show the deployment path. Figure 1: Searching AWS Marketplace for the Cartesia Sonic 3.6 SageMaker model package Figure 2: The Cartesia Sonic 3.6 listing in AWS Marketplace Figure 3: Creating a SageMaker model from the Sonic 3.6 subscription Figure 4: The SageMaker endpoint for Sonic 3.6 The model-package ARN is Region-specific. To verify the Sonic 3.6 package in US East (N. Virginia) with the SageMaker API, run: After the endpoint reaches InService , invoke it with the SageMaker Runtime InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream API and process the returned audio stream in your application. Some teams have existing GPU infrastructure, strict networking requirements, or a need to co-locate Cartesia with other services. For these cases, you can run the model container yourself on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) GPU instances. This gives you full control over the runtime, scaling, and network path. It uses Cartesia’s container image, obtained from Cartesia, rather than the AWS Marketplace model package. Figure 5: Self-managed deployment flow for Cartesia Sonic on Amazon EC2 GPU instances Obtain the container image. Request the Sonic container image and licensing terms from Cartesia. Replicate it into your own private Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repository so your compute plane can pull it with IAM-scoped credentials rather than reaching out to an external registry at scale. Choose your GPU instance family. Sonic runs on NVIDIA GPU instances. The G6 (L4) and G6e (L40S) families are the optimal balance for real-time TTS. The earlier G5 (A10G) also works. Match GPU memory and vCPU to your target concurrency and prefer a single-GPU instance per model replica for simplest scaling. Provision the compute plane (Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) or Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS)). For ECS: register a GPU task definition (set the container’s GPU resource requirement, for example, resourceRequirements with type GPU) and run it as a service behind an Application Load Balancer. For EKS: create a GPU node group (or Karpenter provisioner) using the EKS GPU-optimized AMI, install the NVIDIA device plugin, and deploy the container as a Deployment fronted by a Service/Ingress. Configure networking for low latency. Place inference nodes in a cluster placement group to minimize inter-node latency, keep replicas in a single Availability Zone for the tightest path, and use VPC endpoints for ECR/S3 pulls. For hybrid or on-premises callers, terminate traffic over AWS Direct Connect or a private Network Load Balancer to avoid public-internet hops. Load model weights efficiently.

title: Introducing India-based inference for Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock
abstract: Kimi K3 is a multi-modal, open-weight foundation model (FM) that provider Moonshot AI reported achieved frontier-level coding and general agentic intelligence at release. In addition to global and US-based inference, Amazon Bedrock now supports in-country inference in India for Kimi K3: unblocking local workloads with strict data residency requirements. Customers like Ultrahuman are already seeing the benefits in production: “Jade, an AI Health and Wellness assistant in the Ultrahuman app, answers questions in plain language using each person’s own Ring and glucose data, across more than 14,000 conversations a day. Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock let us add a leading open-weight model through the API we already use, with health data staying inside AWS and Mumbai as a fallback Region. With prompt caching, we’ve cut LLM costs by 80 percent and made multi-turn chats 85 percent faster.” — Aditya Patawari, VP Engineering, Ultrahuman In this post, we explain the different global and geographic inference options available, and share code for an example use case: optical character recognition (OCR) and understanding of Indic-language documents, with follow-up question answering in code-mixed Hinglish. Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock is offered through cross-Region inference profiles . You can invoke the model from any of a wide range of AWS Regions (the “source”). Amazon Bedrock then securely processes your request in one of multiple possible “destination” Regions. Cross-Region inference is fully managed by AWS: Data is encrypted in transit between Regions and remains on the AWS network, never traversing the public internet or requiring you to set up any multi-Region virtual private cloud (VPC) infrastructure. The inference profile ID you invoke controls which destination Regions are eligible: See the Amazon Bedrock Kimi K3 model card for up-to-date information on available inference profiles, which AWS Regions they can be called from, and what destination Regions they can use for inference. Let’s consider an example use case: reading a scanned Hindi document, extracting structured data, and answering follow-up questions in mixed Hindi and English (Hinglish). This need is common in Indian financial services and public sector workflows where know your customer (KYC) forms, utility bills, and similar documents must often be digitized. Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock can directly read and reason about images, including those containing multilingual text. It offers a potential solution with no separate OCR or translation service required. The full source code for this example is available on GitHub . For example, to use Kimi K3 through the ap-south-1 Mumbai Region with India geographic inference, the following IAM policy grants sufficient access. Replace the {ACCOUNT_ID} placeholders with your AWS account ID: For more information about permissions, see Prerequisites for running model inference in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. If your organization restricts AWS Regions, ask your administrator to review the geographic cross-Region inference IAM and SCP guidance . Keep the source Region permitted and allow routing to both India destinations, using a profile-scoped exception where appropriate. The Responses API guide also describes required default-project access. As detailed on the model card , Amazon Bedrock supports multiple APIs for invoking Kimi K3, all under the Bedrock Runtime endpoint: Because the OpenAI-compatible APIs are recommended for this model, we use those in this example and connect through the openai Python Library . Amazon Bedrock supports generating API keys for integrations that require them. However, AWS recommends using short-lived credentials instead where possible. The AWS token generator Python library derives a short-term API key-like token from the standard AWS CLI credential chain. If you use a named profile for your AWS CLI, you might need to set the AWS_PROFILE environment variable first. After CLI credentials are set up, you can invoke the model with the following code: Here, region ( ap-south-1 Mumbai) specifies the source Region to which the request is made. The inference profile in.moonshotai.kimi-k3 ensures that inference is processed in Indian Regions only. A broad range of features like streaming, tool calling, and structured outputs are supported across both the Chat Completions and Responses APIs. See the OpenAI Python API Reference for more examples. Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock supports images as well as PDFs and a range of other file types. You can send input files to the model directly by base64-encoding. For OCR or other use cases where small details are important, consider setting the image detail parameter to high . This improves accuracy, at the cost of more input tokens consumed per image. In some cases, we’ve seen higher output quality for Kimi K3 when images are provided before text inputs. We suggest experimenting with request ordering. Consider the following example code: To demonstrate, we generated an image of a synthetic electricity bill in Hindi. Figure 1: A synthetic Hindi electricity bill from the sample (all sample documents are fictional) Given this image input, the model can answer questions by pulling data directly from the document with no separate digitization step required. For example: Q: Bill kitne ka hai aur last date kab hai? Late hua toh kitna dena padega? A: Bill ka total ₹2,217.20 hai, aur last date 20/10/2026 hai. Late hua toh ₹2,261.54 dena padega. Beyond general question-answering, you can create structured document processing workflows by using static prompts to extract a consistent set of expected fields across many documents. To apply firm constraints on output structure (rather than best-effort prompt-guided generation), Kimi K3 supports structured output on Amazon Bedrock either through function calling or by providing a JSON Schema output format. These options are described in more detail in the OpenAI documentation (for OpenAI-compatible APIs) and the Amazon Bedrock User Guide (for native Converse/InvokeModel APIs). In the full sample code repository , we’ve provided an end-to-end pipeline that: For the same synthetic Hindi electricity bill in the preceding figure, the pipeline returns structured fields such as the following (abbreviated): We’ve also included a KYC form example and an open-ended schema-free mode, where the model selects the most useful fields itself for any other document type. All provided sample documents are synthetic, with fictional names and addresses and masked identity numbers. Download the sample code from GitHub to explore further and try it out on your own images. As with any automated extraction, you should verify the outputs are reliable for your specific use case before relying on them for important decisions. Consider adding post-validation logic or a human review step for critical workflows. Tune your system prompts and schemas against example documents for reliable extractions. Amazon Bedrock Advanced Prompt Optimization (AdvPO) provides a fully managed option to optimize prompt templates based on reference examples. Amazon Bedrock service tiers give you control over price-performance on a per-request basis. For less latency-sensitive cases, you can select the flex tier to enjoy a 50 percent discount on default standard pricing. For latency-critical scenarios, you can select “priority” to request higher queue priority at a higher price. See the pricing page for details. Use cases with long, seldom-changing content in their input prompts can also benefit from prompt caching on Amazon Bedrock. Make sure the static content (system prompt, tool descriptions, and so on) appears at the beginning of the input, before dynamic sections like the current image and question. Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock supports both discounted pricing for cache hits, as well as an explicit caching mode.

title: 機器人幹活，AI當廠長！這家巨頭要造下一代自主智慧倉
abstract: 機器人幹活，AI當廠長！這家巨頭要造下一代自主智慧倉 夢瑤 2026-11-03 21:57:11 來源： 量子位 AI接管排程運營，倉庫越幹越聰明 夢瑤 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI 具身智慧，開始挑戰更複雜的生產場景了。 當一眾廠商還在圍繞揀貨、家務等任務探索時，如今有玩家盯上了具身智慧產業化的一塊硬骨頭： 智慧倉儲 。 而且野心不小，要讓AI接管整座倉庫，實現7×24小時自主執行，還能在真實業務中持續學習、自主進化。 這個玩家的名字大家也不陌生，正是全球智慧機器人的頭部企業 「極智嘉」 （Geek+）。 就在最近，極智嘉正式亮出《24/7自主智慧倉計劃》，目標直指物理AI時代的自進化智慧倉。 從讓具身AI真正幹活，到讓整座倉庫自己運轉，物理AI這次直面的，是產業化更深層的考題。 從會幹活到會自己管，物理AI開始挑戰更難的一關 在AI深入工業場景的過程中，其實一直藏著一個蠻尷尬的事實—— 物理AI的自動化程度越高，對人工的依賴反而越集中在最難的環節。 過去十多年，AMR讓搬運、儲存等大量標準化作業實現自動化，貨物甚至能自己找到人。 可一旦進入複雜揀選，面對成千上萬種SKU、頻繁變化的包裝和擺放位置，機器人依舊容易犯難。 這也暴露出倉儲自動化長期以來的一道瓶頸：單點效率的提升，已經很難支撐整座倉庫的智慧化躍遷了。 也正是在這個節骨眼上，極智嘉對下一代倉儲智慧化的突破口，給出了自己的行業判斷： 下一代倉儲智慧化的關鍵，是實現7×24小時自主執行、持續進化，並依託全球規模化商業能力，讓自主智慧倉成為新一代生產力基礎設施。 這一判斷背後，其實藏著倉儲行業越來越現實的一筆經濟和技術賬。 對客戶來說，倉庫每多一小時自主運轉，就意味著多一小時擺脫 人工班次限制 的產能。 尤其在夜間和訂單高峰，持續穩定的履約能力，直接關係到供應鏈的響應速度。 更重要的是，能讓投入重金的自動化裝置真正跑滿產能，把夜班用工、現場管理的壓力轉化為實實在在的 運營收益 。 但這就意味著，機器人要能處理從未見過的異常，而且整倉系統要能在數百臺裝置同時執行時自主決策、故障恢復、積累經驗。 畢竟，只有整座倉庫具備自主應對不確定性的能力，技術上的自主智慧，才能真正轉化為 商業上持續、可衡量的生產力 ～ 基於這一判斷，極智嘉提出的《24/7自主智慧倉計劃》則將全倉自主化作為下一階段的戰略方向，分三步推進： 打通全流程： 讓具身智慧接手複雜操作，補齊倉儲作業中長期依賴人工的環節。 強化智慧閉環： 讓AI從發現問題走向自主決策、動態調整，推動整座倉庫越幹越聰明。 規模化落地： 憑藉全球交付與本地化運營能力，讓自主智慧倉真正走進更多商業場景。 而這三個方向，恰好對應著物理AI規模化落地必須跨過的三道坎—— 機器人能不能獨立完成複雜作業、整座倉庫能不能自主決策、這套模式能不能大規模複製。 這套龐大的系統性能力，事實上如今也早已在這家公司多年的技術積累與商業化實踐中，長出了真實立體的形狀。 機器人長手腳，AI接管大腦，無人倉開始自主進化 具身智慧解決方案，讓機器人幹真活 要讓一個倉庫真正自主運轉，那就首先要解決一個基礎的問題—— 機器人能否打通端到端的物理作業鏈路，讓自動化從單點突破走向全流程貫通。 單個機器人能幹多少活，決定的是單一作業效率上限；整條作業鏈能否自主閉環，決定的才是無人倉的落地深度。 相比聚焦單機或特定任務的具身智慧方案，深耕具身十餘年的極智嘉，在真實落地的能力上顯然有更深的家底。 其自研的Gravity統一具身智慧框架與Gravity 4D具身世界模型，瞄準的正是機器人在複雜環境中的自主操作難題： 前者讓機器人理解任務、規劃動作，學會先想清楚再動手，後者則讓其理解物理空間的幾何關係、受力與接觸變化。 兩者結合，讓機器人在面對複雜任務和突發變化時，有了更多自主應對的能力： 跨任務泛化： 面對不同材質、形狀的陌生物品，不用逐個訓練，也能判斷怎麼抓。 動態抗干擾： 物品突然移動、被遮擋，也能及時調整動作，繼續完成任務。 長程任務執行： 面對多步驟複雜任務，能夠自主拆解、規劃並逐步完成。 自然語言糾偏： 動作出現偏差，不用重新程式設計，通過語言指令就能調整策略。 此外，基於多模態感知、長程任務推理、4D物理建模與動作規劃等能力，機器人如今也開始走進了真實倉儲作業。 比如其通用人形機器人 Gino 1 ，既能揀貨、搬箱，還能與移動機器人協同，完成連續的揀選任務： 另一邊，極智嘉的 無人揀選工作站 ，也開始接手過去高度依賴人工的揀播環節。 在施耐德電氣上海物流中心的試點中，這套方案的揀選效率達到人工的2倍，準確率超過99.99%。 在這些具身智慧產品之外，其全品類AMR方案也覆蓋料箱、托盤、貨架等不同儲存形式下的大量標準化作業。 這些年積累的端到端技術能力，也恰好為其進一步實現整倉自主執行創造了有利條件。 AI接管排程運營，倉庫越幹越聰明 機器人能把活兒幹完，只解決了第一道難題。 更大的考驗在於，當幾百臺機器人同時開工，整座倉庫還能不能自己管好自己。 極智嘉系統平臺部副總裁 譚文哲 在媒體採訪中，也談到了這個長期困擾行業的問題—— 傳統倉儲系統往往各管一攤，排程系統最佳化機器人路徑，業務系統最佳化訂單執行，資料平臺負責統計報表。 看上去每個系統都有自己的最佳化目標，但實際上很難站在整座倉庫的角度統一決策！！ △AI生成 而極智嘉這次想做的，正是讓原本各自運轉的系統，真正擁有一個能夠統籌全域性的 「倉庫大腦」 。 具體而言，就是將訂單、庫存、機器人、機械臂、工作站等納入統一的執行狀態體系—— 實現從物理執行、資料感知到智慧決策的全流程閉環，進行即時、全域性的最佳化。 在倉庫大腦的底層，由 RMS、WES、IOP 三大系統支撐，分別負責機器人排程、業務執行和運營分析。 IOP負責發現問題，WES負責制定和編排策略，RMS負責排程機器人執行，三者相互協作。 而真正讓這套系統變得更聰明的，是極智嘉在此基礎上構建的全倉智慧，通過AI Agent持續強化兩項能力： 協同智慧： 讓機器人、裝置和業務流程能夠統一排程，根據即時訂單變化靈活調整任務與資源分配。 運營智慧： 讓AI即時監控全倉、自主診斷異常、最佳化策略，逐步減少人工值守。 兩者結合，就意味著AI既要管好眼前的活兒，還得不斷琢磨怎麼把活兒幹得更好。 更關鍵的是，每次調整後的運營結果還能重新反饋給系統，形成「洞察—診斷—決策—執行—學習」的完整閉環。 這樣一來，倉庫也開始從會執行指令，走向自己發現問題、調整策略，並在長期執行中越幹越聰明了～ 值得一提的是，目前極智嘉也已經圍繞這套流程佈局了三類AI Agent—— 監控Agent 負責識別異常， 資料分析Agent 負責追查原因、提出方案， 部署配置Agent 則負責參數調整與策略落地。 這些Agent甚至還結合了極智嘉過去積累的「現場運營經驗」和「效率分析框架」。 過去資深倉管人員需要反覆排查的問題，如今開始有機會轉化為AI能夠呼叫、分析和複用的知識，而且不同層面的最佳化有著不同的節奏。 在效率上，排程層面的調整甚至可以在 幾分鐘 內進行，涉及整體運營策略時，則會結合 每天 積累的資料持續最佳化。 倉庫執行得越久，積累的經驗越多，系統就有機會作出更好的決策，真·閉環了。 從技術到商業交付，全球實踐給出答案 智慧倉儲的產業化競爭，最終還得回到真實場景。 客戶真正關心的，是系統能否長期穩定執行、融入現有業務，以及投入後究竟能帶來多少收益。 而極智嘉過去十多年的商業化實踐，已經積累了不少可供觀察的樣本。 全球市場側，極智嘉連續7年位居AMR市佔率 第一 ，覆蓋40多個國家和地區、超 1000家 客戶，累計部署機器人超 8.1萬 臺。 在今年CeMAT展會上，極智嘉更是把全品類AMR和AI全倉排程串了起來，直接上演了一場整倉協同作業。 譚文哲博士在媒體採訪中，也給出了衡量倉庫「自主進化」能力的幾項硬指標。 包括自主處理異常的能力、複雜工況下的吞吐穩定性、連續執行時長，以及故障後的自主恢復效率。 這些指標背後，恰好也指向了《24/7自主智慧倉計劃》更深層的行業意義： 把資深倉管人員積累多年的隱性經驗，逐步變成倉庫裡「常駐」的智慧。 對企業來說，最頭疼的莫過於花重金建起自動化倉庫，關鍵時刻卻依然離不開人。 而一座真正具備自主運營能力的倉庫，就意味著 每一分自動化投入，都能轉化為持續、穩定的生產力。 未來，極智嘉還計劃將經過真實場景驗證的機器人、AI與系統能力，延伸到更廣泛的物理作業領域。 而在這條從技術走向真實生產力的路上，長期積累與規模化實踐的價值，已然變得越來越清晰。 版權所有，未經授權不得以任何形式轉載及使用，違者必究。 AI 夢瑤 剛剛，DeepSeek重磅開源：Agent底座架構！ 2026-10-31 你的8G iPad裡有12G記憶體！庫克走了但他的刀法追著我砍 2026-10-31 世界模型首次指導設計晶片！超大核NPU700TOPS，99%算力可用 title: 智己LS8純電版背後：8年研發底盤，兩大廠聯合開發電池
abstract: 智己LS8純電版背後：8年研發底盤，兩大廠聯合開發電池 傑西卡 2026-11-03 20:57:35 來源： 量子位 兩位CTO，關起門來吵架 “我們的電池有點貴，有時還貴不少。” 寧德時代CTO高煥，竟然親口承認了自家電池的價格問題。 最近在智己LS8 NEO純電版釋出會後的媒體群訪中，談起寧德時代電池為什麼貴，高煥非常坦誠地回答了這個問題。 不過，貴歸貴，車企提起要求來，可是一點也不客氣。 坐在他身邊的智己汽車CTO項嬌，就是一個典型例子。 高煥透露，兩人相識多年，為了產品效能和技術規格，有時甚至會關起門來吵一吵。 比如，智己希望將93度電池的容量提升到103度，重量卻不能增加；還要求超快充效能更好，但又不能過多佔用整車熱管理資源。 這意味著，寧德時代不僅要提高能量密度，還要進一步降低電池內阻，有些指標甚至需要再降低10%—20%。 容量、重量、充電速度、安全性、壽命，每一項都要兼顧。 而為了滿足這些要求，雙方的研發團隊不得不反覆磨合。 不過，談到最終的技術路線，兩位CTO的態度卻高度一致： 專業的事，交給專業的人做。 這句話放在當下的新能源汽車行業，倒是別有一番意味。 過去幾年，越來越多車企宣佈自研動力電池，希望將這項核心技術掌握在自己手中。 智己卻選擇繼續深化與寧德時代的合作，甚至將全系搭載寧德時代電池，作為LS8 NEO純電版的重要賣點。 在這場群訪中，兩位CTO也把這條路線背後的技術考量，講得更加具體。 兩位CTO，關起門來吵架 一塊電池，要造到什麼程度才算好？ 站在電池廠和整車廠的角度，答案未必完全一致。 對於寧德時代來說，電池必須在能量密度、充放電效能、安全性和壽命之間取得平衡，還要兼顧生產成本和大規模製造的一致性。 而智己作為整車廠，需要考慮的問題更加具體：電池裝在車上佔多大空間、增加多少重量、留給其他部件多少熱管理能力，以及最終能讓使用者獲得多少續航。 雙方的研發分歧，恰恰出現在這些具體指標上。 高煥舉了一個例子。智己希望電池容量進一步提升，提出了103度電池維持93度電池重量的研發要求。 看起來只是多了10度電，但要在重量基本不變的情況下提升容量，就必須進一步提高電池系統的能量密度。 對一臺大型純電SUV而言，這項要求尤其重要。 智己LS8 NEO純電版車長超過5米，還搭載了大量舒適性配置、智慧駕駛硬體和全線控底盤系統。電池容量增加固然可以提升續航，但如果整車重量隨之大幅增加，又會影響能耗、操控和底盤表現。 因而，在有限的重量空間裡爭取更多電量，成為雙方需要共同解決的問題。 另一個難點，則是超快充。 高煥透露，智己希望進一步提升充電效能，卻又不能把整車製冷能力全部分配給動力電池。 這就對電池本身的熱管理能力提出了更苛刻的要求。 一項重要的最佳化方向是降低內阻。 按照高煥的說法，雙方討論過程中，智己曾要求在原有基礎上將內阻進一步降低10%—20%，以減少充放電過程中的發熱。 高煥對此的總結是，雙方其實一直在效能、安全、壽命、能量密度、環境適應性和成本之間反覆尋找平衡。 這樣的聯合研發，最終也體現在LS8 NEO純電版搭載的兩套電池方案中。 其中一套是93度黃金高效電池，採用磷酸鐵鋰體系。 磷酸鐵鋰電池在成本、安全性等方面具有自身優勢，但低溫環境下的效能表現、剩餘電量估算等問題，一直是使用者關注的重點。 這一次，雙方將研發重點放在了電池管理系統與整車控制的協同上。 高煥透露，在低溫場景下，團隊對SOC估算演算法進行了最佳化。 按照其介紹，行業相關估算誤差水平通常約為5%—8%，而智己與寧德時代聯合開發的這套方案，有信心將誤差控制在2%—3%。 換句話說，改善的並不只是儀表盤上的一個數字。 尤其是在冬季、低電量等場景下，電池SOC估算越準確，車輛剩餘續航的顯示也就越有參考價值，能夠降低電量預估不準帶來的使用風險。 此外，兩家企業還對充放電演算法、能量回收和熱管理進行了協同最佳化。 高煥介紹，經過最佳化之後，電池功率輸出能夠更加平滑，減少過去臺階式的功率變化；車輛加減速過程中的能量回收能力，也得到進一步改善。 這些變化涉及電池與整車控制策略之間的配合，很難單靠更換電芯來完成。 一套是103度單晶超能電池。 這套方案更加註重能量密度與整車重量之間的平衡。 高煥特別提到，LS8 NEO純電版搭載了豐富的座艙和舒適性配置，這些都會增加整車重量。 因此，電池系統必須在提供更高容量的同時，儘可能控制重量，讓底盤效能得到更好的發揮。 一套側重成本、效率和日常使用體驗，一套進一步提升能量密度，兩種方案背後都有整車與電池共同開發的考慮。 而在高煥看來，雙方的合作也不能只關注效能指標。 電池的可靠性和長期壽命，同樣需要經過大量驗證。 項嬌提到，雙方曾針對電池進行累計25萬公里的道路試驗，涉及川藏線、漠河等不同環境。按照其披露的測試結果，相關電池經過拆解檢查後，容量保持率仍達到90%。 高煥進一步表示，即便完成了這類嚴苛測試，團隊仍在繼續開展後續驗證。 對於整車廠來說，電池供應商能夠提供什麼樣的產品是一回事，能否根據具體車型持續最佳化，又是另一回事。 兩位CTO之間的爭論，也就有了更實際的意義。 寧德時代，為什麼敢賣得貴？ 談及價格，高煥並沒有迴避寧德時代產品的成本問題。 他給出的解釋，首先是研發投入。 過去多年累計研發投入超過1000億元，擁有6萬多件專利。 這是高煥在群訪中披露的兩組數字。 在他看來，這些投入背後，是動力電池技術仍然存在大量需要突破的工程問題。 雖然近幾年，動力電池能量密度的提升不像早期那樣迅猛，但電池技術遠沒有到成熟期或平臺期。 尤其是安全性、可靠性、壽命，以及不同環境下的效能表現，仍然需要持續投入。 高煥強調，動力電池是汽車上的重要安全部件，研發過程中必須始終保持敬畏。 這與汽車本身的使用週期有關。 手機等消費電子產品可能幾年就會更換，但一輛汽車的使用年限往往達到8年、10年，甚至更長。 動力電池不僅需要在車輛交付時表現良好，還需要經歷長期充放電、高低溫變化，以及不同道路工況帶來的考驗。 而這些要求，不可能只通過一次實驗室測試來驗證。 作為全球動力電池頭部供應商，寧德時代擁有龐大的裝車規模。其電池累計搭載車輛約3000萬輛，電芯累計出貨超過10億顆。 大規模裝車帶來了持續積累的產品執行資料，也對製造一致性提出了更高要求。 畢竟，單顆電芯達到效能標準，與數以億計的電芯在大規模生產中保持一致，是兩件不同的事情。 項嬌也提到了寧德時代的PPB級質量控制標準，即以十億為單位衡量缺陷水平。 對動力電池而言，規模化製造能力不僅影響成本，也直接關係到產品質量能否長期保持穩定。 高煥認為，寧德時代的技術投入和質量要求，正是其產品定價較高的重要原因。 不過，面對車企越來越強的成本控制訴求，僅僅強調自身研發投入，顯然還不夠。 一家整車廠是否願意支付更高的採購成本，最終仍然取決於電池能夠為整車帶來多少價值。 尤其在新能源汽車市場價格競爭持續加劇的背景下，動力電池是整車成本中最重要的部分之一。 按照高煥的說法，動力電池約佔整車成本的30%—40%。 對於主流價格區間的車型來說，電池成本的變化，會直接影響整車定價和盈利空間。 因此，電池廠的技術優勢必須轉化為具體的整車表現，才有可能獲得車企和消費者的認可。 智己此次聯合寧德時代推出93度、103度兩套電池方案，就是這種合作思路的體現。 一方面依靠寧德時代的電芯研發和製造能力，另一方面通過整車熱管理、軟體演算法、底盤協同等技術，進一步發揮電池系統的效能。 電池的價值，也逐漸超出單純的容量和採購價格。 車企自研成風，智己為何堅持寧德時代？ 值得注意的是，智己對動力電池的選擇，與部分車企正在推進的技術路線存在明顯差異。 近幾年，圍繞動力電池這一核心部件，車企不斷增加研發投入。 有的選擇研發自有電芯，有的深入參與電池包和管理系統開發，還有企業通過投資、合資等方式強化對動力電池供應鏈的掌控。 背後既有技術自主可控的考慮，也涉及成本、產品差異化以及供應鏈話語權。 面對相同的行業變化，智己給出的答案是繼續與寧德時代深化合作。 項嬌明確表示：“讓專業的人做專業的事。” 按照他的解釋，智己更看重最終交付給使用者的產品體驗，而不是單純追求某項技術由哪家公司獨立完成。 事實上，上汽與寧德時代的合作也並非最近才建立。 早在2017年，雙方就通過合資方式建立了上汽時代、時代上汽兩家企業，合作涉及電芯和電池包等環節。 經過多年發展，雙方的合作範圍逐漸深入到產品定義和技術研發。 項嬌認為，電池本身的效能只是基礎，要將一塊好電池真正用好，還需要整車整合、全域熱管理等能力配合。 高煥也透露，雙方會分享不同層面的技術資訊。 智己將整車使用經驗、使用者場景等資訊提供給寧德時代，寧德時代則向智己開放相關製程資料與底層技術資訊，以便雙方開展更加深入的協同開發。 這意味著，電池供應商不再只是按照整車廠給出的規格生產產品。 車企同樣需要參與到電池的效能定義和演算法最佳化過程中，甚至對具體工程指標提出新的要求。 雙方的技術邊界正在變得更加緊密。 不過，智己並非所有核心技術都選擇外部合作。 一個頗有意思的對照是，智己在動力電池上堅持聯合研發，卻線上控底盤領域走上了自主研發的路線。 項嬌介紹，上汽從2018年就投入線控轉向技術研究，歷時8年，累計試驗項超過1萬項。 其目的之一，就是將底盤關鍵技術掌握在自己手中。 與傳統底盤相比，全線控底盤需要更深度地協調轉向、制動、驅動等系統。 而通過自研底層技術，智己能夠對這些系統進行更加充分的協同控制，也能減少對外部封閉技術方案的依賴。 如今，這項技術已經逐漸進入智己旗下多款車型。 在LS8 NEO純電版上，全線控底盤實現全系標配，配合後輪轉向等技術，讓一輛車長超過5米的大型SUV，實現了4.85米的轉彎半徑。 在安全方面，項嬌還提到，團隊針對爆胎、複雜附著係數路面等場景進行了大量測試，通過三重冗餘和整車協同控制提高車輛穩定性。 當然，先進底盤技術能否下放到主流價格區間，還需要解決成本問題。 項嬌對此給出的解釋是，上汽通過自主研發掌握底層技術，結合集團供應鏈和規模化製造能力，逐漸實現成本可控。 這也解釋了智己為什麼能夠將全線控底盤作為全系標配，而不是隻提供給價格更高的車型。 兩條研發路線放在一起，智己對核心技術的選擇也就更加清楚了。 對於需要整車深度協同、決定車輛操控和安全表現的底盤技術，智己投入多年自主研發。 而在研發投入巨大、規模化製造要求極高的動力電池領域，則選擇利用頭部供應商的技術積累，同時保留整車層面的研發與整合能力。 不同技術領域，選擇不同的資源投入方式。 事實上，隨著新能源汽車技術不斷深入，整車廠與核心供應商之間的關係也越來越複雜。 電池企業需要理解更多整車執行場景，整車廠則需要進一步深入電芯特性、熱管理和電池控制演算法。 過去相對明確的採購與供貨關係，正在延伸為更加緊密的聯合研發關係。 這樣的合作也有其現實考驗。 技術協同的程度、雙方對關鍵研發成果的掌握，以及供應鏈成本能否持續最佳化，都會影響最終產品的競爭力。 對於智己來說，與寧德時代持續合作，並不意味著可以省去核心技術研發的工作。 恰恰相反，整車廠必須足夠了解電池，才能提出更加具體、也更加苛刻的技術要求。 就像高煥所講的，兩位CTO為了一個性能指標，有時還會關起門來爭論。 電池可以由專業廠商來造，但如何讓它在一輛具體的汽車上發揮出更好的效能，依然需要整車廠給出自己的答案。 版權所有，未經授權不得以任何形式轉載及使用，違者必究。 智己汽車 傑西卡 買車送終身AI？智己LS8純電版25萬起！全系線控底盤寧德時代標配 2026-10-30 24萬開賣！理想重造i6，李想：目標全球暢銷 2026-10-29 0營收估值200億美元，具身版OpenAI又融10億美元
