abstract: I discovered a sound that leaks your exact location (and it’s everywhere)—YouTube ( via ) Genius piece of OSINT by Colsto, who demonstrates how you can take almost imperceptible background noise of planes from a video soundtrack, figure out their Doppler curves, then cross reference them against ADS-B data to find the exact location of the video based on their speed, distance, and gaps between different flights. # 3rd November 2026 , 5:32 am / privacy , youtube How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts ( via ) Parameter Labs describe an exploit they found against ChatGPT's implementation of the artifacts pattern (OpenAI used to call this "Canvas" but it looks like the latest revision is called HTML previews ), where interactive custom HTML apps are displayed in a sandboxed iframe. It's important that HTML in these stays tightly sandboxed to avoid untrusted code interacting with OpenAI APIs and accessing private data. Parameter found quite a complex attack chain. OpenAI use the MathLive JavaScript library as part of their graph support, and that library includes its own virtual keyboard , which can be triggered in the parent page via postMessage() from the sandboxed iframe. That message receiving code uses innerHTML , so anything that sends a message can add custom HTML to the parent - and there was no mechanism to prevent other sandboxed frames, including HTML preview frames, from calling that method. This meant untrusted code in an iframe could insert HTML, and while innerHTML doesn't directly execute script elements it could be used to inject a new iframe without sandbox restrictions. OpenAI’s CSP rules blocked inline scripts entirely, and only allowed script loading from a handful of domains, but one of those was YouTube - and the YouTube oEmbed endpoint could be used to reflect JavaScript back in a way that executed it. Once the attack had JavaScript execution on ChatGPT, it was trivial to fetch private user data from APIs and exfiltrate it via an image reference. The end result: you could create a ChatGPT share URL which, when visited by another signed-in user, could exfiltrate their private data or take actions on their behalf. OpenAI closed the hole and paid out a $5,000 bug bounty, which I think was a bit cheap for a vulnerability this serious. # 31st October 2026 , 11:15 pm / iframes , javascript , sandboxing , security , xss , openai , chatgpt , content-security-policy dbreunig/nesformer ( via ) Inspired by qwenputer by Divyansh Agrawal, Drew Breunig baked a working emulator for a Nintendo Entertainment System 6502 CPU into the weights of Qwen3.5-4B. You can now play NES ROMs such as Super Mario Bros (very slowly) running inside Qwen! In a comment on Hacker News Drew reveals the Opus 5.5 prompts he used to build this system: Read this article and any relevant source code: https://divagr.com/blog/qwenputer. Then explore if you could emulate the chip and ram in a Nintendo Entertainment System (as people do today with FPGAs in MISTRs) using this technique. If so, what size model would you have to build and if you could use smaller faster ones, could you get it to be at the standard clockspeed. I think we should build it! Just for fun. It's okay if it's not fast. We want to be able to have the weights, and a cli to run them that we can point at a ROM. Apparently Opus found and then used this collection of conformance tests for the NES CPU released 15 years ago by Christopher Pow. # 30th October 2026 , 9:59 pm / games , ai , generative-ai , llms , drew-breunig , qwen , conformance-suites API credits benefit for eligible ChatGPT subscriptions . Earlier this month Anthropic announced a generous new benefit for their Max and Team subscriptions: $100, $200, and $500 per month subscribers would get the equivalent quantity of (expiring) credits to use with the Anthropic API. OpenAI have now launched pretty much exactly the same deal: if you have a $100, $200, or $500 subscription plan with them you now get that same quantity of credits to apply to one of your API organizations. I maintain subscriptions with both companies, so this is great news for me! I may even ship some public-facing demos now that the credits are already covered by my existing subscriptions. # 29th October 2026 , 10:48 pm / ai , openai , generative-ai , llms , anthropic , llm-pricing How I Built the Most AI-Pilled Company in the World . Don't be put off by the clickbait headline, this piece by Jacob Sansbury describing how they are building Spawn is a fascinating exploration of the bleeding edge of what's possible with agentic engineering against frontier models. Spawn is a massively multiplayer gaming environment where players can use prompts (to the in-game agent, Savi) to modify the game world. I fired it up on my phone for a few minutes and was able to prompt a castle into existence, then a dragon, then ride the dragon to fly around that castle. By Jacob's telling, Spawn is now being developed autonomously by a swarm of Fable-powered agents costing over $3 million in tokens per month ("we spend 30x payroll on AI tokens"). Our agents change the live code directly and ship to production hourly, so they read every error, bug report and metric themselves. About 60% of our work starts from a production error, a Savi bug report (Savi is the AI you build games with in Spawn), something odd in our logs, or a feature request. Savi files bugs herself. When a user hits one, or Savi hits one in the product, she files it. It goes straight to an agent that decides whether it's a real bug to fix, something we won't fix, or intentional design that needs a decision. Usually it becomes a change, delivered to that user within an hour, with a message in the same chat. This is continuous deployment turned up to 11: A loop this tight only works if it never stops, so we treat an hour without a ship as a SEV-0, our most severe kind of incident. Unshipped changes pile up, and every problem already in production lasts longer. The feedback slows down too. An agent can only keep a few hours of work in its head, so shipping faster than that actually helps it stay coherent. [...] We can roll back a broken change in 30 seconds, exactly where it's broken and nowhere else. When a monitor or a log alert fires, it starts or wakes an agent that owns the incident, and we break things on purpose to test that those recovery paths work. My eyebrows raised at least a dozen times reading this. I have trouble imagining this style of development working on software with higher stakes for when something goes wrong, but for a game this appears to be working surprisingly well. Jacob says that Fable 5 (and then 5.1) was the model that made this level of autonomy possible. Opus 5.5 doesn't quite hack it for them, and when they tried GPT-6 Astra to apply fixes from a security review everything stopped working: Every feature had been disabled and marked to be turned on again once the security fixes were done. Astra had gone through our whole product and made the insecure things secure by turning them off. These kinds of extreme experiments are why I'm excited about game development as a substrate for exploring the edges of what today's coding agents can do. # 29th October 2026 , 5 pm / game-design , ai , generative-ai , llms , claude , coding-agents , agentic-engineering , claude-mythos-fable GitHub Octoverse 2026 . I'm at GitHub Universe today (GitHub gave me a free ticket through their "GitHub Stars" program). EVP Jay Parikh just announced this year's Octoverse report, and highlighted these numbers in particular: This is a pretty stark representation of the impact of agentic engineering on GitHub. In 2026, merged pull requests tripled in less than a year to 220 million per month. Commits more than tripled to 7.38 billion per month, with most of that increase in the second half of this year. New repository rate doubled this year, to 30.3 million per month.

The OpenAI Codex desktop app (since rebranded to just ChatGPT) has 1.7GB of stuff in there in a folder called codex-primary-runtime , including a full Python installation, a full Node.js installation, and native binaries for Poppler , git, and the LibreOffice open source office suite (which forked from OpenOffice.org in 2010): The ~/.cache/codex-runtimes/codex-primary-runtime/plugins/openai-primary-runtime/plugins/documents folder includes skills which tell Codex how to find and use those binaries. # 1st September 2026 , 7:03 pm / codex , generative-ai , openai , ai , llms , openoffice , open-source The key skill required to make productive use of coding agents is being able to confidently instruct them on how to make changes and then confidently verify that those changes have been applied in the correct way. Sometimes this involves reviewing every line of code they have written, but there are other ways to achieve that goal. Eyeballing every line of code has never been the most effective way to validate a change to a piece of software. # 22nd August 2026 , 3:56 pm / code-review , coding-agents , generative-ai , agentic-engineering , ai , llms I started building my markdown-svg-renderer tool in May , but I've since added enough features to it that it's worth talking about here again. It's evolved into my ideal tool for sharing Markdown transcripts that include SVG documents. Given my proclivity for drawing pelicans riding bicycles this is a problem that I needed to solve! The tool is very simple. Navigate to markdown-svg-renderer in your browser and paste in some Markdown to see it rendered... or save that Markdown to a CORS-friendly URL or a GitHub Gist and paste in a URL to that document. The URL option will give you a bookmarkable page, for example https://tools.simonwillison.net/markdown-svg-renderer#url=https%3A%2F%2Fgist.github.com%2Fsimonw%2F6f9e48293be5c916652d29f0dc0b0657 - which bakes in the URL to this Gist . If you visit the Gist you'll see raw SVG: In the rendered tool that looks like this instead: As you can see, that SVG block in the Markdown has been transformed into a rendered SVG (in this case animated) plus several tabs. The tabs are the really fun bit. The PNG and JPEG tabs render that SVG to those image formats in the browser and lets you copy or download them - useful for sharing on platforms that don't support SVG directly. The MP4 tab is new today - it examines the SVG to see if it contains any animations, attempts to guess how long the looped video should be, then renders a whole bunch of frames of the animation and loads 30+MB of ffmpeg.wasm so it can compile those frames into an MP4 video using the full power of FFMPEG compiled to WebAssembly and running in the browser. Being able to turn an animated SVG into a MP4 again makes it easy to share on platforms that can't support SVG animation natively. It's a neat trick! # 16th August 2026 , 11:59 pm / svg , markdown , tools I wrote this summary of the past few weeks of open letters as a section of my sponsors-only newsletter but I've decided to share it here as well. Open Weights and American AI Leadership was shepherded by Microsoft, dated July 24th, and signed by 235 AI-adjacent companies including NVIDIA (see Jensen's first ever tweet ), Amazon, Y Combinator, The Linux Foundation, and (a later signer) OpenAI. It's clearly an argument designed to counter any instincts by the current US government to ban or limit open weight models over "safety" concerns - a reasonable consideration given what happened to Claude Fable 5 !

title: Elsewhere
abstract: Release TIL Research Tool Museum Sighting Comment There's a lot of stuff in this new release of my LLM CLI tool and Python library, representing around two months of accumulated features and fixes. I added gpt-6.1-sol and gpt-6.1-terra , plus a new llm openai endpoint add command to make it easier to configure additional models that use OpenAI-compatible endpoints. I switched the default model (if you have not set your own default) to gpt-6-luna - half the price of the previous default, gpt-5.6-luna . LLM's support for embeddings now accepts that different binary content may have different content-type - necessary for models like Gemini Embedding 2 , which can embed text, audio, images, and video. A lot of open source maintainers complain about a flood of AI-assisted PRs. LLM is my project that has been most affected by this and, to be honest, I'm not finding it to be a problem. That's mainly because I have Opus 5.5 or GPT-6 Astra help me with triage to spot the most useful fixes! This release includes fixes from 12 authors - almost all AI-assisted - and the burden of reviewing them wasn't nearly as great as I expected. I really see them as bug reports with attached examples - sometimes I land them, sometimes I implement my own fix. So thanks to 0d00ciallo0721 , ac1982 , Allen Flux , Bian Yuhan , Bishop Kammeraad , Chen Yufeiyang , Christopher Krah , Ethan Stoner , Jiachen Xie , Olamide Faniyan , Sharat Chandra Sai Boddu , nosmile99 for helping out with (or spending tokens on) this release! I have some big upgrades to Datasette Agent in the pipeline, but in the meantime here's a tiny user experience improvement to the underlying datasette-llm plugin. It now picks up the default model used by LLM , which means you can start using Datasette Agent without needing to explicitly configure a default model: Previously you would also need to specify a model with -s plugins.datasette-agent.default_model gpt-6-astra . webframe is a neat little project from Jeff Lindsay which lets you "run a web page like a program" - you point it at a URL or file and it executes it in a hidden headless web view and outputs console.log() to standard output and any exceptions to standard error. It's written in Go on top of the glaze library, which provides access to a system browser ("WKWebView on macOS, WebKitGTK on Linux, WebView2 on Windows") so it doesn't need to bundle its own browser engine. It reminds me of my own shot-scraper javascript tool, albeit in a much smaller package that doesn't depend on Playwright. I had Claude Opus 5.5 put it through its paces and prepare a research report for me. Here's the prompt I used: Explore https://github.com/tractordev/webframe try running it and put it though its paces, build a few exploratory prototypes, then evaluate it as a potential sandboxing tool and as a tool for scraping web pages using the same patterns encouraged by the "shot-scraper JavaScript" command (see simonw/shot-scraper on GitHub, docs directory) I built this weird and very specific cropping tool - it lets you create a horizontal or vertical cut across an image, then slide the two sides relative to each other. Effectively it lets you crop out a section in the middle of an image. I wanted this because I often use Tailor on my iPhone to stitch several screenshots together into lot long image, but sometimes I find myself wanting to crop out a section in the middle - to redact an irrelevant prompt from a transcript, for example. I added four player online mode to Battledrones - previous maps were limited to two. Here's the initial prompt I used: Add a new map for a four player battle - four way rotational symmetry, up to four AI players, works with the WebSocket non-audio based multiplayer mode so up to four human players can join (any spare slots use AI) Claude Opus 5.5 added a new map called "Compass Rose" and modified the WebSockets multiplayer network code to support up to four players for that map, joining via share links or QR codes. The new teams use robots themed in purple and green, joining the existing blue and red designs. You can preview those colors in the updated model browser . Here's a replay link to watch a four way AI battle with the "Goliath Armada" mutator turned on, where each side starts with four giant Goliath mech units. Prompt to Claude Opus 5.5 High : Build an artifact where you open a photo and it rapidly (in a few seconds) paints a version of that photo using a canvas element and simulated paintbrush See also my previous experiment getting Claude Fable to simulate a watercolor illustration with P5.js. Quick Study uses Sobel edge detection , with no external libraries beyond Google Fonts. When I switched LLM over to httpx2 in LLM 0.33 I forget that this would break any plugins which used httpx without directly depending on it. llm-tools-datasette was one of those plugins, now fixed. I'm working towards a new LLM release, and testing PRs caused me to revisit the llm-echo debug plugin. This plugin provides a "model" which doesn't involve an LLM at all - it just repeats back the prompts that have been fed to it. The new release now updates the simulated token usage counts to take tool calls, system prompts, and reasoning tokens into account. web-edit ( previously ) is my tiny web app for browsing and editing files in a folder. I mainly built it for editing files on different machines via Tailscale. I added a "copy to clipboard" option for both text and image data. I needed this because I was running pelican prompts on a laptop from my phone (here's DeepSeek 4.1 Flash 1017 ) and I wanted an easy way to copy the resulting logs into a Gist. This research task is really an experiment in running Claude Code for web in "Ultracode" mode, as described in Orchestrate subagents at scale with dynamic workflows in the Claude Code documentation. With Ultracode turned on, Claude Code makes aggressive use of dynamic workflows - it generates JavaScript that defines and coordinates a network of subagents to take on complex problems. My initial prompt was this - I meant "hit the rows directly", the word "delete" was an accidental typo on my phone: Write a SQLite extension in Rust that implants SPARQL and runs really fast because it can hit the delete rows directly This caused Claude Code for web to churn for over 12 hours. I checked in on its progress the next day and sent a single follow-up prompt when I noticed how many Rust crates it had built: Every folder in the crates/ directory needs a README Include a tutorial.md teaching users how to install the extension and how to run it in the SQLite CLI and then teaching them SPARQL in addition to how to use the SQLite extension Include a script with the tutorial for populating a SQLite database with useful and realistic example data for that tutorial This project feels like next-level vibe coding - it's not remotely feasible to review the code that was produced here, and even following the documentation is a significant investment in work. I'm not entirely sure what to do with this - I appear to have a full SPARQL implementation in Rust inside SQLite now, but how valuable is that if I created it on a whim and can't (or won't) invest the necessary time to understand what it can do? Another game experiment - I wanted to see if it was feasible to have a two player game on two separate phones running in static HTML where the networking code uses chirps sent via the microphone. It seems to work! Build a two player competitive pong like game where two players use their phones close to each other and the game state is sent via audio noises which the web microphone API can interpret - but add graphical and gameplay twists to make it a lot more fun and intertwine than pong Claude Opus 5.5 Extra in Claude Code .

title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
abstract: Yesterday’s hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a “blog post”, but it’s paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model—literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I’ve been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I’m delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well! Here’s the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights: Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do . And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights . With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x. All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming . The paper combines two topics that I think deserve to be treated separately. The first is what models can do with raw weights without running tools or executing code. The second explores how well models, once armed with code, can run operations to update and improve other models. spaCy author Matthew Honnibal called the paper misleading for conflating the two, and Sean Goedecke deconstructed the Qwen3.5-0.8B update example as taking the same steps that a human ML researcher would use. I’m going to focus on the no-tools question, which I think is the more interesting of the two. The paper presents the first question as Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights? They trained four neural networks to play simplified 10x10 grid versions of four classic computer games—Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Freeway (I had to look that one up , it’s an Atari 2600 game from 1981). Then they fed those weights (as floating point numbers) to an LLM along with the following question: The weights below belong to one policy network that was trained with reinforcement learning to play a game on this grid. Which game was it trained on? Work from the weights. You have no tools: no code execution, no calculator, nothing to run. This is a single response. The GitHub repository that accompanies the paper is RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs . The exp1_which_game folder contains the prompts they used, with weights for the four games: I checked and, aside from the weights, each prompt is identical to the others. The prompts on GitHub are self-contained. My LLM tool has a -f/--fragment option which can be passed the URL to a text file to use as a prompt, which means I can run any of the above like this: This example requires the llm-openrouter plugin installed, and runs the Breakout prompt against Kimi K3.1 Pro via OpenRouter. Here’s what I got back from Kimi K3.1 Pro , which successfully guessed Breakout after 9m 41s and 19,493 reasoning tokens. But how about Qwen 3.8 27B ? That’s still my favorite model to run on my own laptop—it’s just 17GB (I use this version ) and somehow feels close to the leading proprietary models of 2025. I fired up LM Studio , ensured Qwen 3.8 27B was loaded with a long context window (the default 8192 context failed with errors), installed the llm-lmstudio plugin and ran this command: (I had to bump the timeout up using an environment variable, see this issue .) After 46m 12s and 43,506 reasoning tokens, Qwen on my laptop returned a response that ended like this (here’s the reasoning trace ): Game: A simplified Pac-Man-style gridworld: an agent moves through a fixed 8x8 maze with central and corner wall blocks, moving objects/ghosts, and reward targets/pellets. Description: The agent navigates a fixed maze-like 8x8 board, using current agent/moving-object/previous-frame cues to move through corridors, collect reward-target cells, and avoid moving objects or hazards. This is impressive. I tried it on two of the other games as well. It identified Pong ( reasoning ) in 1h 4m 54s: Pong — specifically a Pong-like paddle/ball game where the agent controls a vertical paddle on the right side and must move up/down to intercept or return a moving ball/reward object. The agent moves a right-side paddle vertically to hit or catch a moving ball-like reward target moving across the 8×8 field, while a left-side moving object/opponent and wall borders define the play; reward is obtained by successfully intercepting/returning/scoring the ball, and missing or failing to hit it is penalized. And Breakout ( reasoning ) in 52m 25s: Game: Breakout, or an Arkanoid-like paddle/ball/brick game. Description: The agent is a paddle on the bottom row and moves left/right to keep a ball in play; the ball moves around the upper grid, and bricks/reward targets in the top rows give reward when hit, while missing the ball/hitting the bottom wall ends the episode or gives penalty. Qwen failed at the Freeway prompt, which didn’t surprise me considering that game is more obscure than the other three. Here’s that transcript —Qwen thought it was “A simplified Pac-Man-like grid game: agent moves 4-directionally”. The reasoning traces are fun to skim, and almost incomprehensible. Here’s a sample: What about agent channel0? We see some large channel0 rows near row8 col7/8 and maybe bottom? Let’s list channel0 large: line436 input435 (row8 col7 ch0) -2.107,1.169,0.513...; line441 input440 (row8 col8 ch0) -0.376,0.010,1.564,3.855...; line445 input444 (row8 col8 ch4) 0.142,0.491...; line382? input381 ch0? Wait line382 input381: 381//5=76 (row7 col6), ch1? 381%5=1? 76 * 5=380, ch1. So not. Channel0 large maybe at row8 col7/8 only. Also top row? line44 input43 ch3, line49 ch3. Channel0 large maybe not many. Agent position could be near bottom-right? If the agent is typically at bottom-right? That said though, I expect a sufficiently experienced human being armed with a notepad and a pencil could get there with enough effort. It’s a cool paper, but some of the wider commentary I’ve seen around it does not feel justified. I’m not ready to declare that the age of source code is over and our future involves incomprehensible machines editing their own model weights in incomprehensible ways. This is Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too by Simon Willison, posted on 3rd November 2026 . title: [AINews] LLMs can read & write neural network weights: "Weight Space Programming" cuts Autoresearch out of the RSI loop
abstract: Amid a deepening bear market for AI/tech (worthy of dark humor ) with Anthropic bonds receiving a “junk” rating and OpenAI fundraise headlines , we continue to see very surprising capability finds in the community, such as today. The best way to put today’s blockbuster paper in context is to recall Karpathy’s autoresearch from a mere 8 months ago , which presaged a summer of recursive self improvement fears : Abstractly, the demonstration is that you can take a sufficiently smart model and through running a series of experiments across a compute cluster, train a model autonomously without human expertise or intervention. However, this is usually done by an involved process of writing PyTorch/Jax code and running compute and watching loss curves and reading evals and optimizing kernels and data and…. Well, last month’s guest Alex Zhang comes back to coauthor a MONSTER discovery: what if you just ask a smart model to directly read and edit the weights of a dumber model? In ML this is the equivalent of not looking at source code, just directly seeing the 1’s and 0’s of ( very small ) compiled executables, and being able to 1) tell what they do , 2) oneshot-fix bugs given failed traces or, with 50 steps, improve in a general direction ( possible overstatement here ), 3) writing entire network weights from scratch in one shot , beating some independently trained models. If you believe that LLMs can truly fit and simulate everything given enough parameters (and in fact, LLMs are increasingly better calculators as you grow in size), then something like this was in theory bound to happen, but it is surprising nevertheless to have the ability suddenly emerge, as an independent reproduction seems to already have found: Of course the exact thing we are really modeling is some variant of mechanistic interpretability (which could be done by hand ), and right now unlikely to scale to more advanced tasks than simple games and RL policies, but the world has now gone from 0 to 1 on this very new RSI capability…. which will immediately put to use and explored due to its remarkable efficiency. AI News for 10/31/2026-11/02/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! DeepSeek Open-Sources a "Super-agent" Harness Prototype Release : DeepSeek Harness published a long design article ( article ) and the dsh-superagent-prototype repo ( repo link ). An official English version followed ( @tianyi ). Architecture : One long-lived router session talks to humans and hands out work. Isolated workers run tasks in parallel, triggered by GitHub events ( summary ). Claimed results : In DeepSeek's own test, p95 completion time fell from 29.5 to 15.7 min versus a single session using subagents ( summary ). Design rationale from a reviewer : Final reviewer 崔添翼 (@tianyi) says "Super" means a layer above the working agent, not superior intelligence. He frames the core trade-off as cross-task continuity versus throughput ( Zhihu summary ). Stated limits : The harness has no built-in cross-session long-term memory yet. Separating state, compute and environment is mostly unimplemented. The prototype has only been validated in a small, trusted internal environment, and security, privacy and agent-to-agent communication remain open questions. Prior art : He acknowledges that other teams explored similar architectures months earlier. Practitioner reception : @badlogicgames says the design matches where Earendil is heading: a single long-lived entity, ad-hoc recursive delegation and cross-system event triggers. @omarsar0 calls it a "masterclass" in coordination-execution harness design. DeepSeek also says it aims to support pi and other major harnesses with each model generation ( @tianyi ). Critique : @teortaxesTex calls the write-up "something of a hot mess." He argues DeepSeek builds internal crutches around model weaknesses such as hallucination rather than making the system generally robust. He also notes Bloomberg covered a repo that had no English announcement ( post ). V4.1 naming confusion : A Renmin University FlashRSI README referenced deepseek-v4.1-pro , which prompted release speculation. Teortaxes says it is a placeholder: the real config uses v4-flash and v4-pro, and deepseek-v4.1-flash is not a valid ID ( thread , follow-up ). He also says the API fingerprints for V4.1F-1017 are unchanged ( fingerprints ). Independent Evals and Frontier Model Signals GDPx benchmark (SemiAnalysis) : The benchmark covers 206 agentic tasks across 11 economically valuable domains, including chip design, SWE, finance and biology. The best model scores only 12% ( launch ). Results : Opus 5.5 leads at 12%. Gemini 4 Carbon is close behind at 10.9% at roughly 4x lower cost ( breakdown ). Reactions : @dylan522p apologized to Google, calling Carbon "spikier" but very strong in some areas. @demishassabis welcomed the benchmark. Analysis : @eliebakouch finds that removing safeguard-affected benchmarks changes the picture. In that view Carbon stays cheap, and Sol 6.1 is cheaper still. He also suggests OpenAI has stronger bio safeguards than Anthropic ( note ). Within-family comparison : Sol 6.1 and Astra score very similarly, Carbon beats Argon across the board, and Sonnet is strong at SWE ( comparison ). Possible bug : Some Argon cybersecurity runs may be affected by an Antigravity bug ( report ). Audit concerns : One satirical post complains that GDPx is not open source and is costly to audit ( post ). Epoch Capabilities Index : DeepSeek V4.1F-1017 scores 159, equal to GPT 5.5. That is 3 points above V4.1F-0910 and 10 above V4-Pro; Astra sits roughly 10 points higher ( @teortaxesTex ). Gap to Mythos : @scaling01 notes that no Chinese model has matched Mythos Preview (~161 ECI) after about 7 months. Weighting critique : @wenhaocha1 argues the unweighted ECI exaggerates the gap; weighting coding more heavily shrinks it to about 2 months. Spikiness : Teortaxes calls 1017 extremely spiky. It scores near zero on some SWE evals and approaches the frontier only on cybersecurity and quant trading ( chart ). He also flags "reward-hacking-shaped" behavior ( post ). October release roundup (Vals) : Vals reports 15 releases and more than 500B eval tokens ( @nikilravi ). Open-weight leaders : Kimi K3.1 Pro is #1 among open-weight models, with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 close behind and stronger at cyber. New open models : Meta's Muse Spark Open (816B total, 42B active) is the most capable US open-weight model. Reflection's Beam 1.0 has 500B total parameters, 23B active and 1M context. Mistral's Le Chonk (1T total, 52B active) ranks #5 among open-weight models. Upcoming model rumors (unconfirmed) : GPT-6.2 Astra : Reportedly visible in Codex usage analytics, with a release "very soon" ( @kimmonismus , @TokenGremlin ). Mythos 5.5 : Appears in the HTML of Anthropic's site, which describes Mythos as "our most capable model class for cybersecurity and biology research" ( tip , text ). The tagline covers all Mythos models ( correction ). The mention is absent from an Oct 23 snapshot ( @AiBattle_ ). "Numbat" leak : The alleged Anthropic leak is likely fake, because parts of the weights exactly match random initialization ( @kimmonismus ). Research: Representations, Domain Data and Agent Collectives JEPA and the Platonic Representation Hypothesis : Balestriero and LeCun show that, under certain conditions, separately trained image and text JEPAs converge to essentially the same representation without paired data ( summary ). Claimed results : Their approach matches image-text alignment with 42x fewer samples than next-token prediction (21.6M vs 900M examples). A 109M text JEPA beats LLMs up to 72B on cross-modal alignment ( explainer ). Mechanism : The claimed driver is "two views of the same thing" training signals rather than scale.

against a normal resident run, and reproduced independently on an H100 at 113.00 tok/s in the same
3.32 GB. (Both figures were measured on v0.72.2, before the v0.73.0 correctness repair that cost
−4.8% at 32B. The post-repair run, on another RTX 3050 Laptop 4 GB (@umran666, #1103), reads 208.6 tok/s at 1935–1957 MHz in a 2.40 GB peak . That is 59% of its same-session GEMM ceiling
against 68%: about 14% slower per unit clock, so the raw 1.74x gain is the clock, not a speedup.
Large-layer streaming also changed the memory pattern between the two rows, so even the fraction
is not like-for-like — the record .) Opt-in ( stream_layers: true )
and still BETA — how it works · all measurements · paper · check it yourself on a free Colab T4 (caps the process to
4 GB, then asserts a streamed model is bit-identical to a normal one) Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct + NF4, LoRA, batch 1, seq 512 on an RTX 3050 Laptop 4 GB — 3.32 GB peak, 119.6 tok/s at 952 MHz (pre-repair, v0.72.2; post-#331: 208.6 tok/s at 1935 MHz in 2.40 GB, not directly comparable, @umran666, #1103). Full video (90s) Why Soup? Training LLMs is still painful. Even experienced teams spend 30-50% of their time fighting
infrastructure instead of improving models. Soup fixes that. Zero SSH. Never SSH into a broken GPU box again. One config. A simple YAML file is all you need. Auto everything. Batch size, GPU detection, quantization — handled. Works locally. Train on your own GPU with QLoRA. No cloud required. What's New v0.77.1 — a patch: soup data keeps its input, soup plan agrees with soup train , and
GRPO trains on Apple Silicon. Nothing in v0.77.0 is taken back. That release refuses
settings v0.76 warned about or ignored, so a config that loaded on v0.76 can stop loading:
coming from 0.76.x, run soup doctor --config soup.yaml first and read the v0.77.0 release notes . soup data commands no longer write over their input. Eighteen of them ( dedup , filter , convert , merge , sample , pii , toxicity and the rest) refuse an --output that is the same file as an input, under any spelling, before they read anything, and a
default output name that the input already has is refused too. Write to a new file instead. soup plan and soup apply refuse the configs soup train refuses, with the same
message, and write no plan. GRPO trains natively on Apple Silicon. task: grpo with backend: mlx runs Soup's own
MLX loop on the objective the transformers path trains, with the built-in accuracy or format reward. soup infer --backend mlx generates from MLX bases and native text LoRA
adapters without Torch. One peak-VRAM estimate for soup train 's pre-flight, soup profile and soup plan ,
calibrated on 39 measured runs ( record ). For dense
models up to about 3.5B parameters, the range it was fitted on, the pre-flight now refuses
some long-sequence, large-vocabulary runs it let through, and --allow-oom-attempt still
launches them. Outside that range (a larger or mixture-of-experts model, medium or selective checkpointing, use_liger / use_cut_ce , backend: unsloth ) a run that does
not fit gets the estimate as a warning and starts, unless its weights, the CUDA context and
the gradients and optimizer state of the parameters it trains are more than the card holds
(a 7B full fine-tune on 80 GB, Llama-3.1-70B in 4-bit on 24 GB): that run is refused there
too. LoRA runs and runs that train a subset (Spectrum, LISA, freezing) are judged on fewer
terms, and --allow-oom-attempt still launches a refused run. External programs start by an absolute path found on PATH . The current directory and
relative PATH entries are no longer searched: a tool that only lives there needs its
directory on PATH . Also new. soup ship --progress jsonl ; unknown config keys written the way another
library names them get the Soup field ( learning_rate suggests lr ); and the Docker
example below passes --yes , which a non-interactive soup train needs since v0.77.0. Older highlights live on the GitHub Releases page. Quick Start 1. Install Soup is a command-line application, so the cleanest install gives it its own
environment and puts soup on your PATH : # Light core: CLI + config + data tools, no PyTorch pipx install soup-cli
uv tool install soup-cli # same idea, if you already use uv # Add the training stack (torch, transformers, peft, trl, datasets, …) pipx install " soup-cli[train] " # Everything (train + serve + ui + data) in one shot pipx install " soup-cli[all] " # Or from GitHub (latest dev) pipx install " git+https://github.com/MakazhanAlpamys/Soup.git " Already inside a virtualenv, a Colab notebook, or a Docker image? Use pip directly, with the same names and extras: pip install soup-cli
pip install " soup-cli[train] " pip install " soup-cli[all] " pip install git+https://github.com/MakazhanAlpamys/Soup.git Use pip rather than pipx if you also want to import soup_cli from your own
code, since pipx deliberately isolates the application from everything else. The full extras table ( fast , mlx , serve , eval , ui , vision , audio , …) lives in docs/models.md . error: externally-managed-environment ? That is PEP 668 , not a Soup problem. Debian 12,
Ubuntu 23.04 and later stop pip from writing into the system Python, because apt manages those files too. pipx and uv tool sidestep it by giving Soup
its own environment, which is why they are listed first above. python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate then plain pip works just as well. Double quotes, not single. "soup-cli[train]" is the only spelling that works in every
shell — cmd.exe , PowerShell, bash and zsh. If you copied 'soup-cli[train]' from an older
tutorial and pip rejected it, that is the reason: why, and the exact error . soup init , soup data … , and the other data/inspection commands work on the light install.
Fine-tuning ( soup train ) needs the [train] extra. 2. Create a config soup init # interactive wizard soup init --template chat # or start from a template Templates: chat , code , tool-calling , medical , reasoning , vision , kto , orpo , simpo , ipo , bco , rlhf , pretrain , moe , longcontext , embedding , audio . 3. Train, test, ship soup train --config soup.yaml # LoRA, quantization, batching — all handled soup chat  --model ./output # talk to your model soup push  --model ./output --repo you/my-model

soup merge  --adapter ./output # merge LoRA into the base soup export --model ./output --format gguf --quant q4_k_m # GGUF for Ollama / llama.cpp More export targets (ONNX, TensorRT, BitNet) and deployment options live in docs/serving-and-export.md . Web UI Prefer a browser? soup ui serves a local dashboard for experiments,
training setup, live metrics, dataset exploration and model chat. pip install " soup-cli[ui] " soup ui # Opens http://127.0.0.1:7860/?token=<token> and prints the same URL Web UI documentation Configuration A complete soup.yaml : base : meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct task : sft # backend: unsloth  # 2-5x faster, pip install "soup-cli[fast]" data : train : ./data/train.jsonl format : alpaca val_split : 0.1 training : epochs : 3 lr : 2e-5 batch_size : auto lora : r : 64 alpha : 16 quantization : 4bit output : ./output config/schema.py is the single source of truth for every field.

title: blader/humanizer
abstract:
Humanizer sponsored by cfo.ai Humanizer makes AI-written text sound like a person wrote it, without changing what it says. It is built on Wikipedia's Signs of AI writing , the guide Wikipedia editors use to catch AI-generated text, and it works in Claude Code, Codex, and any other agent that supports skills. Before: I'm thrilled to announce that shared drafts are finally here! 🚀 For months, our own team was drowning in files named final_v7.docx — and we knew there had to be a better way. Now two people can edit the same doc at once, with every change appearing live for both of them. It's not just a feature; it's a whole new way to collaborate. Comments stay anchored to the exact sentence they reference, even as the text around them evolves. And the best part? It's available today on every plan, completely free. Let that sink in. After: Shared drafts are out today. For months our own team passed around files named final_v7.docx, so we built a way for two people to edit the same doc at once, with each person's changes showing up live for the other. Comments stay pinned to the sentence they're about, even when the text around them changes. It's free on every plan. In a blind test, judges preferred Humanizer's rewrite over the original AI text 16 times out of 16 ( #229 ). Humanizer edits for human readers. Getting past AI detectors is not a goal, and detectors still flag most of its output. The five strongest tells These are the most common signs of AI writing, and Humanizer rewrites any of them on sight: Not X but Y: "It's not just a feature, it's a shift." One-line closers: "Let that sink in." Sayings that sound deep: "At its core, what really matters is..." A staged run-up: "Here's the thing." "Honestly?" Arguing with no one: "I'm not saying X, but..." Humanizer checks for 26 patterns in all. Installation Once installed, the skill answers to /humanizer . Claude Code /plugin marketplace add blader/humanizer
/plugin install humanizer@humanizer The plugin answers to /humanizer:humanizer . It needs Claude Code 2.1.142 or newer; on older versions, use npx skills add blader/humanizer --global --agent claude-code . Codex npx skills add blader/humanizer --global --agent codex Claude.ai and Claude Desktop Download this repository as a ZIP ( Code → Download ZIP ) and upload it as a skill in Settings. Other agents npx skills add blader/humanizer --global --agent ' * ' This installs Humanizer for every agent the Skills CLI supports, including Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot, and Windsurf. Leave off --global in any command above to install it only in the current project. For an agent the Skills CLI does not know, copy SKILL.md into its skill folder. Usage Call the skill directly: /humanizer

[paste your text here] Or ask in plain language: Please humanize this text: [your text] To rewrite a file, give Humanizer its path: Humanize the prose in docs/launch-post.md Match your voice If you want the rewrite to sound more like you, include a sample: /humanizer

Here's a sample of my writing for voice matching:
[paste 2-3 paragraphs of your own writing]

Now humanize this text:
[paste AI text to humanize] Humanizer follows the sample's rhythm, word choice, punctuation, and deliberate quirks, including dashes if you use them. How it works A language model writes whatever is most likely to come next, so by default it makes the choice that fits the widest range of readers and subjects. A person chooses for one reader and one subject. Every tell Humanizer looks for is a form of that default choice: a sentence that signals importance instead of adding a fact, rhythm or formatting applied by rule, an ordinary fact dressed as a pivotal one, text left over from the chat, or a reply that re-explains what the reader already knows. "LLMs use statistical algorithms to guess what should come next. The result tends toward the most statistically likely result that applies to the widest variety of cases."
Wikipedia, "Signs of AI writing" Humanizer marks every tell it finds, strongest first. It drafts a rewrite without treating the original structure as fixed, checks the draft against the patterns and the original claims, and then writes the final version. It does not make things up. A name, number, date, quote, citation, or other factual detail must come from the source or the writer, and if a sentence needs a detail that is missing, Humanizer asks instead of inventing one. When you paste text, Humanizer shows its work: the first rewrite, a short critique of anything that still sounds artificial, and the final version. Point it at a file and it changes only the prose, leaving code, data, frontmatter, and link targets alone. Personal writing keeps the writer's opinions and quirks. Technical and reference prose stays neutral and plain. The 26 patterns The patterns are numbered by strength and frequency. The first five justify an edit on a single sighting. Patterns marked weak alone count only when several tells share a passage, because a careful writer may use any one of them on purpose. A. Staging instead of stating # Pattern Before After 1 Not X but Y "It's not just X, it's Y", "This doesn't mean X. It means Y." State the point directly 2 One-line closers and dramatic fragments "That is the real win." after every section; "This shows the importance of..." after an example; "No prior. No nostalgia." Cut the closer that repeats or explains the example; merge fragments into a specific claim 3 Sayings that sound deep "At its core, what matters is...", "Symmetry is the language of trust" Replace the saying with the specific claim 4 Staged run-up before the point "Let's dive in", "Honestly? It depends..." Remove the run-up and state the point 5 Arguing with no one "This isn't mainly about...", "A tempting approach would be..." Remove the unraised objection or fake option; keep any real claim B. Rhythm by rule # Pattern Before After 6 Forced triads "innovation, inspiration, and insights"; three examples plus a lesson Use the number of items the meaning needs 7 Repeated sentence openings "She noted... She noted... She filed..." Merge the sentences or change the subject 8 Dashes as the universal connector ( weak alone ) "institutions—not the people—yet this continues—" Use periods, commas, colons, or parentheses; match a sample that uses dashes 9 Stacked qualifiers ( weak alone ) "could potentially possibly be argued" Keep only qualifiers the source supports 10 Hyphenated pairs everywhere ( weak alone ) "the report is high-quality" Keep the hyphen before the noun or where the dictionary has one 11 Passive voice and missing subjects ( weak alone ) "No configuration file needed" Name the actor when that helps C. Inflation and borrowed authority # Pattern Before After 12 Overused AI words "delve... testament... landscape... showcasing" Use plain words 13 Inflated significance "marking a pivotal moment", "Despite challenges... continues to thrive", "The future looks bright" Keep the fact and drop the significance; end on the last concrete fact 14 Vague connection or association "associated with the leadership of", "in connection with" State the relationship the source gives 15 Shallow -ing riders "symbolizing... reflecting... showcasing..." Keep only what the source supports 16 Sales language "nestled within the breathtaking region" State what the thing is 17 Borrowed authority "Experts believe...", "cited in NYT, BBC, FT, and The Hindu" Name a real source and what it said, or remove the claim or list 18 Avoiding is, are, and has "serves as... features... boasts" "is... has" D. Formatting by rule # Pattern Before After 19 Bold as decoration " OKRs , KPIs "; " Performance: Performance improved" Remove the bold; turn a labeled list into prose 20 Decorative headings "Strategic Negotiations And Partnerships", "🚀 Launch Phase:", "The decision, on one screen" Sentence case; remove emojis and arrows; name what the section holds 21 Curly quotation marks ( weak alone ) said “the project” said "the project" E.

title: github/copilot-cli
agent0ai/agent-zero
abstract: Agent Zero Give your agent a full Linux computer. Agent Zero is an open-source AI agent with its own Linux workspace. It can research, write code, create and work with documents using a terminal, browser, and desktop apps. It runs in a sandbox, but you can step in, and connect it to local files on your own computer when needed. Get started · Installation guide Quick Start | Why Agent Zero | Try These First | Deep Dives | Docs Quick Start Choose A0 Launcher for a desktop computer, or A0 Install for a server or shell-only environment. You will need a supported AI account, a provider API key, or a local model server to start chatting. Desktop setup A0 Launcher is recommended for desktop computers. It guides you through Docker setup, creates your Agent Zero instance, and opens the Web UI. Download A0 Launcher v1.9 for your operating system and processor: Platform Recommended download Other processors Windows Windows x64 · Intel / AMD Windows ARM64 macOS Apple Silicon · M-series Macs Intel Macs only Linux Linux x64 · Intel / AMD Linux ARM64 Open Launcher and follow any Docker setup prompt. Create an Instance , a separate Agent Zero setup. Choose Download Agent Zero or Run Agent Zero , keep the default version and persistent workspace, then click Create . Wait for Running and click Open UI . Continue with your first message , or see the Installation guide for screenshots and help. Servers and shell access A0 Install is recommended when you have shell access but no graphical desktop , such as a server or an SSH session. It runs interactively in your terminal, helps set up Docker where needed, and creates an Agent Zero instance with a persistent workspace. macOS / Linux curl -fsSL https://bash.agent-zero.ai | bash Windows PowerShell irm https: // ps.agent - zero.ai | iex Follow the prompts, then open the Web UI and send your first message . For a local install, use the printed URL. On a remote server, localhost refers to that server; follow the VPS guide for access and authentication before connecting from a browser on your own computer. For setup without installer menus, see scripted installation and the full installer options . Send your first message Send a message from the welcome screen. Try: "Create a one-page plan for a 15-minute team kickoff. Save it as a Markdown file and give me a link." Connect a model when the chat asks. Choose Cloud provider , AI account , or Local model , then select a Main model for conversations and a Utility model for summaries and chat names. They can use the same provider. Click Finish setup , then Continue to close setup. Your original message resumes in the same chat; watch for the reply and open the returned file link. The Codex guide covers ChatGPT account sign-in. If your provider is missing, use the provider-plugin link to find it in the Hub; the OpenCode Go guide walks through installation. Other install options Docker already installed? Run this directly docker run -d -p 127.0.0.1:5080:80 -v a0_usr:/a0/usr agent0ai/agent-zero Open http://localhost:5080 on the Docker host, then send your first message . The a0_usr volume keeps your data when the container is replaced. Keep backups too. This command makes the Web UI available only on the Docker host; see the Installation guide for other setups. Troubleshooting Docker is not running: start Docker Desktop or your Docker service, then reopen the Launcher or rerun the install command. Linux download won't open: allow the AppImage to run as a program in its file properties, then open it again. Port is already in use: choose another in Launcher or A0 Install. For the Docker command above, replace 5080 with a free port and use that port in your browser URL. No first reply: check that setup finished and both models are available through your chosen provider. Read any connection or account error shown in the chat. Still blocked: see the Troubleshooting guide . Try These First Make a plan: "Create a one-page plan for a 15-minute team kickoff, with a goal, three agenda items, and next steps. Save it as a Markdown file and give me a link." Work with a document: attach a document, then ask, "Summarize the main points and list anything I need to follow up on." Research a topic: "Compare three places for a weekend trip by train from Rome. Link your sources and make a shortlist." Once you are comfortable, try the Browser and Desktop: Annotate a design you like: "Open this site in the Browser. I'll point out the parts I like, then help me build something similar for my project." Cowork on a spreadsheet: "Create an editable ODS budget model with assumptions and monthly projections." Drive a desktop app: "Use the Linux Desktop to open Blender and create a simple 3D logo for me." Review a web UI: "Open my local app in the Browser. I will annotate the page with comments; then implement the requested UI fixes." Coming from another agent? Bring chats from Pi, Hermes Agent, or Claude Code into Agent Zero with Migrate Agents . Preview the import before saving it, then continue the conversation here. Project files are copied separately; importing a chat does not move its workspace. Why Agent Zero What you can do Where to start Use desktop apps and work on documents together Desktop and Cowork Browse the web and point out exactly what needs changing Browser and annotations Keep each job's files, instructions, and memory together Projects Add providers, tools, and integrations Plugin Hub Work on files on your own computer Launcher Host access , or A0 CLI Adapt the agent to how you work Agent Profiles and Skills Deep Dives A Real Linux Desktop in the Canvas The Canvas is the panel beside your chat for browsers, documents, and the desktop. Open Desktop there to see Agent Zero's Linux workspace. It can use Blender, a terminal, a file manager, and other desktop apps. You can watch and take over with your own mouse and keyboard. See the Desktop guide for the walkthrough, prompt examples, and how Desktop differs from Browser. Browse and Annotate The built-in Browser opens pages, fills forms, uploads files, and takes screenshots. Open it in the Canvas to follow along. In Annotate mode, click a page element to inspect it, request a change, capture a design reference, or leave a comment for the agent. Browser history keeps screenshots of important steps. You can also install Chrome extensions or connect a browser on your own computer through Launcher Host access or A0 CLI. See the Browser guide for screenshots, settings, host-browser setup, and troubleshooting. Cowork on Documents Markdown Editor With Live Cowork Ask Agent Zero to write a plan or meeting notes as a Markdown file, then open it in the Canvas editor. You can type, format text, and edit tables while the agent works on the same document. LibreOffice Integration Use the Desktop toolbar to create a Writer document, spreadsheet, or presentation. Agent Zero can work on these LibreOffice files alongside you and save the result as ODT, ODS, or ODP. Plugin Hub Open the Plugin Hub to find community providers, tools, memory systems, integrations, and UI additions. Read a plugin's description and setup instructions before installing it. You can also build and publish your own. See the Plugin Hub guide , the Create a Small Plugin tutorial, and the MCP setup guide for connecting external tools. Use Codex with Your ChatGPT Account Sign in with your ChatGPT account, choose Codex models, and continue in Agent Zero. Enable device code sign-in in ChatGPT, open Account in Agent Zero's onboarding, and connect Codex/ChatGPT . After you authorize on OpenAI's page and choose Main and Utility models, your first message resumes in the same chat. Follow the Codex account setup guide for the complete walkthrough with screenshots. A0 CLI Connector: Extend Onto Your Host Machine The A0 CLI Connector connects your terminal to a running Agent Zero instance. It can give the agent access to files, commands, and a browser on your own computer. Using Launcher?

title: jordan-gibbs/hyperresearch
abstract:
The Most Powerful Deep Research Harness: a deep research skill for Claude Code and OpenAI Codex Hyperresearch turns Claude Code into a deep research agent, and it's #1 on the DRACO deep research benchmark, ahead of Claude Research, ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity. It runs in OpenAI Codex too. A tier-adaptive 16-step pipeline takes one prompt and produces an adversarially-audited report with full source provenance. Every source it reads lands in a persistent, searchable vault, so each session starts smarter than the last. Don't want to run it locally? Hyperresearch is the hosted version: the same pipeline, with no Claude Code or Codex install needed. Note New: hyperresearch runs on OpenAI Codex. One command installs the full pipeline for Codex: entry skill, step procedures, the subagent roster as Codex custom agents, and a Stop hook that keeps Codex from skipping steps. Same vault, same ship gate as on Claude Code. pip install hyperresearch && hyperresearch install . --target codex
codex --sandbox workspace-write -c sandbox_workspace_write.network_access=true # then: $hyperresearch <question> Codex support ships in the next PyPI release; until then install from GitHub with pip install git+https://github.com/jordan-gibbs/hyperresearch . Details and what differs on Codex: Codex . See a sample report Read a full report before you install anything. These are unedited Deep runs from the hosted version, and you don't need to log in: Toast vs Square vs Clover : a restaurant POS competitor analysis, built mostly from SEC filings (241 sources) Buying a $2M HVAC business : multiples, SBA loans and diligence (213 sources) Who is winning AI coding agents, October 2026 (259 sources) These are the same kind of Deep runs that put Hyperresearch at #1 on DRACO. Method and per-task scores are on the benchmark page . Why it wins 250+ sources in a single run. The premier scale profile targets 100–130 in the width sweep alone; citation chasing and gap-fill fetches more than double what actually lands in the corpus. Every citation is verified before the report ships. A skeptical cite-checker audits whether each cited source actually supports its sentence. Hallucinated quotes and unacknowledged retractions are hard blocks at the gate. Syndication doesn't count as consensus. An independence audit clusters derivative copies, so five reprints of one press release argue with the weight of one source. Adversarial by construction. Four critics attack every draft in parallel, and a tool-locked patcher can only apply surgical edits. It physically cannot rewrite the report. Eight scholarly sources, one query. hpr scholar search hits OpenAlex, Crossref, CORE, DOAB, ClinicalTrials.gov, SEC EDGAR and FRED through one client layer and returns a single list deduplicated by DOI and title. Books, trials and filings come back alongside papers, each tagged so the pipeline knows which is which. The humanities and social sciences are covered on purpose, not as an afterthought. Paywalled papers get read, not skimmed. A closed paper normally enters a vault as a 1,500-character abstract that the report then cites as though it had been read. Hyperresearch asks Unpaywall, Europe PMC and CORE for a legal open-access copy and stores the full text instead, even when the publisher blocks the fetch outright. Every substitution is disclosed in the note, the frontmatter, and the CLI output. Nothing is thrown away. Every source lands in a searchable markdown-plus-SQLite vault that your next session reuses before it fetches anything new. Crashed runs resume. Each run keeps a manifest; run resume picks up at the exact step where it died. Scales from 30 minutes to a dissertation. Bounded queries auto-route to a 5-step fast path. Opt-in dissertation runs (experimental) write 25K–80K words across chapters, from 300–450 sources. Browse the vault by DOI, venue, citation count, retraction status, or retrieved
manuscript version with scholarly metadata filters . Install Works in Claude Code and OpenAI Codex : same pipeline, same vault. cd your-project
pip install hyperresearch

hyperresearch install # Claude Code, then: /hyperresearch <anything> hyperresearch install . --target codex # OpenAI Codex, then: $hyperresearch <anything> --target all installs both side by side. Codex sessions need write access and network, see below . Prefer a plugin or a single skill? Each route below installs one bootstrap skill, deep-research , that sets the pipeline up in the current project on first use. It still needs pip install hyperresearch . Claude Code OpenAI Codex Plugin /plugin marketplace add jordan-gibbs/hyperresearch /plugin install hyperresearch@hyperresearch codex plugin marketplace add jordan-gibbs/hyperresearch codex plugin add hyperresearch@hyperresearch Skill ( skills.sh ) npx skills add jordan-gibbs/hyperresearch -a claude-code npx skills add jordan-gibbs/hyperresearch -a codex Invoke /hyperresearch:deep-research <question> (plugin) /deep-research <question> (skill) $hyperresearch:deep-research <question> (plugin) $deep-research <question> (skill) Or just ask for deep research in plain words; the skill triggers on its description. Python 3.11–3.14. Power users: hyperresearch install --global makes /hyperresearch reachable from every Claude Code session anywhere, at the cost of ~15 lines in every session's system reminder. Per-project install (above) keeps unrelated CC sessions clean. The bootstrap skill The repo is a Claude Code plugin marketplace, a Codex plugin marketplace, and a skills.sh source, and all three ship the same skill, deep-research . It checks for the hyperresearch CLI, runs hyperresearch install for the agent it is running in ( --target codex under Codex), and hands off to the pipeline. The pipeline itself still comes from the Python package. If Claude Code does not pick up the newly installed skills and subagents, restart it in the same directory and run /hyperresearch <question> . Codex discovers skills at session start, so on first use the bootstrap reads the freshly installed entry skill directly; later sessions can start with $hyperresearch <question> . Codex The same pipeline runs on the OpenAI Codex CLI . cd your-project
pip install hyperresearch && hyperresearch install . --target codex This installs the entry skill at .agents/skills/hyperresearch/ , the step procedures under .hyperresearch/codex/steps/ , the subagents as custom agents in .codex/agents/ , a Stop hook in .codex/hooks.json , and a short block in AGENTS.md . --target all installs the Claude Code and Codex versions side by side. --global --target codex puts the entry skill in ~/.agents/skills/ and the agents in ~/.codex/agents/ . Research needs to write files and reach the network, and Codex allows neither by default. Start the session with both enabled, then invoke the skill: codex --sandbox workspace-write -c sandbox_workspace_write.network_access=true # then, in the session: $hyperresearch < anything > # non-interactive: codex exec --sandbox workspace-write -c sandbox_workspace_write.network_access=true \
  --dangerously-bypass-hook-trust " \$ hyperresearch <anything> " You pass these as flags; hyperresearch never edits your Codex config. codex exec cannot ask you to trust the project's hooks, so without --dangerously-bypass-hook-trust the Stop hook below does not run. Only pass it for hooks you have read ( .codex/hooks.json ). Subagents inherit the session's model. To pin a model per role, add a codex_models override to a profile in .hyperresearch/config.toml and re-run hyperresearch install . --target codex : [ profile . full ] codex_models = { fetcher = " gpt-5.4-mini " , critics = " gpt-5.5 " } What is different on Codex: No browser lane. Codex has no Claude-in-Chrome equivalent, so fetches blocked by a login wall or bot wall stay in the escalation queue, and the final message lists them for you. Tool locks are instructions, not enforcement. Codex custom agents have no per-agent tool allowlist.

title: AminBlg/SimpleEnglish
abstract:
✈️ your AI writes like a LinkedIn post. make it write like a Boeing manual. An agent skill that makes LLMs write plain English with the discipline of ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English , the controlled language aerospace has used since 1983 so that a tired mechanic cannot misread an instruction. Layman-readable by default, STE-strict on request. Works in every agent that reads the Agent Skills standard : Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code Copilot, OpenAI Codex, Gemini CLI, Goose, OpenCode, and about 25 more. One folder, no dependencies, MIT. Install Any agent, with the skills CLI : npx skills add AminBlg/SimpleEnglish This installs the skill only. It does not install the session hook or the output style below, so setting outputStyle to simple-english:simple-english without the plugin does nothing. Use the Claude Code plugin for those. Claude Code plugin, with the session hook and the output style: claude plugin marketplace add AminBlg/SimpleEnglish && claude plugin install simple-english@simple-english The output style is named simple-english:simple-english . The short name does not resolve. Select it with /config under Output style, or put {"outputStyle": "simple-english:simple-english"} in ~/.claude/settings.json . All Claude runs: claude-sonnet-4-6 , low effort, no settings loaded. Judges are Claude models on Claude text, so family bias is possible. Replies, 8 chat questions with a jargon term each, two runs, raw files and tables . Counts are totals over the 16 replies. 95% fewer visible defects (em-dashes, bold, headers, bullets) with 2.0.1 than with no skill (218 → 11). These counts come from the 2026-09-02 runs of 2.0.1, which still had the five-sentence reply cap that 2.1.0 removed. No run exists yet for 2.1.0 or later. With 2.0.1 they went to 5.2 sentences and zero formatting. Documents, the 8 sqlpipe writing tasks scored with the STE linter, one run per cell. One run moves by about 0.5 on this model, so read the rows as parity or better, not as a ranking. Condition viol/100w Reduction no skill 4.09 1.3.0 2.11 48% 2.0.0 1.70 58% 2.0.1 0.91 78% The linter history: 81.3% fewer linter violations across 9 Claude models (144 generations, RESULTS.md ), plus Pi, opencode, and OpenAI runs in evals/results/ . Those numbers reproduce. A 2026-09-02 audit showed that they measure rule obedience, not what a reader sees, which is why 2.0.1 reports the reply counts above. The rules Two registers in SKILL.md , about 1,700 tokens. The 53 numbered rules of Issue 9 live in rule-catalog.md for check mode and Strict mode. The reply, every chat answer: Rule What it kills Prose only: no headers, bullets, bold, tables The wall of formatting around a one-line answer First sentence answers The preamble No em-dashes The spliced half-thought Define a concept term in a few words Jargon the reader has to look up No contractions, openers, or closers "Great question!" and "Hope this helps!" The document: docs, READMEs, runbooks, error messages, release notes: Rule What it kills Max 20 words per instruction, 25 per description The run-on sentence Condition before command Trailing "...if the flag is set" that readers execute too late Simple tenses, active voice "has been updated", ", making it easy to..." No should/would/may/might Hedging. can , will , must survive One word = one meaning, whole document check/verify/confirm/validate roulette Keep articles, keep "that" Telegraph style. STE is short, not terse No bold lead-ins, no heading over two sentences Decoration that hides the fact State the fact, not its importance "crucial", "robust", "not just X, it is Y" Two modes. Plain, the default, is all of the above. Strict adds the STE dictionary discipline from strict-vocabulary.md when you name STE, ASD-STE100, or compliance. The reply stays Plain in every mode. FAQ Does this make output STE-certified? No. Nothing does, because ASD certifies no tool. Strict mode gets close. Word-level rulings live in the official standard, a free download . Will my docs sound robotic? They will sound like Airbus manuals: flat and impossible to misread. For docs that is the whole point. Keep your voice for your blog. Why not just prompt "write clearly"? "Clearly" is an opinion. "No sentence over 20 words" is a spec. Agents follow specs. Why a 40-year-old aerospace standard? It is maintained (Issue 9, January 2025), numbered, and testable. It is also a near-perfect negative of every AI writing tell. How was it built? Against the primary Issue 9 text, not summaries. A community audit ( #4 ) checked the vocabulary tables against the dictionary. Scenarios and recorded results: evals/pressure-tests.md . Star history Word-choice linter evals/ste_lint.py measures the mechanical rules and cannot see word choice. tools/ste-dictionary/ holds an extractor that builds the word lists from your own copy of the free Issue 9 PDF. A linter reads them. The repository ships the tool and no dictionary content, because the standard forbids reproduction without written authority from ASD. Contributing Open an issue for questions and bug reports. Pull requests are welcome. A change that moves a published number ships the raw files with it, and python3 evals/check_numbers.py must pass. Run python3 evals/ste_lint.py --self-test before you push. Say in the PR whether an agent wrote the code, and do not add attribution trailers. License MIT for everything here. The repo paraphrases the rules for teaching and reproduces no spec text or dictionary content. Unofficial project, not affiliated with or endorsed by ASD or STEMG.
