title: spotify/portal-ai-plugins
abstract:
Spotify Portal AI Plugins Bring Spotify Portal into Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and pi. This plugin provides focused workflows for the Portal CLI : set up
authentication, search your software catalog, build service briefings, run
diagnostics, and invoke Portal actions. Highlights Set up the Portal CLI for your current coding-agent environment. Run read-only diagnostics to verify plugin, CLI, authentication, and action readiness. Search the software catalog and technical documentation using natural language queries. Generate concise service briefings with available ownership, health, incident, and documentation details. Discover and safely invoke Portal actions with built-in help, dry-run, and confirmation safeguards. Create, run, check, and troubleshoot Fleetshift shifts, open PRs from completed runs, and stop a run on request. The marketplace also ships shunt (Claude Code only for now): a plugin that routes I/O-heavy agent work — bulk file reads and boilerplate generation — to AiKA modes running cheaper worker models, via the Portal CLI actions registry. See plugins/shunt/README.md . Installation Claude Code claude plugin marketplace add spotify/portal-ai-plugins
claude plugin install portal@portal
claude plugin install shunt@portal # optional: token-saving AiKA delegation Start a new session and run: /portal:setup Codex codex plugin marketplace add spotify/portal-ai-plugins
codex Open /plugins , install Spotify Portal, start a new task, and ask: Set up Spotify Portal for me. Cursor Register the spotify/portal-ai-plugins repository in your Cursor team marketplace, then install Spotify Portal from Cursor Settings → Plugins . pi pi install git:github.com/spotify/portal-ai-plugins Start a new session and run: /skill:setup Workflows Workflow Purpose setup Configure Portal CLI authentication doctor Run read-only readiness diagnostics search Search the software catalog and technical documentation service Produce a concise operational service briefing actions Discover, inspect, preview, and safely invoke Portal actions feedback Submit feedback about the Portal CLI to the Portal team fleetshift-create-shift Draft and create a Fleetshift shift from a goal, with a dry-run preview fleetshift-run-shift Trigger a shift, monitor it with a bounded wait, and stop it on request fleetshift-check-shift Report a shift's progress, targets, and PRs (read-only) fleetshift-troubleshoot-shift Diagnose failed shift jobs from their status and logs (read-only) fleetshift-create-prs Open PRs for completed shift targets after confirmation Portal CLI The workflows invoke the upstream CLI through: npx @spotify/portal-cli < command > Setup verifies the required auth , actions , owner , search , and service commands before proceeding.

title: liguobao/ds-harness-remote
abstract:
English · 中文 · 日本語 · Documentation · Web · Android · iOS Self-hosting · npm · Connect once. Ready whenever you are. Continue using your DeepSeek Harness instance from a phone, computer, or browser. Return to the same Harness session from whichever device is with you. Harness keeps running on your work computer, with the same workspaces, tools, and project setup. DS Harness Remote is simply another window into that environment. The DeepSeek Harness desktop edition is supported. Install the latest release: ds-harness-remote@0.6.2 Features Access your local Harness instance remotely from the web, a PC, or a mobile device: DSH first, with Codex, Cursor, and Antigravity support too. DeepSeek Harness Desktop is ready to use after installation, with its native interface and no separate desktop conversation UI. Create workspaces, configure models, and switch conversation models with the same smooth workflow as local use. No public listening port or public IP is required on the Harness Host. Connect from anywhere with internet access over a bidirectional end-to-end encrypted channel. Prefer P2P connections, use TURN relay nodes worldwide, and fall back to multiple Server Relays when needed. Access workspace files, read-only previews, remote terminals, and authorized local development-service previews through the native Harness sidebar. Remote Tool context injection supports Host and workspace discovery, Harness session creation and management, history reading, waiting for execution, interruption requests, and authorized file transfers. Details . Alongside DeepSeek Harness, access native workspaces for Codex, Cursor, Google Antigravity, Pi, OpenCode, Claude Code, Hermes Agent, and other tools through ACP integrations, with remote file browsing and terminals. Clients are available across Android, iOS, Web, and native DSH. Multiple clients can connect to the same Harness Host simultaneously, with RPC calls and streams isolated per connection. Contents Connect once. Ready whenever you are Features Supported clients Install Quick start Screenshots How it works Experimental ACP workspaces End-to-end encryption Network and transport Security FAQ Documentation Links Star History Project status and trademarks License Supported clients Client Form Status Notes DSH Desktop plugin Remote sidebar Supported Install ds-harness-remote@0.6.2 ; this computer can also be the Host Web Browser page Supported Open https://dsh.r2049.cn ; reuses the native Harness interface Android Native app Supported Download the APK from Releases ; see the Android guide DSH Go A standout app by ccch1mneyyy Supported See ccch1mneyyy/dsh-go: an Android client for DeepSeek Harness. Run it directly on your phone or control DSH on your computer remotely. iOS TestFlight beta Beta Not publicly released; see issue #20 Browser extension Chrome Entry point only Exchanges an already signed-in Web authorization for a separate device credential, lists online Hosts and opens the same-origin Remote Web; it does not host a conversation UI dsh-TUI Terminal-only CLI Supported Can act as a Host; see the dsh-TUI Remote guide . The installer never creates a Web service for it automatically Linux Cloud server Supported Sign in on the official website for unattended installation with a single command and no configuration. Several clients can connect to the same Host at once; RPC calls and streams are isolated per connection. Install DeepSeek Harness Desktop support Open Extensions / Plugin management in DeepSeek Harness Desktop, choose installation
from npm, and enter this package: ds-harness-remote@0.6.2 Restart Desktop afterward. Its official dsh launcher can also install the pinned package
with dsh plugin --profile desktop add -w ds-harness-remote@0.6.2 . Linux one-command installation Visit https://dsh.r2049.cn , sign in, and obtain an installation authorization code to install with one command. dsh-TUI Host For terminal Host setup with dsh-TUI , see the dsh-TUI Remote guide . Native Android client Keep conversations connected across multiple workspaces at once, and use Bot mode , powered by Fei2411/DS-Bot . Download the latest APK from GitHub Releases , and sign in to the same account to see your Hosts. DSH Go — DeepSeek Harness in your pocket: run it locally on your phone or control your computer remotely. ccch1mneyyy/dsh-go has built-in support for the ds-harness-remote protocol. You can run DeepSeek Harness locally on your phone or connect to your computer remotely. After installing the ds-harness-remote plugin in DSH Go on your phone, you can also connect to the phone’s DSH from your computer or the web and use Mobile Use seamlessly. iOS client Join the beta Quick start Open Remote from the DeepSeek Harness sidebar. Choose Zhihu, GitHub, or Google authorization, or sign in with an account and password. Account registration requires an invitation code; email the repository author to request one. On another device, install the same plugin in DeepSeek Harness and sign in as described in steps 1–2. Alternatively, use Remote Web, iOS, Android, or DSH Go directly without installing a plugin. Select an online Host, then choose an existing workspace or browse remote directories to open one. By default, Remote uses this project's hosted Server at https://dsh.r2049.cn . For self-hosting, use the repository's minimal Server . The current version includes P2P coordination and a Relay Server, but does not provide the full hosted Remote Web experience. Screenshots Desktop On another computer, select an online Host and open its workspace. The workspace opens in the native Harness interface, with the active Host and encrypted connection status in the header. To prevent this computer from controlling other Hosts, open the Host list at https://dsh.r2049.cn/ and enable Controlled only . This device will no longer see other devices under your account, while Web and other clients can still connect to it remotely. Android Use text or image prompts, switch models, and access supported workspace files and terminals. The interface follows the system language and supports English, Simplified and Traditional Chinese, Japanese, Spanish, German, and French. In language settings, tap “More ...” to show all languages. See the Android guide for details. Mobile Settings includes a global Compact conversations switch, off by default and applied when a conversation is next opened. Supporting Hosts reduce historical tool details while preserving messages and tool status. Turn the setting off and reopen the conversation to load full history. How it works DSH Desktop / Remote Web / Android
  ↔ authenticated, end-to-end encrypted channel
Remote Plugin on the Host
  ↔ supported Harness or optional Codex workspace support
Harness sessions/workspaces or Codex projects The Harness Host does not need a public listening port. Connect from anywhere with internet access over ds-harness-remote’s bidirectional end-to-end encrypted channel. The client switches to the selected Host’s native Harness API, keeping the original workspaces, tools, and permission flows on that computer. Every settings namespace registered by the Host can also be configured remotely through the official Harness settings API, with full support for most plugin settings. Experimental ACP workspaces The Host runs local ACP-capable Agents and forwards prompts, streamed replies, and approvals through ds-harness-remote. Each Agent keeps its own workspaces and sessions; only session translation for DSH is performed, without writing to Harness storage. Supported backends: Codex — connected through its independent App Server interface, with the same workspace entry. Cursor — connected through the CLI's ACP interface. Antigravity (AGY) — its stream-json CLI is adapted to the ACP gateway.

title: Fission-AI/OpenSpec
abstract:
The most loved spec framework. Our philosophy: → fluid not rigid
→ iterative not waterfall
→ easy not complex
→ built for brownfield not just greenfield
→ scalable from personal projects to enterprises Follow @0xTab on X for updates · Join the OpenSpec Discord for help and questions. See it in action You: /opsx:explore
AI:  What would you like to explore?
You: I want dark mode but I'm not sure how to do it cleanly.
AI:  Let me look at your styling setup...
     Cleanest path here: CSS variables + a small theme context,
     with system-preference detection. No new dependencies. Scope it?
You: Yes, let's do it.

You: /opsx:propose add-dark-mode
AI:  Created openspec/changes/add-dark-mode/
     ✓ proposal.md — why we're doing this, what's changing
     ✓ specs/       — requirements and scenarios
     ✓ design.md    — technical approach
     ✓ tasks.md     — implementation checklist
     Ready for implementation!

You: /opsx:apply
AI:  Implementing tasks...
     ✓ 1.1 Add theme context provider
     ✓ 1.2 Create toggle component
     ✓ 2.1 Add CSS variables
     ✓ 2.2 Wire up localStorage
     All tasks complete!

You: /opsx:archive
AI:  Archived to openspec/changes/archive/2025-01-23-add-dark-mode/
     Specs updated. Ready for the next feature. What do the specs actually look like? Plain Markdown — requirements with concrete scenarios, no special syntax to learn. Here's what goes in the specs/ folder created above: ## ADDED Requirements ### Requirement: Theme selection The app SHALL let users switch between light and dark themes,
defaulting to the system preference. #### Scenario: User toggles dark mode - ** WHEN ** the user clicks the theme toggle - ** THEN ** the app switches to dark mode and persists the choice Your AI writes these; you review the plan before any code is written. OpenSpec is built with OpenSpec — browse this repo's live specs and in-flight changes for real examples at scale. OpenSpec Dashboard Why teams adopt OpenSpec Solo, OpenSpec keeps you and your AI honest on a single repo. On a team, the hard part moves: a feature spans the API server, the web app, and a shared library; requirements are owned by one team and consumed by others; planning starts before any code exists. Stores are the answer — planning in a repo of its own. The same openspec/ shape you already know (specs and changes), shared by git push like anything else. One source of truth your whole team and every coding agent can read, across every repo. Cross-repo features — one change, one plan, even when the code lands in three repos. Shared requirements — a platform team owns the specs; product teams reference them read-only, right where their coding agent can read them. No drifting wiki. Plan before code — capture the plan in the store now; the code repos catch up later. Stores are in beta . Start with the Stores guide . Quick Start Install OpenSpec. On macOS or Linux, in your terminal: curl -fsSL https://openspec.dev/cli/install.sh | sh On Windows, in PowerShell: irm https: // openspec.dev / cli / install.ps1 | iex Prefer a package manager? npm install -g @fission-ai/openspec@latest (needs Node.js 22.12.0 or higher) or the official Homebrew formula , brew install openspec . Then navigate to your project directory and initialize: cd your-project
openspec init Want your AI to do it? Paste the setup prompt into your coding assistant — it installs the CLI, runs openspec init , and verifies the result. Now talk to your AI: Not sure what to build yet? Start with /opsx:explore , a no-stakes thinking partner that reads your code, weighs options, and shapes a plan before any code gets written. ( Quickstart ) Already know what you want? Go straight to /opsx:propose <what-you-want-to-build> . Both are in the default profile. If you want the expanded workflow ( /opsx:new , /opsx:continue , /opsx:ff , /opsx:verify , /opsx:bulk-archive , /opsx:onboard ), select it with openspec config profile and apply with openspec update . /opsx:propose is the canonical name; your tool may spell it /opsx-propose (Cursor, GitHub Copilot), @opsx-propose (Amazon Q) or $openspec-propose (Codex). openspec init prints the right form for the tools you picked — see Supported Tools . Note Not sure if your tool is supported? View the full list – we support 30+ tools and growing. Also works with npm, Homebrew, pnpm, yarn, bun, and Nix. See installation options . Docs Full documentation lives at openspec.dev/docs . → Quickstart : your first change, start to finish → Set up your project : what openspec init installs → CLI : terminal reference → Supported Tools : tool integrations & install paths → Customize : profiles, project config, and schemas → Stores : plan in a separate repo, shared across your team (beta) → Community Showcase : projects and resources built with and for OpenSpec Community schemas Third-party schema bundles distributed via standalone repositories — these provide opinionated workflows that integrate OpenSpec with other tools, similar to how github/spec-kit's community extension catalog handles tool integrations. → Browse the catalog in the customization docs. Why OpenSpec? AI coding assistants are powerful but unpredictable when requirements live only in chat history. OpenSpec adds a lightweight spec layer so you agree on what to build before any code is written. Agree before you build — human and AI align on specs before code gets written Stay organized — each change gets its own folder with proposal, specs, design, and tasks Work fluidly — update any artifact anytime, no rigid phase gates Use your tools — works with 30+ AI assistants via slash commands How we compare vs. Spec Kit (GitHub) — Thorough but heavyweight. Rigid phase gates, lots of Markdown, Python setup. OpenSpec is lighter and lets you iterate freely. vs. Kiro (AWS) — Powerful but you're locked into their IDE and limited to Claude models. OpenSpec works with the tools you already use. vs. nothing — AI coding without specs means vague prompts and unpredictable results. OpenSpec brings predictability without the ceremony. Updating OpenSpec Upgrade the CLI With the standalone install, run openspec install . If you installed with npm: npm install -g @fission-ai/openspec@latest If you installed OpenSpec with Homebrew: brew upgrade openspec Refresh agent instructions Run this inside each project to regenerate AI guidance and ensure the latest slash commands are active: openspec update Usage Notes Model selection : OpenSpec works best with high-reasoning models. We recommend Codex 5.5 and Opus 4.7 for both planning and implementation. Context hygiene : OpenSpec benefits from a clean context window. Clear your context before starting implementation and maintain good context hygiene throughout your session. Contributing Every change starts as an issue. We discuss it there, and if we agree to pursue it, a maintainer implements the change or invites you to build it with us. → CONTRIBUTING.md : the full process, from first issue to merged PR Other Telemetry OpenSpec collects anonymous usage stats. We collect only command names and version to understand usage patterns. No arguments, paths, content, or PII. Automatically disabled in CI. Opt-out (any one is enough): openspec config set telemetry.enabled false (global config; unset means on) export OPENSPEC_TELEMETRY=0 or export DO_NOT_TRACK=1 (env overrides config) Maintainers & Advisors See MAINTAINERS.md for the list of core maintainers and advisors who help guide the project. License MIT

title: mattpocock/sandcastle
abstract:
What is Sandcastle? A TypeScript library for orchestrating AI coding agents in isolated sandboxes: You invoke agents with a single sandcastle.run() . Sandcastle handles sandboxing the agent with a configurable branch strategy. The commits made on the branches get merged back. Sandcastle is provider-agnostic. It ships with native sandboxes that use your OS's own process sandbox (Bubblewrap on Linux and WSL2, Seatbelt on macOS), image-based providers for Docker and Podman, and cloud providers for Daytona, E2B, Fly.io Sprites, Modal and Vercel, and you can create your own. Great for parallelizing multiple AFK agents, creating review pipelines, or even just orchestrating your own agents. Documentation The docs live in docs/guide , one page per major term, with every term defined in the Glossary , and are published at aihero.dev/sandcastle . title: lexmount/moli
abstract:
Moli English | 簡體中文 | 日本語 | Deutsch | Français | Español | 한국어 Moli is a production-ready headless browser for AI agents. Its on-demand layout
and rendering design combines a complete browser runtime with a lightweight
resource footprint. Moli helps your AI agent fetch and extract web pages, search the web, and
automate browser tasks. Use it through the CLI, CDP, WebDriver Classic, or WebDriver BiDi. Moli supports Linux, macOS, and Windows. Quick start Give this prompt to your AI agent: Install the skills under https://github.com/lexmount/moli/tree/main/skills,
follow their instructions to download and install the latest prebuilt Moli
binary, then use moli-webfetch to fetch https://example.com and show me the
result. Direct installation On Linux or macOS: curl --proto ' =https ' --tlsv1.2 -fsSL \
  https://github.com/lexmount/moli/releases/latest/download/moli-installer.sh | sh On Windows, run in PowerShell: powershell - ExecutionPolicy ByPass - c " irm https://github.com/lexmount/moli/releases/latest/download/moli-installer.ps1 | iex " Showcase An HTML5 game rendered by Moli and inspected live through Chrome DevTools. rust-lang.org rendered by Moli, with its live DOM, CSS, and geometry available in Chrome DevTools. CLI usage Extract a page Render the page as Markdown with Moli's default completion strategy: moli fetch \
  --dump markdown \
  --wait-until done \
  https://example.com Or directly return a compact, model-friendly semantic tree: moli fetch \
  --dump semantic_tree_text \
  --wait-selector body \
  https://example.com For visual output, enable on-demand layout and write a viewport PNG, a full-document PNG, or a paginated PDF: moli fetch --layout --dump screenshot https://example.com > page.png
moli fetch --layout --dump screenshot_full https://example.com > full-page.png
moli fetch --layout --dump pdf https://example.com > page.pdf To export a page after an explicit interaction, combine --eval (or --eval-file ) with --dump . The expression runs after page readiness;
promises are awaited, and any pending navigation is followed before export.
Its return value is discarded without serialization. An exception fails the
command without emitting a dump. moli fetch --eval ' document.querySelector("button.show-details").click() ' \
  --dump markdown https://example.com Only the supplied expression performs interactions. Without --dump , --eval retains its expression-value output behavior. Run fetch --help for the complete option list, including output formats,
page-load/response waits, profiles, proxy settings, resource policies, and
tracing options. Start the automation server # Basic automation server for DOM-first workloads moli serve # Enable real geometry, coordinate input, and screenshot/screencast surfaces moli serve --layout # Also fetch optional image, font, audio, video, media, and text-track resources moli serve --layout --resource The same endpoint serves all three protocols: CDP, WebDriver Classic, and
WebDriver BiDi. Playwright can connect directly over CDP: import { chromium } from "playwright" ; const browser = await chromium . connectOverCDP ( "http://127.0.0.1:9222" ) ; const context = browser . contexts ( ) [ 0 ] ; const page = context . pages ( ) [ 0 ] ?? await context . newPage ( ) ; await page . goto ( "https://example.com" ) ; console . log ( await page . locator ( "body" ) . innerText ( ) ) ; await browser . close ( ) ; The WebMCP playground includes a CLI to list
and call any site's native WebMCP tools, plus booking, restaurant, and pizza demos. Why Moli Three qualities matter most for agent workloads, and Moli brings them together: Full-featured — real JavaScript, DOM, CSS, networking, storage, layout,
screenshots, and standard automation protocols, all integrated into one
headless browser. Fast — most automation requests never need visual rendering, so
structure-first operations skip layout and paint entirely. Resource-efficient — layout and pixels are generated only when needed,
so Moli does not have to continuously maintain and update a fully rendered
visual state. What most browser automation tasks actually need is page structure, not a
continuously rendered visual world. Moli treats the native DOM and style state
as the single source of truth, triggering layout or software paint only for
operations that genuinely require them. Agent request What Moli does Extract HTML/Markdown, query the DOM, run JS, inspect network/storage Reads browser runtime state directly — does not trigger layout or paint Read an element's box, hit-test coordinates, send coordinate input Runs one layout calculation and retains only the latest frozen layout tree Capture a screenshot Rebuilds from the current DOM/style, replaces the frozen tree, renders a fresh frame, and discards its paint state after use Poll a screencast Compares generation metadata only; clean state emits no frame, while changed state rebuilds and emits one fresh frame Moli still includes the complete set of capabilities: V8, CSS, layout, text
shaping, hit-testing, software paint, and more. The only difference is when visual work runs and how long its results are retained. This cost model is
especially well suited to crawling, browser-use agents, retrieval pipelines,
evaluation environments, and reinforcement-learning workloads. Current capabilities Complete web runtime — streaming HTML parsing, native DOM, V8 JavaScript,
modules/timers/microtasks/events, iframes and workers, CSS cascade,
Fetch/XHR/WebSocket, cookies, WebCrypto, and profile-scoped storage
(localStorage, IndexedDB, OPFS). Extraction-optimized outputs — the CLI directly produces HTML, Markdown,
JSON, semantic text trees, and frame-aware serialization, with
selector/script/response waits and network tracing. Unified automation binary — CDP, WebDriver Classic, and WebDriver BiDi
share the same kernel and scheduler. No separate ChromeDriver, geckodriver,
or browser installation is required. Real visual capabilities on demand — add --layout to enable complete box
construction, Taffy layout, Parley text layout, layout-backed
hit-testing/input, viewport
screenshots, and low-frequency CPU-rendered DevTools screencast frames. Controllable operational options — profiles, cookies, HTTP cache, proxies,
resource families, connection limits, timeouts, private-network policy,
user-agent overrides, diagnostic logging, and network diagnostics are all
available. Moli's relationship with Lexmount Moli is Lexmount's open-source headless browser; Lexmount Browser is the managed
cloud runtime and control plane built around it. The open-source headless browser is fully usable without Lexmount Browser. Cost controls Expensive browser operations in Moli require an explicit opt-in and are never
enabled by default: Mode or option Behavior Default LayoutPolicy::Mock — deterministic geometry in a compatible format, with no real layout or paint --layout LayoutPolicy::OnDemand — real layout, geometry, hit-testing, coordinate input, screenshots, screencast --resource Fetch all optional visual/media resource families --image , --font , --audio , --video , --media , --text-track Enable one specific optional resource family --profile-dir , --http-cache-dir , --cookie-file Selectively enable the persistence required by the workload Layout is an on-demand snapshot rather than continuously maintained state. The
first geometry request (a cold start) builds a working layout tree from the
current DOM/style, freezes its canonical geometry into an immutable,
DOM-independent FrozenLayoutTree , and retains only that latest tree. Ordinary
geometry reads may reuse it even if the page has changed. Screenshots always
rebuild and replace the frozen tree. Each screencast subscription remembers
only an opaque visual-state token: an unchanged token suppresses the poll,
while a changed token triggers one fresh frame. Paint results are never reused. Architecture Moli is a standalone browser kernel, not a Chromium wrapper.

title: Anthropic's internal AI use, at retail prices, now exceeds its employee pay
abstract:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images 2026-11-01T15:00:01.255Z Read in app This story is available exclusively to Business Insider subscribers. Become an Insider and start reading now. Have an account? Log in . Here's a remarkable milestone in the AI revolution: Anthropic now spends more on internal AI usage than it does paying employees. The company revealed this in its IPO filing . In April, the value of Claude AI used internally, calculated at prices Anthropic charges customers, exceeded its monthly employee compensation costs, excluding stock awards. By September, that internal AI usage had surged more than 250-fold since January. There's an important distinction here. Anthropic isn't actually spending more cash on AI than salaries. It's valuing its internal AI consumption at retail prices. Still, this feels like a watershed moment for the tech industry. In March, I wrote about a new trend : Tech companies are starting to treat AI tokens (the main way to measure usage) as a fourth component of employee compensation, alongside salary, bonuses, and stock awards. Anthropic's numbers show why. More than 90% of the code added to its software in September was written by Claude. Meanwhile, revenue has grown vastly faster than headcount. For decades, talented humans were the most valuable resource in Silicon Valley. Now AI is challenging that assumption. Sign up for the AI Insider newsletter here . title: Oracle files to sell $20B in new stock, bonds to finance AI buildout
abstract:
Key Points Oracle filed plans on Monday to issue $10 billion in stock and $10 billion in bonds, it said in a filing. The plans were outlined last week at its investor day. The Oracle logo is displayed on a building at an Oracle campus in Redwood Shores, California, Sept. 10, 2025. Justin Sullivan | Getty Images Oracle filed plans on Monday to issue new stock and more debt to finance its artificial intelligence buildout. The hyperscaler will sell $10 billion in common stock and $10 billion in senior notes, according to filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. While the fundraising was already outlined at an investor day last week , shares tumbled 8.8% Monday. "This seems to be exactly what they previewed," said Rob Oliver, senior research analyst at Baird. "So I'm not sure why the market is freaking about it." Oracle said it plans to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, which may include capital expenditures, repayments of debt and future investments. Stock Chart Icon Stock chart icon Oracle's one-day performance The hyperscaler's stock initially bounced after last Wednesday's investor day, when Oracle also issued a revenue forecast of at least $225 billion for fiscal 2030. At the time Oracle also said it was limiting its additional capital market funding for the fiscal 2027 to 2030 investment cycle to that $20 billion. "This is a major relief given concerns about the state of debt markets and the cost of capital (although UBS has argued that these debt market concerns have been over-stated)," UBS analyst Karl Keirstead said in a note on Thursday. Oracle plans to turn to vendor financing, customer-provided hardware and customer prepayments to help it transition to positive free cash flow, which it expects to reach in the second half of 2028. Stock and bonds in Oracle, co-founded by former CEO Larry Ellison, have been under pressure amid growing investor concerns about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure. Oracle shares are down 33% in 2026 and 50% over the past 12 months. The yield on its investment-grade 4.95% bond due in 2031 is currently 7.276%. The sentiment shift is also seen in Oracle's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default. The spread sits at 292, up 265% in one year. That's more in line with a high-end junk bond rating, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence's Gavan Nolan. Oracle's five-year credit default swaps on Nov. 2, 2026 While still an investment-grade credit, Oracle was downgraded by S&P to a BBB- in July, one rating level above high yield. It has $125.34 billion in debt, as of Aug. 31, with the bulk in senior notes. What ultimately matters for Oracle is execution, Pat Nerney, head of investment solutions at Dynasty Financial Partners, said in an email to CNBC Monday. "Can they do what they say they are going to do? We view this as the narrative across the AI space," he said. "If this gets executed according to plans laid out, they will be rewarded. If they have to come back to market in the back half of '27 after telling everyone this was the last of the capital needed ... look out." — CNBC's Seema Mody and Ari Levy contributed reporting. title: Egoless Mathematics in the AI Era
abstract:
[This is a guest post by Karthik C. S. , Amit Sahai , and Jie Xue . This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.] This is a good time for mathematicians to think carefully about the purpose of their work. The development of artificial intelligence brings that question before us with unusual force. Much of the discussion concerns which tasks machines will perform and which abilities will remain distinctively human. But our response also depends on a prior question: what do we understand mathematical work to be, and what gives it its worth? If our answer has become inseparable from the production of results and the demonstration of individual ability, the present uncertainty may reveal a difficulty in our conception of the work itself. There are broadly two perspectives on mathematics. According to one, we invent it as we construct it: we introduce concepts, choose axioms, and develop theories. According to the other, mathematics exists independently of these activities, and our task is to discover it. These perspectives need not disagree about every aspect of mathematical practice. We plainly develop formalism and arguments. The deeper question is whether the truths we come to understand owe their existence to these acts, or whether our constructions enable us to recognize something that does not depend on us. While discovery of mathematical truth can sound passive, a paleontologist searching for fossils must decide where to excavate, develop techniques, and recognize the significance of incomplete remains. The fossils existed long before the investigation, but finding them may require extraordinary imagination. Their prior existence gives direction to the investigator’s activity. Similarly, a mathematical discovery may require the invention of an entire language and framework through which a previously unnoticed relationship becomes intelligible. The discovery may require great creativity, but that does not make the truth discovered a creation of the individual. We encounter this distinction whenever our constructions surprise us. A definition introduced for one purpose reveals an unexpected connection elsewhere. A conjecture that seemed to organize our examples admits a counterexample. Two theories developed through different questions turn out to express a common structure. In each case, our thought encounters something it did not freely determine. We can revise our definitions or abandon our conjecture, but we cannot make the original argument valid merely by wishing it so. The Platonic perspective gives a natural account of this independence. On this view, there were infinitely many primes before anyone proved that fact. Mathematical truth neither waits for our recognition nor receives its authority from it. We may choose how to describe a structure, but we do not choose its properties in the same way. This perspective also changes the place of the mathematician. Our intelligence becomes a means through which an order independent of us can be understood. The significance of the work lies in its relation to that order. The distinction between a correct derivation and an understanding of its significance is equally important. An axiomatic system permits indefinitely many deductions, but the ability to produce them does not by itself supply a worthy direction of inquiry. Mathematical statements may be formally correct without being enlightening. We can introduce countless definitions and prove countless statements about them. What makes one definition illuminating? Why does one theorem disclose something fundamental while another merely adds to the available material? These questions concern the relation of a particular investigation to the principles it brings into view. Mathematical taste has a place here, provided we understand it as more than individual preference. We value a theory when it reveals a unity among things previously understood separately, or enables us to recognize why a phenomenon occurs. Although mathematical truths may exist independently of us, their discovery can transform our understanding and enrich our experience of the world. The ability to carry out longer chains of reasoning does not by itself explain such understanding. Reasoning serves understanding by articulating relationships and making their justification explicit. However, the success of reasoning does not mean that all knowledge can be reduced to it. Nor does our ability to reason more extensively determine what is worth knowing or why we seek knowledge. Mathematics is only one field of knowledge. Not everything can be understood mathematically, nor is mathematical achievement the ultimate purpose of intellectual life. Yet we increasingly measure intellectual life through publications, citations, awards, and other indicators of performance. While useful, these measures become problematic when they define the worth of the work itself. We begin to see mathematicians as collections of productive abilities, and mathematics as merely their output. From this perspective, anxiety about being replaced by AI is natural: a machine that performs these tasks better appears to threaten our worth. But the problem began before AI arrived. We had already come to understand ourselves in terms suited to machines. AI merely exposes the consequences of this view. The response cannot simply be to seek refuge in distinctively human abilities such as creativity, intuition, or taste. If we value these abilities primarily because they give us an advantage over machines, we remain trapped in the same conception of intellectual worth. Why should the value of our pursuit depend on being better at it than someone or something else? Mathematics offers an opportunity to reconsider this whole orientation. Its truths do not become more true through the distinction of the person who expresses them. In understanding a proof, we bring our thought into conformity with a relationship whose validity does not belong to us. The particular path by which we arrive may bear the marks of our individuality. What is understood is available beyond that individuality. We can allow this experience to loosen the belief that knowledge has its highest value as an achievement attributable to ourselves. Egoless mathematics begins with taking that possibility seriously. Humility then reaches beyond modesty about our accomplishments or generosity in sharing credit. It concerns the place from which we pursue knowledge. We may seek truth to serve our existing purposes, or allow what we discover to change those purposes themselves. If we approach truth on the condition that its discovery must preserve our importance, we have already made it subordinate to ourselves. Accomplishing this reordering can be demanding, as intellectual sophistication can furnish elaborate defenses of the very attachments that prevent us from understanding. What matters is whether our abilities remain answerable to truth, including when it requires us to reconsider what we have been using those abilities for. From this perspective, the possibility of mathematical discoveries through AI need not be a source of sadness about our purpose. A truth has become accessible; its worth is not diminished by the absence of our authorship. We need not immediately turn the event into a judgment about our relative importance. The search can continue without requiring every advance to vindicate the seeker. Indeed, the demand for such vindication has always burdened the pursuit, whether the competing claim came from another mathematician or from a machine. The opportunity before us is therefore more substantial than a rearrangement of mathematical labor. It invites us to reconsider what gives an intellectual life its worth, and to let the pursuit of truth shape not only our work but also how we approach life. This may sound like asking us all to become saints.

title: Just a little AI resistance, as a treat
abstract:
At the recent EMFCamp, I bumped in to Professor Kate Devlin who was talking a little about the AI Resist List . I think one of the useful things we can do is loudly complain about shitty uses of AI. Here's an example. As mentioned in a previous post, I'm contacting companies which send malformed calendar invites . One of the organisation I contacted was the British online supermarket Ocado. They don't have an easy way to contact their technical team, and no obvious paths to raise a bug report, so I filled in their usual customer service feedback form. I included a clear statement of the problem and a detailed technical analysis of why I thought it was a problem with their service. After sending in my message, I received this back from "Lulu" at Ocado: Thanks for getting in touch and sharing this feedback about our calendar files. You're entirely right—having a technical glitch pop up when you're trying to organise your delivery is a real pain, so I've made sure to pass your feedback on to our technical and webshop team. We really appreciate you taking the time to help us improve our service. I hope you have a wonderful rest of your day I mean, that's AI right? It starts with the classic tell of a sycophantic agreement . Next up is the em-dash. Beloved by chatbots but almost unheard of in British English style guides. Finally (and this is hard to quantify) it just doesn't feel like a customer service response. They're usually poorly spelled, have dodgy grammar, and ask a bunch of irrelevant questions. The message gave me no confidence that anyone had looked at the problem and I doubted it had been passed on to a technically competent human. I immediately got a customer satisfaction survey. Usually I give top marks to humans because, even though Net Promoter Score is bullshit , I don't want customer service agents to suffer the indignity of a bad review. But in this survey I vented my spleen - giving crappy 1 ⭐ scores on every metric and complaining vociferously about how rude it is to use an AI to deal with a genuine complaint. I was both surprised and delighted to receive this back a few days after my invective was sent: I saw your survey comment about getting a robotic, AI-generated response previously, and I wanted to reach out personally to apologise. There is nothing more frustrating than pointing out a legitimate bug only to feel like you're talking to a brick wall. I promise you there is a real person typing this out! Second, I wanted to send a massive thank you for the incredibly detailed diagnostic. It is rare to get feedback that tells us exactly what is broken and how to fix it. I can assure you that this has been passed to our team to look into. Your feedback is going to make things much smoother for a lot of people, and we really appreciate you taking the extra time to help us get it right. Thank you again, I do hope that this issue is resolved quickly. If there is anything else I can help with in the meantime, please don't hesitate to get in touch. Perhaps I'm being touchingly naïve, but that feels a lot more human, right? The grammar isn't perfect, the sentences are a bit more rambly, and it appears to have actually engaged with the contents of my message. I get that having a million irate customer service messages is a hassle. Using AI to triage them probably makes business sense, summarising the verbose ones could be useful for customer service agents, and totting up general themes is almost certainly a sensible way to gather metrics without overloading the workforce. But using an AI to reply to a human is just disrespectful. It says the organisation values their customer's time at less than their own. It's OK to call out shitty AI responses and insist that a human engages with you. Share this post on…

title: AI is destroying my CS degree
abstract:
AI is destroying my CS degree 03 Nov, 2026 I am a computer science student. I got a scholarship to study computer science and AI last year and I love it! It's something that I wanted to do since I was a kid but couldn't afford it. It's been a huge learning curve. I only had a B in maths from GCSE (which is the exam you take at 16 for non UK folk) and no technical training other than the funny little games I made on OpenProcessing*. Regardless of how hard it's been, I have enjoyed the challenge. I wouldn't have signed up to study computing if I thought it would be an easy ride. The problem is that my university seems to be having an existential crisis because of AI, and it's making the experience much shittier than it was before. The flip flopping makes everything uncertain During my studies, my uni has flip flopped between YOU MUST NEVER USE AI and YOU MUST USE AI and also YES WE'RE USING AI BUT THAT DOESN'T MEAN YOU SHOULD! They seem to have made an art of choosing the worst possible use cases for AI (marking and feedback, course content creation, and student engagement emails) and going all in on them, only to roll back the decision 3 months later. Students are mandated to use AI in assignments, only to reach the next module where you lose marks for even touching an LLM. Coursework design has gone down the toilet I mean, it was never perfect to begin with. Assessing skill in computer science is a difficult problem to solve, but getting Claude to crank out bloated assessment briefs is not the solution. Whereas before, assignments were designed by a person who thought them through at least once, then approved by other people in the department, now I doubt they're getting read more than once (if that). Errors abound, often with corrections coming a week or two before the deadline. The amount of work involved has also tripled - LLMs don't know how much effort it takes for a student to learn new material then complete technical tasks, and professors are too far along in their careers to notice this when skim reading an AI generated brief. So those of us with less technical experience are forced to speed run content, which SUCKS! I am here to learn, god damn it, not barely scratch the surface of the 15 deliverables I have for a 3,000 word assignment. Tutors are overloaded (even more than usual) You know what university financiers love to hear? SCALE! Learning at scale, preferable automated, so they can milk the cash cow as much as possible without paying for extra staff. There has always been tension between educational and commercial interests in every institution, but the AI hype has forced through a level of workload that is unethical and unsustainable for tutors and lecturers. I only hear from my tutor these days when I haven't accessed the online portal in a while, because their data dashboard flagged me as 'at risk' T_T Doomers left, right and centre I don't care if computer science and maths are over! I still want to learn about them! OK, I do care about my future career, but it still doesn't mean I want to forget everything I learned or stop progressing on this journey. There are so many interesting avenues to explore (some AI, some not), but I can't move for headlines about how software engineering is over/not using AI makes you obsolete/blah blah blah. Can't a girl learn statistics for fun? I could go on, but I won't. It'll give me indigestion. Maybe I'll go back to OpenProcessing for a bit and make some more silly games now I actually know how to do a bit of programming. Give em a go! Click in the browser frame to activate keyboard controls. [Simple space shooter with awesome music] https://openprocessing.org/@u304330/1557487 [Moogle meow. It meows, that is all] https://openprocessing.org/@u304330/2205896 [Make a sound to scare the fish away] https://openprocessing.org/@u304330/1651274 #tech #uni

title: Octomind – open-source AI harness that saves your tokens, static rust
abstract:
Open-source coding agent harness. One Rust binary, any model, every surface. Interactive, stdin, daemon, WebSocket, or ACP — one engine, one config. A supervising model plans and checks the work. Policy lives in TOML guardrails, not approval prompts. Website · Docs · Tap Registry · Benchmarks · Issues Octomind is an open-source coding agent harness. It gives an LLM real access to your repo — reading and writing files, running shells, searching code, delegating to sub-agents — through MCP tools. The same harness runs interactively , non-interactively through stdin , as a background daemon , over WebSocket , or as an ACP agent inside your editor or another agent's stack. # Interactive octomind run developer:general # Piped — CI, scripts, automation echo " Explain the auth module " | octomind run developer:general --format plain # Daemon — keep it alive, talk to it from another terminal echo " watch the build " | octomind run --name watcher --daemon --format jsonl
octomind send --name watcher " run the test suite " Why Octomind? Most coding agents assume a human is watching the screen. Octomind is built for the work that keeps going after you leave. Policy as code, not approval popups. Deterministic guardrails — pre-call guards, post-result hooks, post-turn validators — live in TOML and scripts, so they work in CI, daemons, and scheduled runs. Proven on real PRs. It solved 24 of 25 held-out tasks at lower cost than the closest competitor. See the benchmarks . Ready-made specialists. octomind run developer:general pulls a packaged agent (prompt, model, MCP servers, tool permissions) from a tap . Publish your own with one repo. Sessions that stay sharp. Adaptive compression keeps long tasks moving while retaining task knowledge and the live exchange. Remembers your rules. Rules and corrections you state in a session become lessons, grounded in your own words and scoped to the project and role, that come back in later sessions. See learning . Any model, any budget. Use Octomind Cloud or your own key (OpenRouter, Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepSeek, Ollama, and more), pick a model per role, and cap spend per request and per session. Over budget, a terminal session asks y/N; a non-interactive run stops with exit code 75. One config. Models, tools, roles, guardrails, budgets: all TOML, no framework code. Quick Start 1. Install (macOS, Linux): curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/muvon/octomind/master/install.sh | bash On Windows, in PowerShell: irm https: // raw.githubusercontent.com / muvon / octomind / master / install.ps1 | iex On macOS, you can also install with Homebrew: brew install muvon/tap/octomind 2. Get model access. The fastest path is Octomind Cloud, which includes models and needs no configuration: octomind login Prefer your own provider key? Skip login and export one (also OPENAI_API_KEY , ANTHROPIC_API_KEY , DEEPSEEK_API_KEY ), then follow Model access to point the config at it: export OPENROUTER_API_KEY= " your_key " 3. Run a specialist in your project: cd ~ /your/project
octomind run developer:general You're now in a session with an agent that can read your code, run commands, and edit files. The interface is a plain line prompt with markdown rendering — no TUI to learn, so it works over SSH, in tmux , and in CI logs. The first time you run a specialist, it may install its tools and ask for credentials. developer:general comes from the default tap muvon/tap , not your local config. Plain octomind run starts the config's default role, assistant:concierge . Try the recorded bug-fix demo : two failing tests, an agent fix, and an independent test rerun. Benchmarks Measured on octobench against 25 tasks harvested from merged pull requests across Python, PHP, Rust, C++, and JavaScript. Each agent works in the pre-fix repo; held-out tests from the merged fix decide pass or fail. These are the published July 30, 2026 results, not a measurement of this checkout. solved judge Σ / 2500 cost wall time octomind + glm-5.2 24/25 2264 $63.43 3.6h claude code + claude-opus-5 23/25 2262 $81.79 6.7h codex + gpt-5.6-sol 21/25 2127 $14.86 1.0h opencode + glm-5.2 19/25 2093 $129.54 3.3h The harness matters. opencode used the same model and endpoint; octomind solved 24 vs 19 at roughly half the cost. All four agents ran stock invocations with no tuning, so this measures the whole harness, not individual features. Worst-case pricing, still ahead. glm-5.2 ran without prompt caching while Opus billed ~97% of context re-reads at cache rates — and octomind still led on solves, cost, and wall time. Reproducible. Per-case table, artifacts, and reproduction guide: BENCHMARK.md . Background: blog post . Guardrails: Policy as Code Drop a .agents/guardrails.toml in your repo. Octomind enforces it deterministically, with no code to compile and no plugin to install. # Pre-call deny — block a class of calls before they execute [[ guard ]] match = " shell(command=^rm \\ s+-rf?) " message = " rm -rf blocked. " # Conditional rule — only fires after the agent ran git status this session [[ guard ]] match = " shell(command=git push) " when = [ " +shell(command=git status) " ] message = " Review changes before pushing. " Layer When it runs What it does Guards Before a tool call Deny by capability, argument regex, and session history. A match returns a denial instead of executing the call. Hooks After a tool result A non-zero exit injects stdout into the agent's inbox — lint and format failures become automatic corrections without restarting the turn. Validators After a turn Scripts the agent reads on its next turn. This replaces "approve this change?" prompts in autonomous loops. If you know Claude Code hooks: guards are PreToolUse denies declared in TOML, hooks are PostToolUse , validators are Stop — no scripts required for the common cases. Hook and validator script examples: Guardrails guide . One Harness, Five Surfaces The same harness, exposed wherever your workflow needs it. Surface Use it for Docs Interactive CLI Daily work, any domain Sessions Non-interactive ( --format plain / jsonl ) CI, scripts, scheduled jobs CLI reference Daemon + send Background agents, continuous monitoring Daemon & hooks WebSocket ( octomind server ) IDE plugins, dashboards, integrations WebSocket server ACP ( octomind acp ) Agent inside Zed, JetBrains, VS Code, Neovim, or any ACP editor ACP protocol Need machine-readable results? Pass --schema schema.json to constrain the final response to a JSON Schema (requires a model with structured-output support). See Structured output . Features Feature What you get Learn more Specialists & taps Packaged agents with model, prompt, MCP servers, and permissions; installs their tool dependencies on first use Tap system Roles Per-role model, temperature, system prompt, tools Roles Workflows Multi-step pipelines, each step with its own model and toolset Workflows MCP client stdio and Streamable HTTP servers, with OAuth; enable/disable servers mid-session MCP tools Agent Skills Standard SKILL.md skills from .agents/skills/ , ~/.config/agents/skills/ , and taps; they activate on demand, so your context stays small Skills Local project tools Executable scripts in .agents/tools/ auto-register as tools Local tools Plugins & AGENTS.md Agent Plugins ( plugin.json + skills + mcp.json ) from taps, .agents/plugins/ , or ~/.config/agents/plugins/ ; project AGENTS.

title: LLMs are not superhuman at reading and writing neural network weights
abstract:
A recent paper argues that frontier LLMs can work with neural network weights directly. This seems superhuman, but it isn’t. The paper shows that GPT-6 Astra can take a small neural network and interact with its weights directly, “well past what we’d expect from humans or conventional algorithms”. Specifically, Astra was able to identify what games a small network 1 was trained to play just by looking at the weights, and even tweak the weights itself. The most impressive result is Astra significantly improving a 0.8B Qwen LLM’s ability on mathematics by natively editing its weights. The reason to be excited here is that “superhuman ability to improve language models” is precisely the kind of thing that could cause recursive self-improvement. I think a smart human ML researcher could perform all of these tasks . Figuring out what game a model was trained to play based on the network sounds impressive until you consider three points: The input channels of the model directly listen to each 8x8 grid cell The input channels are labeled (e.g. “agent”, “moving objects”) It’s thus relatively trivial to calculate 2 which parts of the grid the first layer of weights cares about and why Here’s that calculation expressed as a heatmap in three lines of Python: d = np.load("a9f535cc.npz")
W1 = d["actor/dense1/kernel"]
norms = np.linalg.norm(W1.reshape(10,10,5,32).transpose(2,0,1,3), axis=-1) # 5 x 10 x 10 And here’s the heatmap for each game: If someone showed you that heatmap without the game labels, I think you’d be able to immediately identify at least the first three games purely by noticing where the player is (e.g. for Breakout, in a horizontal line at the bottom) and where the moving objects are (e.g. for Pac-Man, in the distinctive Pac-Man maze). It’s neat 3 that Astra was able to calculate the norms in its head without executing Python, but not that impressive, and certainly not something that should shock anyone who’s been paying attention. I’m not going to go through each example 4 in the paper, so let’s skip straight to the most impressive one: fixing a 0.8B Qwen model’s ability to do mathematics. 0.8B is a lot of parameters, and “mathematics” is way more complicated than “guess what the game is based on how the player moves”, and editing weights is arguably harder than parsing them. What happened here? First, note that the Qwen model was not “bad at mathematics” in a pure capabilities sense. It had a specific problem where after 32k tokens it would get stuck in loops, so any mathematical task that needed more than 32k tokens would automatically fail 5 . If you had a model that looped like this, how would you update the weights to fix it? Personally, I would try steering : I would write some reasoning texts that looped and some reasoning texts that didn’t, calculate the difference between the looping and non-looping residuals, measure how much each weight contributed to that difference, then try manually trimming those top weights. This is basically the Heretic abliteration playbook. And this is exactly what Astra did! It wrote four pairs of texts, measured 6 the weights that contributed to looping, started cutting them down and testing if it worked, and ended up finding a patch that stopped the Qwen model from looping, thus making it able to work on mathematical problems for more than 32k tokens. Again, this is exactly what a competent human researcher could have and would have done. It’s cool that Astra was able to make direct weight updates. But we shouldn’t think of this like a radically new capability that will change how AI research is done. We should think of this as analogous to the ability of LLMs to emit machine code and tweak compiled binaries: it’s an impressive trick, but the best way to work with binaries is still to write source code and compile it. Likewise, the best way to update the weights of a model is to train it normally. To the extent that intelligent LLMs help with AI research, they will help by improving training , not by magically tweaking model weights directly. edit: this post got some comments on Hacker News. One commenter disagrees that the heatmaps are obvious, though I think this reflects unfamiliarity with what toy RL game maps look like and what games are likely to be implemented in toy RL projects. Another commenter complains that I’m not impressed enough. To be clear, I am very impressed! It just doesn’t update me much beyond “these models can solve Navier-Stokes and find better bounds on the Riemann Conjecture”. Around 17k weights. ↩ By taking the L2 norm of each input across the 32 weights in the first layer. ↩ Note that this is superhuman mental mathematics, not superhuman AI research. ↩ The most impressive one I’m skipping is hand-writing a neural network from scratch. While cool, if you can express a task as a simple program, we already know it’s possible to express that program as a NN , even by unaugmented humans . ↩ All the <32k token problems were solved successfully on the original Qwen model. ↩ Unlike with the toy game networks, it had access to Python. ↩

title: Launch HN: Momentic (YC W24) – Agents that catch bugs by using your app
abstract: Hey HN, we’re Wei-Wei and Jeff. We’re building Momentic, QA agents that autonomously plan, explore, and bug-bash controls and user flows in your web, iOS, Android, and (soon) desktop apps to catch bugs. Here’s a demo:  https://youtu.be/BFsM-Se1Fh8  We’re both software engineers that spent our careers on dev tooling and infra across companies like Robinhood, Retool, WeWork, and Qualtrics. Testing was always a pain in the ass (esp Playwright and Selenium), so we built agents to do it for us. Modern day software has a ton of bugs and the change failure rate is only growing faster as coding agent adoption scales. LLMs are really good at generating code, but reinforce their own assumptions, write a ton of useless tests, and are bad at visual understanding. On DeepSWE v1.1, Sonnet 5.5 hit 66.2% pass rate when banned from writing tests, versus 65.3% when allowed. OSS end-to-end testing frameworks like Playwright, Selenium, or Maestro force you to hardcode implementation details like XPath, text, or aria-* attributes in your tests. Even with agents, these take a nontrivial amount of time and tokens to build and maintain. In 2023, we saw Nat Friedman drive a browser with GPT-3 via natbot. We were inspired to use this technology to automate the most painful and tedious parts of software engineering: testing. We started with using LLMs to generate and maintain Playwright, but quickly realized that those primitives were fundamentally misaligned with the agentic SDLC. We think the future of QA is agents testing themselves, not writing scripts. Mo is a custom agent harness for catching bugs that builds on the past 3 years of Momentic and millions of test traces from complex, real-world applications. Mo is built for recall: it finds the most real bugs, though Codex is a bit more precise at 86% vs 84%. The tradeoff is cost: Mo costs $2.67 per bug vs $0.80 for Codex, less than Claude Code and Devin. - Self-organizing agent graph. Mo builds a directed acyclic graph (DAG) as it explores. Large product areas automatically fork into parallel sub-agents, each with their own browser or device for concurrent execution. - Specialized agents for domain specific tasks. Planner agents reason over screenshots and video while dedicated locator agents inspect page structure to resolve plain-English interaction targets. Others include image analysis, video understanding, audio generation, and more. - Parallel agents coordinate through cooperative resource leases. Agents can announce that they’re “using” or “modifying” overlapping resources or fixtures. Multiple “using” claims can coexist, but only a single “modifying” claim can be active on any particular one. - Scaled infrastructure. Mo ships with a tunnel that lets users expose private sites and local apps to our hosted agents and infra. A single bug bash can spin up 100s of concurrent browsers and devices. We benchmarked Mo against coding agents on 4 popular open-source apps: Gitea (58.8k stars), Metabase, Twenty (YC), and Saleor, with 1,396 human-labeled bugs. Each agent got the same brief, a fresh E2B sandbox, and no access to source code. Codex and Claude Code used hosted Browserbase browsers, while Devin used its built-in browser. For evaluators, we implemented LLM as a judge (GPT-6.1 Sol) with a human reviewer. Results from a time-boxed 60-minute run: - Mo: 269 bugs, 19.3% recall, 84% precision, $2.67 per bug - Codex (GPT-6.1 Sol + Playwright MCP): 86 bugs, 6.2% recall, 86% precision, $0.80 per bug - Claude Code (Opus 5.5 + Playwright MCP): 59 bugs, 4.2% recall, 80% precision, $4.09 per bug - Devin: 27 bugs, 1.9% recall, 84% precision, $3.89 per bug Mo finds more bugs the more time it has. From 30 to 60 minutes, it went from 177 to 269 bugs (+52%), while Codex gained only 16%. Results:  https://momentic.ai/qa-bench  Write-up:  https://momentic.ai/blog/qa-bench  Dataset:  https://huggingface.co/datasets/momentic/qa-bench  Harness:  https://github.com/momentic-ai/qa-bench  We just shipped PR testing for Vercel and Cloudflare deploy previews and we’re giving every new signup $250 in Mo spend. Paid plans have higher infra capacity and included usage along with options to top up. We’d love for you to try it out and give us feedback. Feel free to comment here, we’ll be around all day!

title: Ubuntu still has not released patch for Linux 0day RCE in almost 3 weeks
abstract:
Ubuntu has not shipped fixed kernels for CVE-2026-98432 , a critical vulnerability scored CVSS 9.8, leaving the 22.04, 24.04, and 26.04 LTS releases without a vendor update. Operators running those releases therefore have no official kernel package that closes the hole. The gap matters most for internet-facing and multi-tenant self-hosted systems that rely on Ubuntu’s LTS kernels for isolation and privilege boundaries; until packages appear, those hosts remain exposed to whatever remote or local attack the CVE enables. Ubuntu has not announced an ETA for the fixes. In the interim, affected administrators are left to decide whether to stay on the stock kernel, apply out-of-tree mitigations if any exist, or move workloads onto releases or kernels that already carry the patch.

title: Show HN: Subvocal – Talk to your computer without making noise
abstract: Hi HN, we're Aarush and Arnav from The Subvocal Company (YC F26) ( https://subvocal.company/ ). We’re building smart glasses that let you talk to your computer without talking out loud. You can mouth words silently and discreetly and the glasses decode them to text at the speed of speech. Here's a video of Dave from YC trying it out:  https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9QdX1eObVYI  (Edit: you don't actually have to move your lips or even open your mouth for this to work! Since the RF can see inside your mouth the system can be fine tuned on "internal speech". This isn't the automatic tongue movements that occur when "thinking" words to yourself, but more like mouthing with your lips closed. It's a bit weird to do, but with practice, we have been able to get it down pretty well.) Arnav and I were studying CS at Georgia Tech at the beginning of the year, with no experience in silent speech or sensing. We were both AI-native builders and power users of Wispr Flow. What bugged us was not being able to use these tools in the library (or an office) or in public. At Stanford’s TreeHacks in February, we decided to build the most technically ridiculous thing we could think of. We’d read about AlterEgo, a silent speech system out of MIT’s Media Lab, and wanted to recreate it in 36 hours. We built a crude prototype, sticking EMG electrodes onto my face:  https://drive.google.com/file/d/1mwhv5HZMz3UTevdrgwS5O7g2jWV...  We got it to kind of work at a letter level in a very janky way. It wasn’t good enough to win the hackathon, but convinced us to go all in. The first time I typed a sentence without anyone noticing, I felt the magic of the technology. We quickly realized EMG (reading muscle electrical signals) wouldn’t work: - Signal changes due to sweat - Electrical interference - Placement variability - Most importantly, no one wants to stick electrodes onto their face!! So we switched to RF and built the glasses you see now. They emit radio waves, similar to Bluetooth, that pass through your face. As they cross the tongue, lips and soft palate, they’re modulated by silent mouthing. We train foundation models on this data to decode these perturbations to text. Despite prior academic research, getting this to work was a huge engineering challenge. First we built an extremely low noise RF sensing stack. Then we had to place antennas so their fields overlapped maximally with the articulators. Our first attempt on glasses failed completely, so we reverted to old habits and taped antennas on our face:  https://drive.google.com/file/d/1ks0dS0eZiTV9EqSFsyB_w5BBjpc...  Since taping antennas consistently in the same spot and angle was hard, we created this weird but effective head rig to hold them in place:  https://drive.google.com/file/d/1rhzNFpdDzr7oHk0isFY70dkoV4C...  This worked, but obviously wasn’t a product yet. So we worked deep in simulations to design glasses that could hold the antennas. That evolved into our design now, with antennas embedded within the frames. Once we established there was a signal, the next hurdle was cross-user generalization. Everyone’s facial anatomy, and hence RF signal patterns, are vastly different. We tried algorithmic workarounds but realized the only lever was to massively scale pretraining data. So that’s what we did. We set up booths in our office and paid people to read prompts wearing our glasses, to pretrain our models on. This produced a beautiful scaling curve, with errors falling quickly as we scaled our dataset and cross-user performance becoming genuinely compelling (as you see in the video above; Dave only had a short 20-sentence calibration). We always heard about building things from first principles but never understood it before this. We tried tackling it top down but completely failed. Only when we broke each component (the antenna, electronics, ML) down to its fundamentals to understand and optimize it did we get it to work really well. Over the next few months we’re continuing R&D to turn our prototype glasses into the slick product on our website and ship in Q1 2027. We’re also scaling up our dataset to improve performance on edge cases. For anyone who loves voice dictation but hates using it around people, we’ve opened preorders for our first batch of 500 units, with a $200 discount off the final price. Allocation is running out quickly, so get yours at  https://subvocal.co/preorder !

title: Show HN: Warsaw in voxels – An interactive 3D map of the city centre
abstract:
Explore central Warsaw in voxels - slightly inspired by Minecraft, and MagicaVoxel. 
You can change the date, time of day and weather, explore the city, or click on a pedestrian to control them (here a bit of inspiration from Dungeon Keeper). Works best on desktop, but I tried to make it usable on mobile too. The initial load can take a while. It's based on several open datasets, including: - OpenStreetMap ( https://www.openstreetmap.org/#map=6/52.02/19.14 ) - buildings, streets, sidewalks, tram tracks, etc - GUGiK / Geoportal ( https://www.geoportal.gov.pl/ ) - LiDAR for building heights and trees, aerial imagery for colours - Warsaw's city tree database ( https://mapa.um.warszawa.pl/ ) - individual tree species, used for seasonal foliage Open-source ( https://github.com/stared/warsaw-vibe-voxel ), so feel invited to (re)use it as you wish!

title: Tell HN: Please Vote
abstract: The strongest sign of a healthy democracy is that people participate in it.  It's up to you to decide who to vote for, but no matter who you support, please show up and cast a ballot.  A democracy with 75% voter turnout is healthier than a democracy with 50% voter turnout even exactly the same politicians got elected, because citizens participating in a democratic process signals that they value the process and want to keep it. (Obviously, this only applies to people eligible to vote in ongoing elections.  If you're not eligible to vote, please don't vote.)

title: Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen
abstract:
We find that frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at natively reading and writing neural network weights , using a variety of recent tools and algorithms or even via direct weight editing. These results show sparks of Weight-Space Programming, which may extend beyond what we’d expect from humans or conventional algorithms. This might be a big deal for both optimization and interpretability. Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do . And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps. Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights . With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x. All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming . Throughout the history of deep learning, we encoded our simplistic inductive biases into tiny symbolic optimizers like Adam or Muon. This is changing: our neural network weights will soon be natively optimized by LLMs that deliberately reason about their weights . If you were asked to handcraft a neural network that plays Go, what would you do? If you were handed raw neural network weights and asked to predict their behavior, where would you even start? For almost any human, this is practically impossible. Today, weights are written by optimization , by custom networks trained to write them , or by compilers from formal programs . In this post, we find that the current generation of frontier LLMs, used natively in natural language, are starting to become eerily good at understanding and crafting neural network weights around natural-language goals. For a few years now, we’ve all been using LLMs to optimize text artifacts like prompts and the programs built around them . More recently, we’ve started using them to optimize whole harnesses and the training code and hyperparameters that train ML models . We often justified these methods by reference to the fact that we don’t know other principled ways to hill-climb on text artifacts, unlike for updating the weights of differentiable neural networks . After all, humans can “optimize” code by hand, for example, so it made sense to ask LLMs to do it, but they can’t “optimize” neural weights by hand, so those remained largely in the realm of symbolic algorithms. In this post, we share very early results that allow us to argue that the paradigm of reasoning-driven optimization is now coming even for differentiable neural networks . In Weight-Space Programming , a general-purpose LLM reads and writes a network’s weights directly (i.e., not through an optimizer, and in particular not with gradient descent) around some natural language spec, sometimes even with no environment feedback at all. In natural language, it’s becoming possible to “just ask” an LLM to natively find a hidden trait or failure inside the weights of a neural network, to fix that failure, or to write a new network from scratch . We report early, exciting results on each of these below, first on small networks and then even on real language models: We start with a small-scale experiment to see if LLMs can understand the continuous weight space, which is essentially just a list of numbers. In our first experiments, we train some neural network with some algorithm. It would be extremely exciting if the LLM is able to tell its behavior just from the weights. We trained neural network policies with PPO to play four computer games. All four networks take the same input channels, choose from the same actions, and have exactly the same network dimensions, so that it is not able to tell unless the weights are read. For each of these networks, we pass its raw weights into Astra as a prompt, and ask: Which game was this neural network trained on? Without revealing the options of the games we consider, Astra was still able to name the right game for all four networks. This is exciting particularly because there are so many games out there that Astra could choose from. It seems that Astra was able to work out what game each network was built to play, just from features of its weights. For example, where each input channel’s first-layer weights concentrate (e.g., for Breakout, the agent’s weights lie along the bottom row, a paddle), and which actions the output layer tells apart. Next, we wanted to see if this generalizes to other tasks and models. We train diffusion models (DDPM) to generate circle, triangle, and square images independently. We then ask Astra if it could tell what the DDPMs are trained to generate, just from the weights alone. We do not allow tool use or forward passes. Astra was able to tell what each model generates, from the weights alone. It finds the shape in the output layer, where each hidden unit’s weights draw one piece of the shape’s edge, and it draws just those edges. Interestingly, it draws every shape as an outline, ignoring that the actual models generate filled shapes. This mistake kind of shows it does not rely on calculating the forward pass, but rather it actually reads the structure/geometry of the weights. Now, in the first two experiments above, Astra was not really looking at the full network and could get away with only reading the first or the last layers. This is not a scalable strategy for larger (particularly language) models and problems we really care about, as how they process and think through their input often happens in the intermediate layers. So next, we take the first and last layers away and leave Astra with only the middle layers. We train three small language models (7.2M parameters) to predict the next character, one each on Python code The Python code dataset, as a list of its files with a script that rebuilds it: GitHub . , Japanese in alphabet (romaji) , and English . We then remove the input and output layers and give Astra only the four transformer blocks in between. Without these two layers, nothing in the weights says which character is which, and the model cannot be run on any text. Astra may analyze the weights with Python, but it may not run the network or any of its layers on any input. We ask: which language was this network trained on, and what each of its 24 attention heads does . Astra names the right language for all three networks, in both of its attempts. It also finds every copying head (induction head), the heads that let a model repeat text it has seen earlier, and names no other head as one. The reasoning went like this. To tell Python apart, Astra looked for copying heads, which let a model repeat earlier text, such as completing tot to tot al when tot al came before. Without running anything, it found a first-layer head that looks one character back and then, by multiplying weight matrices, the later heads that search using what that head brings along ( Figure 1 ). We find that this is actually a method presented by Elhage et al. , which we never mentioned to Astra. Code repeats names far more than prose, so many copying heads pointed to Python. Romaji stood out instead because the last of the four blocks it was given (not the output layer, which was removed) writes in fewer distinct directions, as if the model had fewer letters to tell apart. Indeed, romaji never uses some letters like q, l, v and x. So far, Astra has only read weights. Now, we ask if Astra knows how to write the weights. We train a PPO network to operate a car such that it can scale a ramp in a Kinetix environment .
